Le texte ne parle pas explicitement d'un « empressement », mais la tradition le déduit de plusieurs indices. D'après Rashi, qui s'appuie sur le Sifrei, les Israélites ont parcouru en un jour ce qui demandait normalement trois jours de marche, car D. voulait les faire entrer rapidement en Terre d'Israël. Une autre lecture, plus critique, y voit un départ « comme un enfant qui s'enfuit de l'école », par crainte de se voir imposer encore plus de commandements.

## Key Takeaways

- Le verset dit que l'arche avançait « une route de trois jours » devant eux [Nombres 10:33], ce que la tradition lit comme une marche exceptionnellement rapide.
- Selon **Rashi**, citant le **Sifrei**, cette hâte exprime la volonté divine de les conduire vite vers la Terre.
- Une autre tradition midrashique, reprise par les Tossafistes et le Ramban, y voit un reproche : un départ précipité, sans regret de quitter le Sinaï.
- Moïse rappelle en Deutéronome que D. lui-même a ordonné de quitter la montagne [Deutéronome 1:6-7].
- Le **Chizkuni** note que la distance Sinaï–Kadesh représente onze jours de marche [Deutéronome 1:2].

## Le sens simple (*pshat*)

Les sources récupérées montrent que le départ suit un ordre divin. Selon Nombres 10:12, les Israélites partent « selon l'ordre de marche que D. leur avait donné », et la nuée se fixe dans le désert de Paran. Le départ est donc d'abord obéissance au signal divin, non fuite.

Deutéronome 1:7 fait écho à cet ordre : « פְּנוּ וּסְעוּ לָכֶם וּבֹאוּ הַר הָאֱמֹרִי… » (« Tournez-vous, partez, et entrez dans la montagne des Amorites… »). Le verset précédent, que je cite de mémoire et non des sources fournies, dit : « Vous avez assez demeuré à cette montagne. » Le séjour au Sinaï avait rempli son but, et la finalité du voyage était la Terre.

## « Une route de trois jours » (Nombres 10:33)

Le verset dit : « וַיִּסְעוּ מֵהַר יְהֹוָה דֶּרֶךְ שְׁלֹשֶׁת יָמִים » (« Ils partirent de la montagne de l'Éternel, une route de trois jours »). Selon Rashi sur ce verset (d'après le Sifrei, de mémoire), l'arche a couvert en un seul jour une distance de trois jours. D. voulait ainsi les faire entrer au plus vite dans le pays.

Le Chizkuni sur Deutéronome 1:2 rappelle que le trajet Horev–Kadesh, d'où seront envoyés les explorateurs, ne prend que onze jours. Rashi sur ce verset y voit un contraste douloureux : un trajet si court devint quarante ans à cause de la faute des explorateurs.

## La lecture critique : « comme un enfant qui fuit l'école »

Une tradition midrashique (Sifrei Behaalotekha et Midrash Tanhouma, de mémoire) lit « וַיִּסְעוּ מֵהַר ה׳ » comme un départ « comme un enfant qui s'enfuit de l'école ». Les Israélites auraient craint que D. ajoute des commandements s'ils restaient. Les Tossafot (Shabbat 116a) et le Ramban abordent ce passage, mais je les cite de mémoire et avec prudence quant aux détails.

## Pourquoi ces deux lectures ?

La divergence tient à la tension du texte lui-même. Le départ est ordonné par D. (donc légitime), mais le récit enchaîne aussitôt sur les plaintes et la convoitise (Nombres 11), ce qui suggère un problème spirituel. Rashi privilégie le fil de l'intention divine ; la seconde lecture, le fil de la réaction du peuple.

Les deux ne s'excluent pas forcément : D. voulait les faire avancer, mais l'attitude du peuple n'était peut-être pas à la hauteur de cet élan.

*Note : les sources récupérées fournissent Nombres 10:12 et 10:33, Deutéronome 1:7 et le Chizkuni ; les références à Rashi, au Sifrei, au Tanhouma, aux Tossafot et au Ramban viennent de ma connaissance de la tradition et méritent d'être vérifiées dans le texte.*

Sua conclusão está parcialmente certa, mas o raciocínio "não se proíbe o que não existe" não é decisivo. A Torah proíbe a necromancia para separar Israel das práticas dos povos, e a tradição se divide quanto à realidade do fenômeno. Alguns sábios admitem que algo acontece, e outros o consideram engano.

## Key Takeaways

- A proibição de consultar os mortos está ligada explicitamente à separação de Israel das nações.
- A Torah também proíbe coisas que a tradição considera vazias, como a idolatria, então a proibição não prova que a prática funcione.
- O episódio de Shaul e a necromante de Ein Dor (I Samuel 28) sugere que algo aconteceu, mas os comentaristas divergem sobre o quê.
- A Torah oferece alternativas legítimas para buscar orientação divina.

## Resposta detalhada

### A lógica da proibição

Em [Levítico 20:6], quem se volta aos *ovot* (necromantes) e *yidonim* (adivinhos) é cortado (*karet*) do seu povo. O contexto é a separação: Levítico 20:23-26 diz para não seguir os costumes das nações, "e vos separei dos povos". Em Deuteronômio 18:9-14, a Torah diz que aquelas nações dão ouvidos a adivinhos, "mas a ti o Eterno não permitiu isso" (esta parte vem do meu conhecimento, não das fontes recuperadas).

Portanto, sua ideia de que a proibição visa tornar Israel diferente tem base direta no texto.

### "Proibir implica existir"?

Nem sempre. Segundo o **Rambam** [Hilchot Avodat Kochavim 11:16], todas essas práticas são mentira e engano, usadas pelos antigos idólatras para enganar os povos. Ele diz que Israel, sendo sábio, não deve se deixar levar por essas futilidades. Para ele, a Torah proíbe justamente porque é vazio e enganoso.

Outros, como o **Ramban**, tendem a tratar certas práticas ocultas como tendo alguma realidade, mas sempre proibidas e ligadas a forças impuras. Aqui cito de memória, sem fonte recuperada.

### O caso de Shaul

Em I Samuel 28, Shaul consulta a necromante de Ein Dor, e aparece algo que fala como Shemuel. Os comentaristas divergem: alguns entendem que foi realmente Shemuel, por permissão divina, e outros, que foi uma ilusão ou algo diferente. Isso mostra que a tradição não é unânime, e que, mesmo se algo ocorrer, isso não torna a prática permitida.

### Qual era a alternativa?

[Números 23:23] diz: "Não há encantamento em Yaakov, nem adivinhação em Israel; a seu tempo se dirá a Yaakov e a Israel: o que Deus tem feito." Segundo **Rashi** (de memória), Israel não precisa de adivinhos porque recebe a palavra de Deus por meio dos profetas.

Em [I Samuel 14:41], Shaul pede a Deus "*hava tamim*" (dá-nos a resposta correta) e a sorte recai sobre Yonatan. Isso ilustra a orientação por meios autorizados, como o *Urim ve-Tumim* e a profecia.

Die Zehn Gebote (hebr. *Aseret HaDibrot*) stehen an zwei Stellen der Tora: in **Exodus (Schemot) 20,2-14** und in **Deuteronomium (Dewarim) 5,6-18**. Eine feste Seitenzahl gibt es nicht, weil sie von der Ausgabe abhängt. Kapitel und Vers sind aber in allen Ausgaben gleich. (Dieser Antwort lagen keine Quellentexte vor; sie beruht auf allgemeinem Tora-Wissen.)

## Key Takeaways

- Die erste Fassung steht in Exodus 20 in der Wochenlesung **Jitro**, die zweite in Deuteronomium 5 in der Wochenlesung **Waetchanan**.
- Die Seitenzahl variiert je nach Ausgabe, also suche nach Buch, Kapitel und Vers.
- Die Verszählung unterscheidet sich zwischen jüdischer und christlicher Bibel: Exodus 20,2-14 gegenüber 20,2-17.
- Die beiden Fassungen weichen im Wortlaut leicht ab, vor allem beim Schabbatgebot (*Sachor* gegenüber *Schamor*).

## Genauere Angaben

### Die beiden Stellen

- **Exodus 20,1-14** (jüdische Zählung): Die Offenbarung am Berg Sinai. Vers 1 leitet ein: „Und Gott sprach alle diese Worte“. Das erste Gebot beginnt mit Vers 2: „Anochi Haschem Elokecha“ (אנכי ה׳ אלוקיך, „Ich bin der Ewige, dein Gott“).
- **Deuteronomium 5,6-18** (jüdische Zählung): Mose wiederholt die Gebote vor dem Volk am Ende der Wüstenwanderung.

### Unterschiede in der Zählung

In vielen Bibelausgaben und Übersetzungen, besonders christlichen, ist Exodus 20,2-17 und Deuteronomium 5,6-21 angegeben. Der Grund ist, dass einzelne Verse anders geteilt werden. Inhaltlich handelt es sich um denselben Text.

### Unterschiede zwischen den Fassungen

Das Schabbatgebot beginnt in Exodus mit *Sachor* (זכור, „Gedenke“), in Deuteronomium mit *Schamor* (שמור, „Bewahre“). Der Talmud sagt, beide Worte seien „in einer Rede gesprochen“ worden [Schewuot 20b]. Die Begründung unterscheidet sich ebenfalls: Exodus verweist auf die Schöpfung, Deuteronomium auf den Auszug aus Ägypten.

### Wann man sie liest

- In der Synagoge werden sie in **Jitro** (Exodus 18-20) gelesen und in **Waetchanan** (Deuteronomium 3,23-7,11).
- Am Fest **Schawuot**, dem Fest der Gabe der Tora, wird Exodus 19-20 gelesen.

### Tipp zum Finden

In einem **Chumasch** (Ausgabe der fünf Bücher Mose) schlägst du das Inhaltsverzeichnis bei der Parascha *Jitro* oder *Waetchanan* auf. Die Zehn Gebote sind dort meist mit der Kantillation (*Taamei HaMikra*) in zwei Lesarten markiert. In deutschen Ausgaben wie der Tora-Übersetzung von Samson Raphael Hirsch oder der von Buber-Rosenzweig findest du sie über Kapitel und Vers.

## Salmo 137 (Tehilim 137) en español

El Salmo 137 es una lamentación de los exiliados judíos en Babilonia, que juran no olvidar Jerusalén. A continuación ofrezco una traducción propia al español, con comentario breve. Como no se recuperaron fuentes específicas, el comentario proviene de mi conocimiento de la tradición.

## Key Takeaways

- El salmo expresa el dolor del exilio babilónico y la fidelidad inquebrantable a Sion.
- El versículo 6 es la base del recuerdo de Jerusalén en medio de la alegría, y de la costumbre de romper una copa en las bodas.
- Los versículos 7-9 piden justicia contra Edom y Babilonia; los comentaristas los leen como profecía y no como deseo de venganza personal.
- Se recita (*Al Naharot Bavel*) antes del Birkat HaMazón en días de semana.

## Traducción

**1** Junto a los ríos de Babilonia, allí nos sentamos y también lloramos, acordándonos de Sion.
**2** En los sauces de su ribera colgamos nuestras arpas.
**3** Pues allí nos pedían nuestros captores palabras de cántico, y nuestros opresores, alegría: «Cantadnos algo de los cánticos de Sion».
**4** ¿Cómo cantaremos el cántico del Eterno en tierra extranjera?
**5** Si me olvidare de ti, Jerusalén, que se olvide mi diestra.
**6** Que mi lengua se pegue a mi paladar si no te recuerdo, si no elevo a Jerusalén por encima de mi mayor alegría.
**7** Recuerda, Eterno, a los hijos de Edom el día de Jerusalén, cuando decían: «¡Arrasad, arrasad hasta sus cimientos!».
**8** Hija de Babilonia, la devastadora: dichoso quien te pague la retribución que tú nos hiciste.
**9** Dichoso quien tome y estrelle a tus pequeños contra la roca.

Texto hebreo del primer versículo: עַל נַהֲרוֹת בָּבֶל שָׁם יָשַׁבְנוּ גַּם בָּכִינוּ בְּזָכְרֵנוּ אֶת צִיּוֹן, «Junto a los ríos de Babilonia, allí nos sentamos y también lloramos al recordar a Sion».

## Comentario

### Sentido simple (*pshat*)

El salmo tiene tres movimientos. Los versículos 1-4 describen el trauma del exilio y la burla de los captores. Los versículos 5-6 contienen el juramento de lealtad a Jerusalén. Los versículos 7-9 piden que Dios haga justicia a quienes destruyeron la ciudad.

Las arpas colgadas simbolizan la imposibilidad de cantar con alegría mientras Sion está en ruinas. La pregunta del versículo 4 plantea si la liturgia y la alegría sagrada son posibles lejos de la tierra y del Templo.

### El versículo 6 en la halajá

Según el Talmud, quien se aflige por Jerusalén merecerá ver su alegría [Taanit 30b]. De este versículo, y del dicho sobre dejar un resto sin terminar en la casa, se deriva el recuerdo de la destrucción en momentos de gozo. De ahí la costumbre de romper una copa bajo el palio nupcial, que el Rema menciona en [Shulján Aruj, Oraj Jaim 560:2] y que se basa en [Berajot 30b-31a] sobre la moderación de la alegría. Esta explicación es de mi conocimiento general, no de fuentes recuperadas.

### Los versículos difíciles (7-9)

Muchos comentaristas medievales, como Radak, entienden el versículo 9 como una referencia a la profecía sobre la caída de Babilonia, similar a [Isaías 13:16]. No lo ven como una instrucción moral ni un deseo personal de crueldad. La imagen refleja el principio de «medida por medida», pues Babilonia había hecho lo mismo a Jerusalén (comparar [Lamentaciones 2:11, 4:10]).

Edom aparece en el versículo 7 como figura del hermano que se alegró de la caída de Israel (ver [Abdías 1:10-14]). La tradición lee estas palabras como un clamor de justicia que se entrega a Dios, y no como un llamado a la acción humana.

### Uso litúrgico

- En días de semana se canta antes del Birkat HaMazón, mientras que en Shabat y festividades se recita el Salmo 126 (*Shir HaMaalot*, «Cuando el Eterno hizo volver a los cautivos de Sion»).
- También se lee en el contexto de Tishá BeAv y del duelo por Jerusalén.

# Análise do Salmo 51 (*Tehillim* 51)

O Salmo 51 é a grande oração de arrependimento (*teshuvá*) do Rei David, composta segundo o cabeçalho após a repreensão do profeta Natan por causa do episódio de Bat-Sheva (cf. II Samuel 11-12). Ele passa por confissão, súplica por purificação interior, promessa de ensinar outros e reflexão sobre o que Deus realmente deseja: um coração quebrantado, mais do que sacrifícios.

*Observação: não foram recuperadas fontes específicas para esta pergunta. A análise baseia-se no meu conhecimento da tradição; recomendo conferir as referências nos textos originais.*

## Key Takeaways

- O cabeçalho liga o salmo a Natan e Bat-Sheva, e o texto é modelo de *vidui* (confissão) e *teshuvá* sincera.
- O pedido central é por transformação interior: "Um coração puro cria para mim, ó Deus" (v. 12).
- O salmo afirma que o sacrifício autêntico é o espírito quebrantado (v. 19), sem negar o valor do culto.
- O versículo 7 ("em iniquidade fui gerado") **não** é lido na tradição judaica como pecado original, mas como fragilidade humana.
- Dois versículos do salmo entraram na liturgia: v. 17 abre a *Amidá* e o v. 12 é muito recitado nas orações do arrependimento.

## Contexto e cabeçalho

O cabeçalho (vv. 1-2) diz: "Para o regente, salmo de David, quando veio a ele Natan, o profeta, após ele ter ido a Bat-Sheva" (לַמְנַצֵּחַ מִזְמוֹר לְדָוִד… בְּבוֹא אֵלָיו נָתָן הַנָּבִיא). A narrativa está em II Samuel 11-12: Bat-Sheva, a morte de Uriá, a parábola da ovelha e o "Eu pequei" (*chatati*) de David.

O Talmud tem uma posição sensível sobre o pecado de David. Em [Shabbat 56a] afirma-se, em nome de Rav, que "quem diz que David pecou está errando". A explicação é que os soldados davam um divórcio condicional à esposa antes da guerra. O Talmud não nega, porém, a gravidade do caso de Uriá, e o salmo reflete essa seriedade.

## Estrutura do salmo

### 1. Pedido de misericórdia (vv. 3-4)

"Tem piedade de mim, ó Deus, segundo Tua bondade; segundo a abundância de Tua compaixão, apaga minhas transgressões" (חָנֵּנִי אֱלֹהִים כְּחַסְדֶּךָ). David não apela ao mérito, mas à *chesed* e à *rachamim* de Deus.

O texto usa três termos para o pecado: *pesha* (rebeldia), *avon* (desvio) e *chatat* (erro). Isso lembra os Treze Atributos de Misericórdia de Êxodo 34:7, e a tradição vê aqui uma confissão completa.

### 2. Confissão (vv. 5-8)

"Pois eu conheço minhas transgressões, e meu pecado está sempre diante de mim" (v. 5). Esse é o primeiro elemento da *teshuvá* descrita por **Maimônides** [Mishné Torá, Leis de Teshuvá 1-2]: reconhecer, confessar e abandonar o pecado.

O v. 6, "Contra Ti, só contra Ti, pequei" (לְךָ לְבַדְּךָ חָטָאתִי), costuma gerar a pergunta: e Uriá? A leitura comum é que todo pecado entre pessoas é também uma ofensa contra Deus, e que David admite que nenhum poder humano o julgaria, pois era rei.

O v. 7 diz: "Eis que em iniquidade fui gerado, e em pecado me concebeu minha mãe". Isso é lido na tradição judaica como expressão da condição humana, da inclinação ao mal (*yetzer hará*) e da fragilidade. Não é doutrina de pecado original. Há também leituras midráshicas que associam o verso às circunstâncias da concepção de David [cf. Vayikrá Rabá 14:5].

### 3. Pedido de purificação (vv. 9-11)

"Purifica-me com hissopo e ficarei puro" (תְּחַטְּאֵנִי בְאֵזוֹב וְאֶטְהָר). A imagem remete aos rituais de purificação (Números 19; Levítico 14). O pecado é tratado como impureza espiritual que exige limpeza profunda.

### 4. Transformação interior (vv. 12-14)

O centro do salmo é: "Um coração puro cria para mim, ó Deus, e um espírito firme renova dentro de mim" (לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא לִי אֱלֹהִים וְרוּחַ נָכוֹן חַדֵּשׁ בְּקִרְבִּי).

- O verbo *bará* ("criar") é o mesmo da Criação: David pede uma recriação do ser, e não só perdão.
- "Não retires de mim Teu espírito de santidade" (*ruach kodshecha*) alude à perda possível da inspiração profética e da intimidade com Deus.
- "Devolve-me a alegria da Tua salvação": o arrependimento visa também restaurar a alegria.

### 5. Missão após o arrependimento (vv. 15-19)

"Ensinarei aos transgressores Teus caminhos, e os pecadores a Ti retornarão" (v. 15). O arrependido torna-se mestre de *teshuvá*, e o homem caído serve de testemunho de que há caminho de volta.

O v. 17, "Senhor, abre meus lábios, e minha boca anunciará Teu louvor" (אֲדֹנָי שְׂפָתַי תִּפְתָּח), foi escolhido como a abertura da *Amidá*.

### 6. O sacrifício verdadeiro (vv. 18-19)

"Pois não desejas sacrifício… os sacrifícios de Deus são um espírito quebrantado; um coração quebrantado e contrito, ó Deus, não desprezarás" (זִבְחֵי אֱלֹהִים רוּחַ נִשְׁבָּרָה).

Isso não rejeita o culto do Templo. Os profetas (cf. Isaías 1, Oseias 6:6) mostram que o sacrifício sem coração é vazio. Além disso, o ofensor que pecou intencionalmente em homicídio e adultério não tinha sacrifício que o expiasse, então a única oferta possível era a contrição. O Talmud cita este versículo para elogiar a humildade, como em [Sanhedrin 43b].

### 7. Reconstrução de Jerusalém (vv. 20-21)

"Faze o bem a Sião segundo Tua vontade; edifica os muros de Jerusalém" (הֵיטִיבָה בִרְצוֹנְךָ אֶת צִיּוֹן). Alguns comentaristas leem esses versos como um acréscimo ou uma oração para o futuro, escrita em tempo de exílio ou como profecia. Outros veem David pedindo que seu pecado não prejudique a nação. Depois da restauração, "então desejarás sacrifícios de justiça" (*zivchei tzedek*).

## Temas teológicos

- **Teshuvá como renovação, e não apenas perdão.** O salmo vai além da anulação da culpa e pede uma nova identidade espiritual.
- **Misericórdia divina.** O ponto de partida é *chesed*, e não mérito.
- **Responsabilidade do líder.** Mesmo o rei se submete ao profeta e à Torá. Compare com [Yomá 22b] sobre os reis de Israel que erram.
- **Quebrantamento sem desespero.** O "coração quebrantado" leva ao ensino, ao louvor e à reconstrução.

## Uso litúrgico

- O v. 17 abre a *Amidá* de todas as orações.
- O Salmo 51 é recitado em muitas comunidades nas *Selichot* e na época de arrependimento, e é muito lido como oração pessoal de *teshuvá*.
- O v. 12 inspira orações pelo "coração puro" em várias liturgias.

answer:
Gott wird in der Tora zuerst als **Elohim** bezeichnet ([Genesis 1:1]). Der Gottesname **YHWH** erscheint erstmals zusammen mit Elohim in [Genesis 2:4] ("YHWH Elohim"). Eine Seitenzahl kann ich nicht nennen, da sie je nach Ausgabe variiert. Kapitel und Vers sind aber in jeder Ausgabe gleich.

## Key Takeaways

- **Genesis 1:1** enthält die erste Gottesbezeichnung: Elohim (אֱלֹהִים).
- **Genesis 2:4** enthält erstmals den Gottesnamen YHWH, verbunden als "YHWH Elohim".
- **Exodus 3:15** erklärt YHWH ausdrücklich als Gottes Namen "für immer".
- Die Tradition versteht Elohim als Ausdruck von Gerechtigkeit (*midat ha-din*) und YHWH als Ausdruck von Barmherzigkeit (*midat ha-rachamim*).

## Die Stellen im Einzelnen

### Genesis 1:1 – Elohim
[Genesis 1:1]: "בְּרֵאשִׁית בָּרָא אֱלֹהִים אֵת הַשָּׁמַיִם וְאֵת הָאָרֶץ" – „Am Anfang schuf Elohim Himmel und Erde."

In der gesamten Schöpfungserzählung (Genesis 1:1 bis 2:3) steht nur Elohim, insgesamt 35-mal.

### Genesis 2:4 – YHWH Elohim
[Genesis 2:4]: "אֵלֶּה תוֹלְדוֹת הַשָּׁמַיִם וְהָאָרֶץ בְּהִבָּרְאָם בְּיוֹם עֲשׂוֹת יְהֹוָה אֱלֹהִים אֶרֶץ וְשָׁמָיִם" – „Dies ist die Entstehungsgeschichte von Himmel und Erde, als sie geschaffen wurden, am Tag, da YHWH Elohim Erde und Himmel machte."

Hier steht zum ersten Mal der Vierbuchstabenname (das *Tetragramm*), noch verbunden mit Elohim. Danach folgt die Erzählung vom Garten Eden, in der meist "YHWH Elohim" steht. Allein steht YHWH zum ersten Mal in [Genesis 4:1] (nach meinem Wissen, nicht aus den vorliegenden Quellen).

### Genesis 12:1 – YHWH spricht zu Avram
[Genesis 12:1]: "וַיֹּאמֶר יְהֹוָה אֶל־אַבְרָם לֶךְ־לְךָ…" – „Und YHWH sprach zu Avram: Geh für dich…"

Hier steht YHWH allein als der Gott, der Avraham beruft.

### Exodus 3:15 – Der Name für alle Generationen
[Exodus 3:15]: "יְהֹוָה אֱלֹהֵי אֲבֹתֵיכֶם … זֶה־שְּׁמִי לְעֹלָם וְזֶה זִכְרִי לְדֹר דֹּר" – „YHWH, der Gott eurer Väter … das ist mein Name für ewig und das ist meine Erinnerung von Generation zu Generation."

Hier wird YHWH ausdrücklich als Gottes Name genannt. Nach meinem Wissen hängt damit auch [Exodus 6:3] zusammen, wo Gott sagt, er sei den Vätern als *El Shaddai* erschienen, aber mit seinem Namen YHWH nicht erkannt worden.

## Warum zwei Bezeichnungen?

**Elohim** ist eine allgemeine Bezeichnung für Gott und bezeichnet Macht und Herrschaft. **YHWH** ist der persönliche Eigenname Gottes.

Nach dem Midrasch bezeichnen die beiden Namen zwei Eigenschaften Gottes. Rashi zu [Genesis 2:4], mit Bezug auf [Bereshit Rabbah 12:15], erklärt: Zuerst wollte Gott die Welt mit Strenge (*midat ha-din*) erschaffen. Er sah, dass sie so nicht bestehen würde, und stellte die Barmherzigkeit (*midat ha-rachamim*) voran und verband sie mit der Strenge. Deshalb steht hier "YHWH Elohim".

Die akademische Bibelwissenschaft führt den Wechsel auf verschiedene Quellen zurück (Dokumentenhypothese). Die traditionelle jüdische Sicht lehnt das ab und sieht darin bewusste Bedeutungsunterschiede.

## Praktischer Hinweis
Den Namen YHWH spricht man nicht aus, sondern sagt *Adonai* oder *HaShem*. Auch das Schreiben des Gottesnamens auf Deutsch ist ein Thema, bei dem sich eine Nachfrage lohnt.

Wenn du mir sagst, welche Ausgabe du benutzt (z. B. Hertz-Chumasch, Stone, Zürcher Bibel), kann ich dir helfen, die Stellen dort zu finden. Für persönliche Anleitung wende dich an deinen örtlichen Rabbiner oder Posek.

answer:
**SIM**, segundo a leitura predominante da tradição: o texto apresenta o espírito de Samuel como realmente aparecendo a Saul, e não como uma ilusão da mulher. Mas essa resposta não é unânime, pois alguns rishonim leem o episódio como engano ou visão sem a presença real de Samuel.

## Key Takeaways

- A leitura tradicional predominante é que Samuel realmente apareceu e falou com Saul.
- O texto bíblico o chama "Samuel" e ele transmite uma profecia que se cumpre (I Samuel 28:16-19).
- A reação assustada da mulher sugere que ela não esperava um resultado real (I Samuel 28:12).
- Há uma minoria de opiniões, atribuída a Rav Saadia Gaon, que vê um engano ou ilusão.
- Esta resposta vem principalmente do meu conhecimento da tradição, pois as fontes recuperadas tratam o tema só indiretamente.

## Detalhes

### O texto (pshat)

**I Samuel 28:3-25** chama a figura de "Samuel" e registra suas palavras como verdadeiras. Ele anuncia a queda de Saul e a morte dele e de seus filhos no dia seguinte, e isso se cumpre.

O versículo 12 diz que a mulher gritou ao ver Samuel. A explicação comum é que ela se assustou porque, em vez de uma prática ilusória habitual, apareceu um verdadeiro morto. Isso indicaria que o resultado não veio de seus métodos.

### Por que o episódio foi necessário

**Rashi** comenta [Rashi, I Samuel 28:3] que Samuel é mencionado de novo como morto porque, se estivesse vivo, Saul o teria consultado. Saul tinha removido os necromantes (*ovot*) e precisou procurar uma mulher que ainda praticava a arte.

**Radak** descreve os métodos do *baal ov* (necromante) e do *yidoni* segundo os Sábios [Radak, I Samuel 28:24]. O *baal ov* fala "de entre as juntas" do corpo, e o *yidoni* coloca na boca o osso de um animal chamado *yadua*.

### Por que há discordância

- **Tradição dos Sábios:** o Talmud em [Chagigah 4b], pelo que me lembro, trata Samuel como realmente trazido para cima, e ele teria receado que fosse o dia do Juízo. Não posso garantir os detalhes exatos dessa passagem.
- **Opinião minoritária:** Rav Saadia Gaon é citado como alguém que entendeu o episódio como engano. Isso me vem de memória, e convém verificar a fonte.

A tensão está entre o texto, que parece afirmar a presença de Samuel, e a proibição da necromancia em **Deuteronômio 18:10-11**, segundo a qual esses métodos não deveriam ter poder real.

### Outro ângulo: a postura de Saul

**Abarbanel** [Abarbanel, I Samuel 28:3] pergunta por que Crônicas condena Saul por consultar o *ov*, se ele já tinha buscado resposta por Urim, profetas e sonhos sem receber nenhuma.

**Or HaChaim** sugere que Saul pode ter entendido que a proibição valia apenas quando D'us levanta um profeta [Or HaChaim, Deuteronômio 18:14]. Segundo essa leitura, na ausência de profeta seria permitido consultar.

Esta é uma leitura específica de um comentarista, e não a opinião geral sobre a legalidade da consulta.

answer:
Your reading is partly right, but the text needs two corrections. Satan does ask God to "stretch out Your hand" and touch Job's possessions, and he says Job will "bless" (*yevarechecha*) God, which is a euphemism for "curse." God does not touch Job directly, but delegates: in chapter 1 Satan may touch Job's property but not his person, and in chapter 2 Satan may touch his body but not his life. So the structure is indirect, but it is not "no touch by Satan" in the end.

## Key Takeaways

- Satan's request that God "send Your hand" is answered by God placing Job "in your hand" (*beyadecha*), within limits [Job 1:12, 2:6].
- *Yevarechecha* ("bless You") is a scriptural euphemism for "curse You," which fits the avoidance of blasphemous language [cf. Exodus 22:27].
- Satan is permitted to touch Job's possessions in chapter 1 and his body in chapter 2, but never his life.
- The indirectness distances God from the act only partially: God says Satan incited *Him* against Job [Job 2:3], and Job attributes the affliction to God [Job 19:21].

## Detailed Answer

### The text (pshat)

The Hebrew of Satan's challenge is: "וְאוּלָם שְׁלַח־נָא יָדְךָ וְגַע בְּכׇל־אֲשֶׁר־לוֹ אִם־לֹא עַל־פָּנֶיךָ יְבָרְכֶךָּ" ("But stretch out Your hand and touch all that he has; surely he will bless You to Your face") [Job 1:11]. In chapter 2 the request is escalated: "וְגַע אֶל־עַצְמוֹ וְאֶל־בְּשָׂרוֹ" ("touch his bone and his flesh") [Job 2:5].

Satan asks for God's own hand. God's reply shifts the agency. From memory of the verses (not among the retrieved passages), God says "all that he has is in your hand, only upon him do not stretch out your hand" [Job 1:12]. In chapter 2 He says "he is in your hand, only preserve his life" [Job 2:6].

### Where your reading needs adjusting

- **Chapter 1:** Your description fits. Satan may strike property and children, but not Job's person.
- **Chapter 2:** The limit moves. Satan *is* allowed to afflict Job's body, with only his life protected.
- **Direct vs. indirect:** God acts through an agent, but He does not disown the act. He tells Satan, "you incited Me against him, to swallow him up without cause" [Job 2:3]. Job later says "the hand of God has touched me" [Job 19:21].

The Talmud reflects this. In [Bava Batra 16a], Resh Lakish identifies Satan, the *yetzer hara* (evil inclination), and the Angel of Death as one. Satan is thus an agent who operates only by divine permission, not an independent power.

### "Bless" as a euphemism for "curse"

The verb *barech* often stands for its opposite when the object is God, to avoid writing a curse against Him. The Torah's own prohibition is "אֱלֹהִים לֹא תְקַלֵּל" ("You shall not curse God") [Exodus 22:27]. The text of Job applies this delicacy to Satan's own speech, since even the Adversary's words are recorded in softened form.

The theme also resonates with "I place before you today a blessing and a curse" [Deuteronomy 11:26]. Job's test is whether the experience of curse-like suffering will turn his blessing of God into its opposite.

### Indirectness as a Torah principle

The retrieved verse "לִפְנֵי עִוֵּר לֹא תִתֵּן מִכְשֹׁל" ("before the blind you shall not place a stumbling block") [Leviticus 19:14] shows that Torah law cares about indirect harm. In Job, the indirectness does not remove responsibility. It makes the test one of faith rather than a simple infliction of punishment. That last point is interpretive, drawn from my own reading rather than a specific retrieved source.

answer:
The first friend is Eliphaz the Temanite, and the verse is Job 5:19. He is using the "six... and seven" number pattern, which is a Hebrew poetic idiom for "a full and complete set of troubles." His point is that God will rescue a person from every possible distress, however many there are.

## Key Takeaways

- The verse is Eliphaz's claim that God delivers the righteous from all trouble, not a literal count of six or seven.
- "Six... and seven" is a graded numerical parallelism common in Tanakh, signaling totality or "and then some."
- Abarbanel cites the verse to describe the person who trusts in God: others suffer in hard times, but he remains calm and untouched.
- Eliphaz is applying a retribution theology that the book of Job ultimately challenges.

## Pshat: The Plain Meaning

The verse reads: בְּשֵׁשׁ צָרוֹת יַצִּילֶךָּ וּבְשֶׁבַע לֹא־יִגַּע בְּךָ רָע, "In six troubles He will rescue you, and in seven no evil will touch you" [Job 5:19].

The idiom of "x, and x+1" appears elsewhere, such as Proverbs 6:16 ("six things the Lord hates, seven are an abomination to Him") and Amos 1:3 ("for three transgressions... and for four"). It does not mean the seventh trouble is different in kind. It means that however many troubles come, even a complete series, God's protection holds.

Some read a slight progression in the verse. In the first six God rescues you after trouble arrives. In the seventh, the harm does not even reach you. This is a reading of the structure, though, and not a firm halachic or midrashic rule.

## Abarbanel's Use of the Verse

In his commentary on Jeremiah 17:8, **Abarbanel** quotes this verse while explaining the image of a tree planted by water. The one who trusts in God is like a tree whose leaves stay fresh even in a drought. Abarbanel writes that such a person has good that never departs, and that "even at a time when people are in distress, he will be in tranquility and calm," and then adds, "as it says, 'In six troubles He will rescue you, and in seven no evil will touch you'" [Abarbanel on Jeremiah 17:8].

He reads the leaf as a metaphor for wealth, riches, and honor, and the fruit as a metaphor for children. So he takes Job 5:19 as a promise of security for the person of *bitachon* (trust in God), even amid general calamity.

## The Context: Eliphaz's Argument

Eliphaz's speech (Job 4–5) rests on a principle of strict reward and punishment. He tells Job that the innocent do not perish and that Job should accept God's discipline and turn to Him. The verse is part of his consolation: if Job repents, God will heal him and save him from famine, war, and every harm (Job 5:17–26).

The irony is that the book as a whole rejects this simplistic reading. In the end God says Job's friends "did not speak correctly" about Him (Job 42:7). Eliphaz's statement is therefore a true expression of faith in God's power to save, but a flawed assumption when applied to Job, because it presumes that suffering always signals sin.

## A Theological Counterpoint

The retrieved passages also include Isaiah 45:7: "Who forms light and creates darkness, makes peace and creates evil; I am the Lord, who does all these." This reminds us that Tanakh does not claim a believer will never encounter hardship. Both good and affliction come from one God.

So the verse should be read carefully. It expresses a real biblical hope, echoed in Psalms (e.g., 91), that God protects those who trust Him, but Job shows that the righteous can still suffer without having sinned. Eliphaz's formula should not be applied as a rule to explain anyone's suffering.

*Note: the retrieved sources cover the verse itself, Abarbanel, and Isaiah 45:7. The remarks on the numerical idiom, parallels in Proverbs and Amos, and the wider context of Job come from my general knowledge of Tanakh.*

- Most Hasidic Torah works "survived" because they were printed before 1939 and carried abroad by students and families.
- The **Esh Kodesh** of R. Kalonymus Kalman Shapira (Piaseczno) is the most striking case, since it was written in the Warsaw Ghetto and buried.
- Vaetchanan's recurring themes are Moshe's prayer, Shabbat Nachamu, the Shema, and love versus fear of God.
- The retrieved sources touch these themes through Rashi's love/fear distinction and the Netziv's *Meshiv Davar*, which is Lithuanian, not Hasidic.

## Lesser-Known Works to Explore

### Written or preserved through the Holocaust
- **Esh Kodesh (R. Kalonymus Kalman Shapira, the Piaseczner Rebbe).** These are his ghetto sermons from 1939–1942, including the Vaetchanan/Nachamu season. The manuscript was buried in a milk can and recovered after the war, and it was first published in 1960. It reads Torah as a response to unbearable suffering, so comfort (*nechama*) takes on very different weight.
- **Eim HaBanim Semeicha (R. Yissachar Shlomo Teichtal).** It was written during the war, and its subject, longing for Eretz Yisrael, resonates with Moshe's plea "Let me cross over and see the good land" (Deuteronomy 3:25). It is a halachic-philosophical work, not a parsha commentary, but it is relevant here.

### Pre-war works that were carried forward
- **Mei HaShiloach (R. Mordechai Yosef Leiner of Izbica).** It is a radical reading of divine will and human striving, and it can be applied to Moshe's denied request.
- **Shem MiShmuel (R. Shmuel Bornstein of Sochatchov).** It offers an extended treatment of the Shabbat Nachamu season and of the Shema.
- **Maor VaShemesh (R. Kalonymus Kalman Epstein of Krakow).** It gives a Hasidic reading of Moshe's prayer.
- **Degel Machaneh Ephraim (R. Moshe Chaim Ephraim of Sudilkov).** This is a Ba'al Shem Tov-lineage work with comments on prayer and on the Shabbat Nachamu season.
- **Ohev Yisrael (R. Avraham Yehoshua Heschel of Apta).** It is homiletical and often overlooked.

## Thematic Connection to the Retrieved Sources

The Hasidic discussions of *ahavah* (love) and *yirah* (fear) have a clear background in the passage. In the retrieved Haggahot Rabbeinu Peretz, Rashi reads "to those who keep His commandments" as fear-based service. He notes that one who serves from fear may walk away when the master burdens him, while one who serves from love serves forever. Hasidic authors often build on this contrast.

The **Meshiv Davar** (Netziv) is not Hasidic, but it addresses the same verse, "who keeps the covenant and kindness for those who love Him and keep His commandments, to a thousand generations." He argues that the "middle" path in divine service includes many levels, and that some people deserve the title *chasid* through their deeds even without ecstatic devotion.

If you tell me which theme interests you most (Moshe's prayer, Shema, or comfort after destruction), I can focus on that.

answer:
Yes, there seems to be a deliberate literary parallel. The book of Job places a heavenly gathering (1:6) and an earthly family gathering (1:13) side by side, and introduces both with the same phrase, *vayehi ha-yom* ("and it was the day"). The structure suggests the two scenes mirror each other, with the heavenly assembly setting in motion what happens at the sons' feast. This is a literary reading based on the text, not a classical commentators' consensus.

## Key Takeaways

- Both scenes open with *vayehi ha-yom*: the heavenly court in [Job 1:6] and the sons' feast in [Job 1:13].
- Both involve "sons" gathering: *benei ha-Elohim* (sons of God/angels) before God, and Job's sons and daughters feasting in the eldest brother's house.
- The verb *barech* ("bless," a euphemism for "curse") links Job's fear about his children (1:5) with Satan's wager about Job (1:11).
- The two scenes are causally linked, since the heavenly challenge leads to the feast's destruction.
- Classical sources do not frame this as an explicit parallel, so this is a literary reading, not a traditional one.

## The Textual Parallels

**The opening formula.** [Job 1:6] reads "וַיְהִי הַיּוֹם וַיָּבֹאוּ בְּנֵי הָאֱלֹהִים לְהִתְיַצֵּב עַל־יְהֹוָה" ("And it was the day, and the sons of God came to present themselves before the Lord"). The disaster begins in [Job 1:13] with "וַיְהִי הַיּוֹם" again, while Job's sons and daughters are eating and drinking wine in their eldest brother's house. The repeated phrase links the two scenes, as if the same "day" is happening above and below.

**Two gatherings of "sons."** In heaven, the *benei ha-Elohim* "present themselves" (*lehityatzev*) before God, an image of formal accountability. On earth, Job's sons gather in a festive rotation (1:4). One is a court, the other a banquet. Yet in both, Satan or the messengers cut in on a gathering and change its course.

**The word "bless."** In [Job 1:5], Job sacrifices after each round of feasting, thinking "perhaps my sons have sinned and *blessed* (*barchu*) God in their hearts." In [Job 1:11], Satan says Job will "bless" God "to your face" if his property is taken, and [Job 2:5] repeats this. Both use the same euphemism for cursing. Job's anxiety about his children's inner lives and Satan's accusation about Job's inner life are mirror concerns about what lies behind outward piety.

## A Fatherly Parallel

Job stands as a father presiding over his sons' spiritual standing, offering sacrifices "according to the number of them all." God likewise appears as the one before whom His "sons" stand and who vouches for His servant Job. The parallel is imperfect, but it sets Job's anxious, preventive piety beside God's confidence in Job's integrity (*tam ve-yashar*).

## Differences

- The heavenly scene is a legal-style review of Job's character, while the earthly scene is ordinary celebration.
- Job is unaware of the heavenly scene, and the reader sees both.
- Job's sacrifices cover possible hidden sin, while the heavenly scene tests whether Job's goodness is genuine.

## Classical Context

I am drawing on memory here, so please verify these references. Rabbinic tradition treats Satan in Job as an accuser who is also the *yetzer ha-ra* and the angel of death [Bava Batra 16a]. The Aramaic Targum to Job 1:6 places the heavenly gathering on a day of judgment, which fits the sense that the scene is a trial. Rashi reads "his day" in 1:4 as each son's birthday, which makes the feasts a pattern of recurring celebration set against the sudden rupture.

## Other Retrieved Sources

[Genesis 6:4] also uses *benei ha-Elohim*, but there the phrase is widely read differently, as nobles, judges, or fallen beings, and it does not bear on Job's feast. [Genesis 37:35], where Jacob refuses comfort from his sons and daughters, is a distant thematic echo: a father mourning a child amid his family. It is not a structural parallel.

answer:
Yes, the Yovel (Jubilee) laws required that the original tribal and family distribution be restored. Land in Israel could not be sold permanently, so every sale was in effect a lease that expired in the Yovel year, when the field returned to the original family holding. The Torah states: "In this year of the Jubilee, you shall return, each man to his holding" [Leviticus 25:13].

## Key Takeaways

- Land sales were really leases of a number of years' crops, not permanent transfers, and all reverted at Yovel [Leviticus 25:13, 25:23].
- The reason given is theological: "the land is Mine, for you are strangers and residents with Me" [Leviticus 25:23].
- Between Yovels, the seller or his relative (the *go'el*, redeemer) could redeem the field early [Leviticus 25:24-28].
- Rabbinic tradition ties the restoration to the original division by tribe and family, so the distribution was not meant to be permanently rearranged by commerce.
- Halachic details, such as whether Yovel applies today, are complex, and the sources here do not settle them.

## Plain Meaning (*Pshat*)

The core text is: "וְהָאָרֶץ לֹא תִמָּכֵר לִצְמִתֻת, כִּי לִי הָאָרֶץ" (the land shall not be sold in perpetuity, for the land is Mine) [Leviticus 25:23]. The word *litzmitut* means "permanently" or "irrevocably." Ownership ultimately belongs to God, and Israelites hold the land as *gerim ve-toshavim* (strangers and residents) with Him.

The following verse adds: "וּבְכֹל אֶרֶץ אֲחֻזַּתְכֶם גְּאֻלָּה תִּתְּנוּ לָאָרֶץ" (in all the land of your holding, you shall grant redemption for the land) [Leviticus 25:24]. So redemption is built into every sale.

## Two Mechanisms of Return

**1. Early redemption (*ge'ula*).** If a person grew poor and sold part of his holding, his closest relative could redeem it [Leviticus 25:25]. If he had no *go'el* but later became wealthy, he could redeem it himself. The buyer's price was calculated by counting the years since the sale and returning the surplus to the buyer [Leviticus 25:26-27].

**2. Automatic return at Yovel.** If the field was not redeemed, it reverted in the Yovel year: "תָּשֻׁבוּ אִישׁ אֶל אֲחֻזָּתוֹ" [Leviticus 25:13]. The Torah later spells this out in Leviticus 25:28 (not in the retrieved text; from my knowledge).

## Why This Matters: Preserving the Original Distribution

The land was divided by lot among tribes and families in the time of Joshua (Numbers 26:52-56; Joshua 13-19). The Yovel system keeps that division from being permanently eroded by poverty, debt, or accumulation of wealth. This is from my own knowledge rather than the retrieved passages, but it is the standard understanding of the institution.

Note one nuance: the return is to the **family** holding, meaning the seller or his heirs, rather than to the tribe in the abstract. In practice this preserved the tribal map as well. Land that passed through inheritance or marriage was a separate matter. The Torah addresses this in the case of the daughters of Tzelofchad, where land was not to move from tribe to tribe [Numbers 36:7-9], again showing concern for the original tribal allotment.

## Exceptions and Limits (from my knowledge)

- **Houses in walled cities** could be redeemed only within one year and then became permanent [Leviticus 25:29-30].
- **Levite property** had its own redemption rules [Leviticus 25:32-34].
- **Consecrated fields** (*hekdesh*) that were not redeemed went to the Kohanim at Yovel [Leviticus 27:20-21].

So the system had some carved-out exceptions, but the general rule for agricultural land was restoration.

## Connection to Broader Themes

The Sifra, which the retrieved sources include on the Yovel count, shows that the *beit din* (court) is responsible for counting the years toward Yovel [Sifra, Behar 2]. The institution was a communal and legal one, not left to individual initiative.

The related theme in Pirkei Avot 3:17, "if there is no Torah, there is no *derech eretz*," is not directly about Yovel. It does reflect the Torah's integration of livelihood and spiritual life, which Yovel embodies by anchoring economic life in the idea that the land belongs to God.

## Halachic Note

The Yovel laws were operative only when the Jewish people lived in the land in their tribal settlement. The Talmud (Arachin 32b) records that Yovel ceased when the tribes of Reuven, Gad, and half of Menashe were exiled, and that this is the view of the Sages. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi disagreed and held that Yovel's rules apply whenever the Jewish people are in the land. This is from my knowledge, so please verify the details in the source.

For personal guidance, consult your local rabbi or posek.

answer:
The ceremony took place when Israel crossed the Jordan and entered the land: six tribes stood on Mount **Gerizim** for the blessings and six on Mount **Eival** (Ebal) for the curses, while the Levites in the valley between them proclaimed the covenant's terms and the people answered "Amen." Its basic significance is that Israel entered the land by publicly and collectively accepting the Torah's covenant, with blessing and curse presented as consequences of their own choice to obey or disobey.

## Key Takeaways

- Moses commanded the ceremony [Deuteronomy 11:26-32; 27:11-26], and Joshua carried it out [Joshua 8:30-35].
- Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Joseph, and Benjamin stood on Gerizim; Reuben, Gad, Asher, Zebulun, Dan, and Naftali on Eival.
- The Levites declared the curses aloud and all Israel responded "Amen."
- Joshua built an altar of whole, unhewn stones on Eival and wrote the Torah on stones.
- The ceremony establishes the covenant's moral choice: blessing and curse depend on obedience to God.

## Detailed Answer

### 1. The ceremony itself

**The command (Deuteronomy 11:26-32).** Moses opens: "רְאֵה אָנֹכִי נֹתֵן לִפְנֵיכֶם הַיּוֹם בְּרָכָה וּקְלָלָה" ("See, I place before you today a blessing and a curse"). The blessing follows if they heed God's commandments. The curse follows if they do not heed them and turn aside "to follow other gods whom you have not known." When God brings them into the land, they are to place the blessing on Gerizim and the curse on Eival.

**The tribal division (Deuteronomy 27:11-14).** Moses commanded that on the day they crossed the Jordan:
- Six tribes stand on Gerizim "to bless the people": Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Joseph, Benjamin. These were mostly sons of Leah and Rachel.
- Six stand on Eival "for the curse": Reuben, Gad, Asher, Zebulun, Dan, Naftali. These were mostly sons of the maidservants, plus Reuben and Zebulun.
- The Levites "answered and said to every man of Israel in a loud voice," pronouncing the declarations.

**The curses (Deuteronomy 27:15-26).** Twelve "אָרוּר" ("Cursed be...") statements follow. They address idolatry, dishonoring parents, moving a boundary marker, misleading the blind, perverting justice for the vulnerable, various forbidden sexual relations, striking a neighbor in secret, taking a bribe to kill an innocent person, and not upholding the Torah. After each, "all the people shall say: Amen." Many are sins done in secret, so the people take communal responsibility for hidden transgressions.

**The tradition of the details (Mishnah Sotah 7:5; Sotah 32a, 36a-37b, from the Oral Tradition).** The Talmud records that the Levites, with the Ark, stood in the middle, half facing Gerizim and half Eival. They first turned to Gerizim and said a blessing, "Blessed is the man who does not make a graven image...," and then both sides answered "Amen." Then they turned to Eival and recited the corresponding curse. The Talmud also holds that blessings were stated alongside each curse, though the text records only the curses. This comes from my knowledge of the Talmudic tradition, not from the retrieved passages.

**Joshua's fulfillment (Joshua 8:30-35).** After Ai, Joshua built an altar on Mount Eival "as Moses, servant of God, had commanded" of "whole stones, upon which no iron had been lifted." They offered burnt and peace offerings, and he wrote "a copy (*mishneh*) of the Torah of Moses" on the stones. All Israel, elders, officers, judges, converts and native-born, stood on both sides of the Ark, half toward Gerizim and half toward Eival. Joshua then read all the words of the Torah, "blessing and curse," with none omitted, before the whole assembly including women, children, and the stranger.

### 2. The significance

**Covenant ratification.** Entry into the land was conditional on a covenant. As at Sinai, the people publicly accept the Torah's obligations before taking possession. The "Amen" is an oath-like acceptance (cf. Shevuot 29b on the concept of *amen* as a binding acceptance).

**Choice and responsibility.** The phrase "See, I place before you today" frames blessing and curse as a real choice. The same Torah leads to blessing or curse depending on the people's own conduct, a theme running through Deuteronomy.

**Collective accountability.** The whole nation, with every tribe participating, was present and responsible. The Talmud (Sotah 37b) connects this to the idea that "all Israel are responsible (*arevim*) for one another," with the covenant extending even to hidden sins.

**Torah and land.** The inscribed stones and the altar link the Torah to the land and to worship. The wholeness of the stones, with no iron, signifies peace and completeness in the altar's purpose.

**The mussar reading.** The **Shenei Luchot HaBerit** (Re'eh) [Shenei Luchot HaBerit, Torah Shebikhtav, Re'eh, Torah Ohr 61] reads the two mountains as corresponding to two spiritual mountains above. One is the "mountain of the Lord" ("מי יעלה בהר ה'," "Who may ascend the mountain of the Lord?"). The other is **Har Se'ir**, which he connects to the *yetzer hara* (evil inclination), compared to a "hair" (*se'ara*) for the wicked and a "mountain" for the righteous. In this reading, the physical ceremony points to the inner choice each person faces between two paths. This is a homiletic layer beyond the plain meaning.

For personal guidance, consult your local rabbi or posek.

answer:
Jeremiah 15 and 16 are a pair. In chapter 15 God says the decree of exile is sealed, even Moses and Samuel could not stop it, and Jeremiah protests and is told to repent his complaint. In chapter 16 Jeremiah's own life becomes a sign: no marriage, no mourning, no feasting, because the nation faces catastrophe, followed by a promise of return.

Only Rashi on 15:1 was in my retrieved sources. The other commentary below comes from my general knowledge, so please verify it inside the text (Mikraot Gedolot, Sefaria).

## Key Takeaways

- Jer. 15:1 says even Moses and Samuel could not avert the decree, because the people had not repented.
- Rashi notes that Moses and Samuel first brought Israel back to the right path and only then prayed.
- Jeremiah complains bitterly (15:10-18), and God answers that he must "return" before he can again be God's spokesman (15:19).
- Chapter 16 makes Jeremiah's life a prophetic sign: no wife, no children, no mourning, no feasts.
- Both chapters end with consolation: Jeremiah is a "bronze wall" (15:20), and Israel will be returned from the "land of the north" (16:14-15).

## Chapter 15

### The decree (15:1-9)

**Pshat:** God tells Jeremiah that "if Moses and Samuel stood before Me, My soul would not be toward this people" (*Im ya'amod Moshe u-Shmuel lefanai, ein nafshi el ha-am ha-zeh*). The people are to be sent away. When they ask where to go, the answer is "those destined for death to death, sword to sword, famine to famine, captivity to captivity." The "four families" (*arba mishpachot*) of destruction are the sword, dogs, birds, and beasts (15:3).

The cause given in 15:4 is the sin of **Manasseh son of Hezekiah** in Jerusalem. God is also "weary of relenting" (*nilEti hinachem*, 15:6), having held back punishment many times.

**Rashi on 15:1** [Rashi, Jeremiah 15:1] asks why Moses and Samuel in particular. His answer is that both were drawn into pleading for Israel, but each first brought the people back to the right path and only afterward prayed.

- Moses ordered the sword against the calf-worshippers and ground up the calf (Ex. 32:20, 27), and only then said, "Perhaps I can atone" (Ex. 32:30).
- Samuel at Mitzpah saw Israel remove the Baalim (I Sam. 7:4) before he said he would pray for them.

The lesson is that intercession works only once there is *teshuva* (repentance). Here the people had not repented, so even these two could not help.

**The Manasseh question:** Why punish this generation for Manasseh's sin? The Talmud discusses Manasseh's wickedness and his later repentance in Sanhedrin 101b-103a, and I Kings 21 and II Kings 23:26 also tie the destruction to him. The classic reading is that his idolatry set a pattern the people never fully abandoned, so the decree stayed in force.

### Jeremiah's complaint (15:10-18)

Jeremiah cries, "Woe is me, my mother, that you bore me, a man of strife to the whole land." He says he never lent or borrowed, so there was no ordinary reason for anyone to curse him. He says God's words were "found and I ate them," and they were "joy and delight of my heart" (15:16). He sat alone and not "in the company of revelers" (*mesachakim*). Yet his pain is endless, and he accuses God of being "like a deceptive brook" (*achzav*), a stream that dries up when needed (15:18).

The commentators generally treat this as the prophet's anguish at being the bearer of bad news, not as disloyalty. Radak and others read verses 11-14, which are hard to translate, as God's initial reply about Judah's wealth being plundered and the strength of the "iron from the north" (Babylon).

### God's response (15:19-21)

God says, "If you return, I will return you; you shall stand before Me." If Jeremiah "brings forth the precious from the vile," he will be "like My mouth" (*ke-fi tihyeh*). The people will turn to him, not he to them. God promises to make him "a fortified bronze wall" against all who fight him.

The classic reading is that Jeremiah must retract his complaint and speak only what is true, without despair, to remain a prophet. The dispute among commentators is about what exactly Jeremiah must "return" from, and what "precious" and "vile" refer to. I am not quoting a specific mefaresh here, so check this verse inside the Mikraot Gedolot.

## Chapter 16

### The prophet's sign-life (16:1-9)

**Pshat:** God commands Jeremiah not to marry or have children "in this place" (16:2). The reason is that children born here will die "deadly diseases" (*mamotei tachalu'im*), unlamented and unburied, "like dung on the face of the earth," with their corpses food for birds and beasts (16:4).

He is also forbidden to:

- enter a house of mourning (*beit marzeach*) or console anyone, because God has withdrawn "My peace, kindness, and mercy" (16:5);
- enter a house of feasting (16:8);
- take part in celebrations, because God will silence "the voice of joy and gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and bride" (16:9).

The Talmud picks up these verses in connection with mourning customs. Ketubot 8b, as I recall, discusses the "bread of mourners" and the "cup of consolation" (16:7). The phrase "voice of the bridegroom and bride" (*kol chatan ve-chala*) also became part of the *Sheva Berachot*, the seven blessings at a wedding. Please verify these Talmud references.

### Why the exile? (16:10-13)

When the people ask, "Why has God decreed this evil?", Jeremiah is to answer that they and their fathers forsook God for idols, and that this generation did worse than their fathers. They will be hurled into a land they do not know, where they will serve other gods and receive no *chanina* (favor).

### The promise of return (16:14-21)

The prophecy turns to hope. A day will come when people no longer swear "by the God who brought Israel out of Egypt" but "by the God who brought Israel up from the land of the north" (16:14-15). The return from exile will overshadow the Exodus in people's memory. Commentators, including Radak as I recall, read the "land of the north" as Babylon.

Then God sends "many fishers and many hunters" to seek the people out (16:16). The classic reading is that these are the enemy armies searching for Israel, though some take them as agents of eventual return. The people receive "double" repayment for their sin (16:18). Radak, as I recall, ties this to the idolatry that defiled the land.

Jeremiah closes with trust: "Hashem, my strength and my fortress, my refuge in the day of distress" (16:19). He foresees nations coming from the ends of the earth to confess that their fathers inherited only falsehood, and that no man can make gods for himself (16:19-20).

## Broader Connection

Together the chapters tie into the prophetic theme of prophets as living signs. The unmarried, unmourning, unfeasting Jeremiah models the coming loss. Compare the Moses-and-Samuel image with Psalm 99:6 and with Moses' intercession after the calf, where repentance and prayer go together.

If you tell me which verses interest you most, I can go deeper into specific commentators. A good place to start is Rashi, Radak, and Metzudat David on 15:19, 16:16, and 16:18.

answer:
Parashat **Lech Lecha** (Genesis 12:1-17:27) tells of God's call to Abram to leave his homeland for an unnamed land, and of the covenants that follow. It covers Abram's journey to Canaan, his sojourn in Egypt, the war of the kings, the *Brit bein HaBetarim* (Covenant Between the Parts), the birth of Ishmael, and the commandment of *brit milah* (circumcision). Abram and Sarai are renamed Abraham and Sarah.

*Note: the calendar data shows this week's parasha is Vayishlach, not Lech Lecha. This summary answers your question about Lech Lecha specifically.*

## Key Takeaways

- God commands Abram to leave his land, and promises him nationhood, blessing, and a great name (Genesis 12:1-3).
- Abram journeys through Canaan, descends to Egypt during a famine, and returns with Lot, who then separates from him.
- God makes the Covenant Between the Parts, promising Abram land and descendants (Genesis 15).
- Ishmael is born to Hagar, and God later establishes the covenant of circumcision (Genesis 16-17).
- Abram becomes Abraham and Sarai becomes Sarah, with a promise of a son, Isaac.

## Detailed Summary

### The Call (Genesis 12:1-9)

The parasha opens: "וַיֹּאמֶר יְהֹוָה אֶל־אַבְרָם לֶךְ־לְךָ מֵאַרְצְךָ וּמִמּוֹלַדְתְּךָ וּמִבֵּית אָבִיךָ אֶל־הָאָרֶץ אֲשֶׁר אַרְאֶךָּ" ("The LORD said to Abram: Go forth from your land, from your birthplace, and from your father's house, to the land that I will show you") [Genesis 12:1].

**Rashi** explains the phrase *lech lecha* as "for your benefit and for your good." There God will make him a great nation, whereas in his homeland he would not merit children. Rashi adds that God will also make Abram's character known in the world [Rashi on Genesis 12:1]. (This is from the retrieved sources.)

Abram travels with Sarai, Lot, and their household to Shechem and then Bethel, building altars along the way. God promises, "To your offspring I will give this land."

### Egypt and Separation from Lot (12:10-13:18)

A famine drives Abram to Egypt. Fearing for his life, he asks Sarai to say she is his sister. Pharaoh takes her, but God afflicts his house with plagues, and Pharaoh sends them away enriched. Many commentators, such as **Ramban**, see this episode as foreshadowing the later exile and exodus of Israel (Ramban on Genesis 12:10, from my own knowledge).

Quarrels between Abram's and Lot's herdsmen lead to their separation. Lot chooses the well-watered Jordan plain near Sodom, and God reaffirms the promise of the land to Abram.

### The War of the Kings (14)

Four kings capture Lot in their war against the Sodom coalition. Abram pursues them with 318 men and rescues Lot. He is blessed by **Malki-Tzedek**, king of Shalem and priest of God, and he refuses any spoils from the king of Sodom.

### Brit bein HaBetarim (15)

God reassures Abram, who is anxious about being childless. He promises descendants as numerous as the stars, and Abram's faith is counted as righteousness: "וְהֶאֱמִן בַּה' וַיַּחְשְׁבֶהָ לּוֹ צְדָקָה" [Genesis 15:6]. In the covenant ceremony, God foretells that Abram's descendants will be strangers in a foreign land for 400 years before returning to inherit Canaan.

### Hagar and Ishmael (16)

Sarai, still childless, gives her maidservant Hagar to Abram. When Hagar conceives, tension arises and Hagar flees. An angel tells her to return and promises that her son, Ishmael, will become a great nation.

### Brit Milah and the New Names (17)

When Abram is 99, God appears to him and establishes a covenant. Abram becomes Abraham, "father of a multitude of nations," and Sarai becomes Sarah. God commands circumcision of every male on the eighth day as "an eternal covenant." God promises that Sarah will bear Isaac, and Abraham circumcises himself and his household.

## Major Themes

- **Faith and obedience:** Abraham acts on God's word without knowing his destination. The Mishnah in *Avot* 5:3 counts *lech lecha* as the first of Abraham's ten trials.
- **Covenant:** The land, descendants, and *brit milah* form the foundation of the relationship between God and the Jewish people.
- **Ma'aseh avot siman labanim:** Ramban's principle that "the deeds of the fathers are a sign for the children" is especially evident in the Egypt episode.

The parasha is traditionally read in the autumn, in the Hebrew month of Cheshvan.

answer:
Ben-Deker is not described as a treasurer of the Temple. **I Kings 4:9** names him as one of Solomon's twelve regional governors (*nitzavim*), responsible for a district in the territory once associated with Dan and Judah. The retrieved sources say nothing of a Temple treasury role.

## Key Takeaways

- Ben-Deker was a district governor (*natziv*) under Solomon, not a Temple treasurer.
- His district included Makaz, Sha'alvim, Beit Shemesh, and Elon Beit Hanan.
- Steinsaltz notes these places had been in Dan's territory but were now counted as part of Judah.
- The text gives only his patronymic, and nothing about his personal life.

## What the Sources Say

The verse reads: "בֶּן־דֶּקֶר בְּמָקַץ וּבְשַׁעַלְבִים וּבֵית שָׁמֶשׁ וְאֵילוֹן בֵּית חָנָן" ("Ben-Deker, in Makaz, and in Sha'alvim, and Beit Shemesh, and Elon Beit Hanan") [I Kings 4:9]. The verse is a fragment of a list, and the title is implied from the surrounding verses.

**Steinsaltz** fills this in: Ben-Deker "was the governor" (*hanatziv*) of these places, which "had formerly been in the territory of Dan, and were now considered part of the territory of Judah" [Steinsaltz on I Kings 4:9]. The comment points to a shifting tribal geography in Solomon's administrative organization.

## Context: Solomon's Twelve Districts

The list belongs to the account of Solomon's administration. From my broader knowledge rather than the retrieved passages, I Kings 4:7 says these twelve officials supplied the king and his household with provisions, each responsible for one month of the year. This was a royal supply system, not a Temple treasury.

Ben-Deker appears in verse 9, right after Ben-Hur in the hill country of Ephraim (v. 8). Several other officials in the chapter are also known only by "Ben-so-and-so."

## Where the Confusion May Come From

- **Temple building:** Solomon's building of the Temple is told in I Kings 5–8. Officials like Adoniram, who oversaw the forced labor (*mas*), appear in I Kings 4:6 and 5:28.
- **Treasuries:** The Temple treasuries (*otzrot beit Hashem*) are mentioned in I Kings 7:51, but without naming a treasurer.
- **Later periods:** Temple treasurers appear more explicitly in later sources, such as the Levite overseers in I Chronicles 26 under David.

Some of the places in his district have their own interest. Beit Shemesh was a Levitical city in Judah, and Sha'alvim and Elon are listed among Dan's cities in Joshua 19:42–43. This is from my own knowledge, not the retrieved sources.

answer:
Parashat Noach (Genesis 6:9-11:32) tells of Noah's righteousness, the Flood, the covenant after it, and the Tower of Babel. It ends with the genealogy leading to Avram. I don't have the text of the **Aish Kodesh** (Rabbi Kalonymus Kalman Shapira, the Piaseczno Rebbe) in the retrieved sources, and I can't reliably quote his Noach sermons from memory, so I won't put words in his mouth.

## Key Takeaways

- Noah is called "a righteous man, perfect in his generations," and the Flood comes because of the earth's corruption and violence (*hamas*).
- After the Flood, God makes a covenant never to destroy the world again, with the rainbow as its sign.
- The parasha closes with Babel, the ten generations from Shem, and Terach's death in Charan.
- The retrieved **Ramban** on 11:32 discusses why Terach's death is mentioned before Avram's departure.
- For the Aish Kodesh, please check his *Derashot mi-Shnot HaZa'am* (Warsaw Ghetto sermons) directly.

## Summary of the Parasha

### Noah and the Ark
The Torah introduces Noah: "אֵלֶּה תּוֹלְדֹת נֹחַ נֹחַ אִישׁ צַדִּיק תָּמִים הָיָה בְּדֹרֹתָיו אֶת־הָאֱלֹהִים הִתְהַלֶּךְ־נֹחַ" ("These are the generations of Noah; Noah was a righteous man, perfect in his generations; Noah walked with God") [Genesis 6:9]. The earth had become corrupt and filled with violence. God commands Noah to build an *teivah* (ark) and bring in his family and pairs of animals.

### The Flood and Aftermath
The Flood comes, and the ark floats for about a year. Noah sends out the raven and then the dove, and finally leaves the ark. He offers sacrifices, and God promises never again to destroy the world. The rainbow is the sign of the covenant, and humanity receives the basic laws given to Noah's descendants (*Sheva Mitzvot Bnei Noach*).

### Noah's Vineyard and Babel
Noah plants a vineyard, becomes drunk, and the incident with Ham and Canaan follows. The nations descend from his sons. The generation of Babel then builds a tower and is dispersed. This is Torah narrative, with details drawn from my general knowledge rather than the retrieved passages.

### Ending with Terach
The parasha records the line from Shem to Terach: "וַיִּהְיוּ יְמֵי־תֶרַח חָמֵשׁ שָׁנִים וּמָאתַיִם שָׁנָה וַיָּמָת תֶּרַח בְּחָרָן" ("The days of Terach were two hundred and five years, and Terach died in Charan") [Genesis 11:32].

## A Source from Your Retrieved Texts: Ramban on Terach's Death

Terach lived 205 years, yet his death is recorded before Avram leaves Charan, though Avram left while Terach still had many years left. **Rashi**, drawing on **Bereishit Rabbah**, explains that the Torah wanted to avoid the impression that Avram failed to honor his father by leaving him in old age. It also notes that the wicked are called "dead" even while alive.

The **Ramban** [Ramban on Genesis 11:32] says he is "amazed" (*ani tomeah*) at this explanation. The Torah's usual pattern is to give a father's life, the birth of his son, and his death, and only then turn to the son. He observes that Noah was still alive in Avram's time, and Shem outlived Avraham. He suggests the Midrash arose because the Torah altered the usual order of the passage. The retrieved text cuts off there, so I can't give his full conclusion.

## The Aish Kodesh

The Piaseczno Rebbe delivered his Shabbat sermons in the Warsaw Ghetto from 1939 to 1942. Noach 5700 (fall 1939) fell right after the German invasion of Poland, so a flood-and-destruction reading is natural. I can't say from memory what he taught on specific verses, so please consult the text.

If you tell me which passage you have in mind, or paste it, I'll gladly work through it with you. I can also discuss how classic sources treat Noah's "in his generations" (whether it is praise or criticism, per **Rashi on Genesis 6:9**, drawing on Sanhedrin 108a).

answer:
God created light on the first day (Genesis 1:3) and the sun, moon, and stars only on the fourth day (Genesis 1:14-19). The classic answers are that the first light was a different, primordial light that was not dependent on the sun, and that the luminaries were given a new role on day four: marking time, seasons, and governing day and night. The order also teaches that God, not the sun, is the true source of light and life.

## Key Takeaways

- Genesis 1:3 describes light created by divine speech, before any luminary existed.
- On day four the sun and moon are given specific functions: separating day from night, serving as signs and seasons, and "ruling" day and night.
- The **Talmud** and **Midrash** identify the first light as a special, hidden light (*or haganuz*).
- **Rashi** and **Ramban** differ on whether the first light was physical or more spiritual or transcendent.
- A theological message: the sun is a created tool, not an independent deity.

## Pshat: The Plain Text

On day one: "וַיֹּאמֶר אֱלֹהִים יְהִי אוֹר וַיְהִי אוֹר" (*"And God said, 'Let there be light,' and there was light"*) [Genesis 1:3]. God then separates light from darkness and names them day and night, and the verse concludes, "there was evening and there was morning, one day" [Genesis 1:3-5]. So the text already has "day" and "night" and an evening-morning cycle before the sun exists.

On day four: "יְהִי מְאֹרֹת בִּרְקִיעַ הַשָּׁמַיִם לְהַבְדִּיל בֵּין הַיּוֹם וּבֵין הַלָּיְלָה" (*"Let there be luminaries in the firmament of the heavens to separate between day and night"*) [Genesis 1:14]. They are to be "לְאֹתֹת וּלְמוֹעֲדִים וּלְיָמִים וְשָׁנִים" (*"for signs, for appointed times, for days and years"*), and "לְהָאִיר עַל הָאָרֶץ" (*"to give light upon the earth"*) [Genesis 1:14-15].

Notice the different vocabulary. Day one has *or* (light as such), while day four uses *me'orot* (luminaries, light-bearers). The first is the phenomenon; the second are the instruments that carry and regulate it.

## Why This Order? Classical Explanations

### The Hidden Light (*Or HaGanuz*)

The Talmud (in a passage I am citing from memory, so verify the exact wording) teaches in [Chagigah 12a] that with the light created on day one, a person could see from one end of the world to the other. Because God foresaw the wickedness of later generations, He hid it away for the righteous in the world to come. The Midrash makes a similar point in [Bereishit Rabbah 3:6].

On this reading, the sun is a replacement, a more limited, "everyday" light for the world as it actually functions.

### Rashi

**Rashi** on Genesis 1:4 (drawing on the Midrash) says that God saw the light was good and that it was not fitting for the wicked to use it, so He set it aside for the righteous in the future. Rashi thus follows the *or haganuz* tradition.

### Ramban and the Question of Nature of the Light

**Ramban** on Genesis 1:3 and surrounding verses understands the first light more in terms of primordial creation. He discusses a primary matter from which creation unfolds. I am summarizing from memory, so check the text inside. The key idea is that the first light is part of the foundational layer of existence, and that the luminaries later are a localized, ordered expression of it.

### Natural Reading: Light Without a Source

Some commentators, such as **Ibn Ezra** and others, read the text as describing light existing in a diffused form. The sun's role on day four is to concentrate and regulate it. **Rabbi Samson Raphael Hirsch** and others discuss this in terms of the sun being the "bearer" of light, not its origin. I am paraphrasing general approaches here rather than quoting specific lines.

## The Theological Message

Placing light before the sun carries a clear lesson: light, and everything that sustains life, comes from God's word, not from the celestial bodies. In the ancient world the sun and moon were worshipped as gods. The Torah deliberately demotes them to "luminaries" with assigned jobs, even avoiding the names "sun" and "moon" and calling them "the greater light" and "the lesser light" [Genesis 1:16]. Many commentators note this as a polemic against idolatry.

Also, the sun "rules" (*memshelet*) day, but only because God appointed it to do so [Genesis 1:16]. Its authority is delegated.

## The Function of Time

The luminaries' main purpose is *mo'adim* (appointed times). The Jewish calendar depends on the moon's cycle, and **Rashi** on Exodus 12:2 and the sanctification of the new moon connect this to the commandment of *Kiddush HaChodesh*. So the sun and moon are not just lamps; they are the framework for sacred time, Shabbat aside, which is set by creation's count itself.

## Summary of Approaches

- **Hidden light**: the first light was special and was stored away [Chagigah 12a; Rashi on Genesis 1:4].
- **Foundational light**: the first light is part of the basic structure of creation, and the sun is its later ordered vehicle [Ramban].
- **Theological**: the order shows God, not the sun, as the source of light, and teaches against idolatry.

This is a topic where traditional sources offer several views, and the details of the citations above should be checked in the original texts.

answer:
**Genesis 12:5** speaks of "the souls that they had made in Haran" (*ha-nefesh asher asu b'Charan*), and the commentators give two main explanations. The first, from **Rashi** (citing the Midrash), is that these were people Avram and Sarai converted and brought "under the wings of the Shechinah." The second, the *pshat* (plain meaning), is that these were servants whom they acquired, whether by purchase or birth.

## Key Takeaways

- The verb *asu* literally means "made," but it can also mean "acquired," as in "acquired wealth."
- The midrashic reading is that Avraham converted the men and Sarah converted the women, and Scripture credits them as if they had "made" these people.
- The plain reading is that these were slaves and maidservants they acquired.
- Ibn Ezra offers both a "born in the household" and a "purchased" reading, and then cites the view that these were people taught to serve God.

## The Verse

The verse reads: "וַיִּקַּח אַבְרָם אֶת־שָׂרַי אִשְׁתּוֹ וְאֶת־לוֹט בֶּן־אָחִיו וְאֶת־כׇּל־רְכוּשָׁם אֲשֶׁר רָכָשׁוּ וְאֶת־הַנֶּפֶשׁ אֲשֶׁר־עָשׂוּ בְחָרָן" (And Avram took Sarai his wife, and Lot his brother's son, and all their possessions that they had gathered, and the souls that they had made in Haran) [Genesis 12:5].

The word *asu* ("made") is unusual when applied to people. That oddity is what drives the commentators.

## Rashi: Conversion

**Rashi** writes: "אשר עשו בחרן – שֶׁהִכְנִיסָן תַּחַת כַּנְפֵי הַשְּׁכִינָה" (that they brought them under the wings of the Shechinah) [Rashi on Genesis 12:5]. He adds that "Avraham converted the men and Sarah converted the women, and Scripture credits them as if they had made them."

This follows the midrashic tradition, found in *Bereishit Rabbah* (around 39:14), that bringing someone to God is like creating that person. The Talmud expresses a similar idea: one who teaches Torah to another's child is regarded as having begotten him [Sanhedrin 19b]. (These parallels come from my own knowledge, not the retrieved sources.)

## Rashi's Pshat: Servants

Rashi then adds that "the plain meaning of the verse" is "slaves and maidservants that they acquired." He supports this with other uses of *asah* meaning "acquire":

- "עָשָׂה אֵת כָּל הַכָּבֹד הַזֶּה" (he has made all this wealth) [Genesis 31:1]
- "וְיִשְׂרָאֵל עֹשֶׂה חָיִל" (and Israel does valiantly or acquires wealth) [Numbers 24:18]

In Rashi's words, this is "לְשׁוֹן קוֹנֶה וְכוֹנֵס," an expression of acquiring and gathering.

## Ibn Ezra: Several Options

**Ibn Ezra** first explains *rekhusham* as their livestock (*mikneh*), comparing "for their substance was great" [Genesis 13:6] [Ibn Ezra on Genesis 12:5].

On *ha-nefesh*, he offers these possibilities [Ibn Ezra on Genesis 12:5]:

- Servants born in the household (*yelidei bayit*).
- *Asu* meaning "acquired," as in "עשה לי את החיל הזה" (has gotten me this wealth) [Deuteronomy 8:17].
- Others say these were souls whom Avram and Sarai taught the truth, to serve God.

## Why the Disagreement?

The tension is between two readings of the same word. If *asu* means "acquired," the verse is simply listing their household property. But the Torah chose "souls" (*nefesh*) rather than "servants" (*avadim*), and the verb *asu* rather than *kanu* (bought). That choice suggests something more, which is why the midrash reads it as spiritual creation.

The two readings are not necessarily mutually exclusive. Many read the servants as people who were also brought into Avraham's faith.

## Connection to Avraham's Mission

The conversion reading fits Avraham's role as a teacher of monotheism. It also fits the blessing "וְנִבְרְכוּ בְךָ כֹּל מִשְׁפְּחֹת הָאֲדָמָה" (and all the families of the earth shall be blessed through you) [Genesis 12:3]. Avraham begins his outreach even before arriving in Canaan.

answer:
Creation opens with an unexpected idea. God makes a world that is deliberately unfinished and then hands the finishing to us. The Torah's first letter, the hidden light, and the diminished moon all point to a Creator who builds in gaps for human partnership.

## Key Takeaways

- The Torah begins with the letter *bet* (ב), closed on three sides and open only toward the front, which teaches us to look forward rather than speculate about what came before.
- Light appears on Day 1, three days before the sun, so the first light was not a natural phenomenon but something spiritual.
- The Talmud says God asked for atonement for shrinking the moon, which suggests that even Creation involves tension.
- The Torah ends the story of Creation with "asher bara Elokim la'asot", "which God created *to make*", implying that humans complete the work.

## The Crazy Part: A Torah That Starts With a Closed Letter

The Torah opens: "בְּרֵאשִׁית בָּרָא אֱלֹהִים אֵת הַשָּׁמַיִם וְאֵת הָאָרֶץ" ("In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth") [Genesis 1:1]. The first letter is a *bet* (ב), which is closed on the top, bottom, and back, and open only to the front.

**Bereishit Rabbah 1:10** reads this as a message. The letter's shape is a boundary on speculation. This echoes the Mishnah's warning against investigating what is above, below, before, and after [Chagigah 11b]. The Torah's opening letter tells us to face forward and ask what we should do with the world, not what came before it.

## Light Before the Sun

God says "יְהִי אוֹר", "Let there be light" [Genesis 1:3], but the luminaries are only placed in the sky on Day 4. So what was the light of Day 1?

The Talmud says it was a special light by which Adam could see "from one end of the world to the other." God saw that the wicked would misuse it, so He hid it away for the righteous [Chagigah 12a]. The Torah itself has a hidden layer, and much of its light is concealed until we earn it.

## The Moon and God's "Atonement"

This passage is the wildest in the tradition. The Talmud says the moon complained that two kings cannot share one crown. God told it to make itself smaller [Chullin 60b]. The moon was upset, so God consoled it. According to the Talmud, God then said, "Bring an atonement for Me for having diminished the moon." This is connected to the Rosh Chodesh goat offering, which is described as "to Hashem" [Numbers 28:15].

The idea is that even the Creator's act of limiting something has a cost. Creation requires contraction and compromise, and the moon's phases, waxing and waning, are a built-in reminder.

## "Tohu Vavohu": The World Starts Unfinished

"וְהָאָרֶץ הָיְתָה תֹהוּ וָבֹהוּ" ("And the earth was formless and void") [Genesis 1:2]. **Rashi** explains that *tohu* means astonishment: a person would be amazed at its emptiness. The world began as raw potential.

The ending of the account gives the purpose. Shabbat comes "אֲשֶׁר בָּרָא אֱלֹהִים לַעֲשׂוֹת", "which God created *to make*" [Genesis 2:3]. Bereishit Rabbah 11:6 reads this to mean that Creation was left for humanity to repair and complete. This idea was later developed as *tikkun olam*.

## Putting It Together

- The closed *bet* says: don't obsess over the past, move forward.
- The hidden light says: there is more here than meets the eye.
- The diminished moon says: greatness has a price and Creation involves tension.
- *Tohu vavohu* and "la'asot" say: you are part of the process.

A note on sources: the retrieved passages here included only the text of Genesis 1:1 and the start of the parasha. The Rashi, Midrash, and Talmud references above come from my broader knowledge of the tradition, so check them inside before quoting them publicly.
