answer:
## Direct Answer

The opening Mishnah of Berakhot (2a) asks, *"Me'eimatai korin et Shema be'arvit?"* (from when may one recite the evening Shema?). It answers "from the time the priests enter to eat their *terumah*," which is nightfall, and then records three views on when the time ends. Rabbi Eliezer says the end of the first watch, the Sages say midnight, and Rabban Gamliel says dawn. The Gemara then asks why the tractate begins with the evening and why it uses the priests' eating as the marker.

## Key Takeaways

- The start of the evening Shema is tied to the time a *tevul yom* (a priest who immersed but awaits nightfall) may eat terumah, which is nightfall.
- The three views on the end of the time are: the first watch (R. Eliezer), midnight (the Sages), and dawn (Rabban Gamliel).
- Rabban Gamliel's sons' story shows that the Sages' "midnight" is a protective fence, while the mitzvah actually lasts until dawn.
- The Ibn Ezra on Leviticus 22:7 shows that the "sunset" of the verse is the biblical source for the terumah marker.
- Reciting Shema before nightfall is a long-debated practice, discussed in the responsum from your retrieved sources.

## The Mishnah (Berakhot 2a)

**Hebrew:** מֵאֵימָתַי קוֹרִין אֶת שְׁמַע בָּעֲרָבִין? מִשָּׁעָה שֶׁהַכֹּהֲנִים נִכְנָסִים לֶאֱכוֹל בִּתְרוּמָתָן
**Translation:** From when do we recite Shema in the evening? From the time the priests enter to eat their terumah.

The Mishnah then gives the three views, quoted in the retrieved passage:

- **Rabbi Eliezer:** until the end of the first watch (*ashmurah*).
- **The Sages:** until midnight (*chatzot*).
- **Rabban Gamliel:** until the pillar of dawn rises (*amud hashachar*).

## The Story of Rabban Gamliel's Sons

His sons returned from a feast and said they had not recited Shema. He answered, "If dawn has not yet risen, you are obligated to recite." He then taught that wherever the Sages said "until midnight," the mitzvah actually lasts until dawn.

The Gemara explains that the Sages set an earlier limit *l'harchik adam min ha'aveira*, to distance a person from transgression. This is a protective fence (*seyag*), so that people do not delay and fall asleep.

## Why the Priests and Terumah?

The Mishnah uses the priests as its time marker rather than simply saying "when the stars appear." The Gemara explains that the Mishnah is also teaching a law about the *tevul yom*, the impure person who has immersed and waits for nightfall.

Ibn Ezra on Leviticus 22:7 addresses the verse "u-va hashemesh ve-taher" (when the sun sets he shall be pure). He notes that the verse never mentions "day," but our Sages received the law that he may not eat until dark. They used the verse as a mnemonic ("the day clears away") [Ibn Ezra on Leviticus 22:7, citing Berakhot 2a].

This ties the Shema's start to a Torah-based, observable moment. It is not an arbitrary hour.

## The Question of Reciting Early

The *Teshuvot Min HaShamayim* 19:1 discusses the common custom of reciting Shema before the stars appear. People rely on repeating the first paragraph before bed. The responsum questions this, because:

- The blessings before and after Shema are then said at the wrong time.
- Shema at the proper time is then said without blessings and with only one paragraph.

Some sages do not recite the blessings with the earlier Shema. The retrieved passage cuts off there, so I cannot say more about its conclusion from the source itself.

## Further Points (from my general knowledge, not the retrieved passages)

- The Gemara continues by asking why the Mishnah begins with the evening. It answers that Scripture's order, "and it was evening and it was morning" (Genesis 1:5), makes the Jewish day begin at night. It also notes that Deuteronomy 6:7 says "when you lie down" before "when you rise."
- Rabbi Eliezer's "watch" depends on a discussion on 3a about how many watches the night has.
- Halachically, the accepted practice follows the Sages' midnight as the preferred time, with dawn as the outer limit after the fact (*bedieved*), as ruled in the Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim 235.

If you tell me which part you want to learn (the Gemara's question, the watches, or the tevul yom), I can go through it line by line, in Hebrew if you prefer.

For personal guidance, consult your local rabbi or posek.

answer:
The retrieved sources don't include the Tosafos you mention, so I can't confirm its exact wording. The story of Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Yosei seeing the *paroches* (curtain) in Rome also appears, as far as I recall, in Yoma 57a, not 58a. Assuming Tosafos does raise the first-Temple possibility, the likeliest answer is that Temple items taken by Bavel did not stay there, and Rome later inherited them through the successive empires.

## Key Takeaways

- The Babylonian exile did not necessarily end the objects' journey, because Bavel's treasures passed to Persia, then Greece, then Rome.
- The Tanakh itself says Temple vessels remained in foreign royal treasuries, and only some were returned under Cyrus.
- The simple reading is that this is the Second Temple *paroches*, taken by Titus, as in [Gittin 56b].
- The first-Temple view would need to explain how an item survived and traveled, which is a historical-transmission question rather than a halachic one.

## The Simple Reading (*Pshat*)

Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Yosei lived in the second century CE, after the Churban. Titus plundered the Second Temple, and [Gittin 56b] describes him entering the Holy of Holies and slashing the *paroches* with a sword: "וְנָטַל סַיִיף וְגִידֵּר אֶת הַפָּרוֹכֶת" ("he took a sword and cut through the curtain"). There "a miracle occurred and blood spurted out." Blood stains on the *paroches* in Rome fit this account naturally.

## How the First Temple Could Be Possible

Your question assumes that what Bavel took stayed in Bavel. The Tanakh suggests otherwise, though this is from my own knowledge and not the retrieved passages:

- **Bavel took the vessels.** Kings II 25 and Jeremiah 52 describe Nebuchadnezzar carrying off the Temple vessels. Chronicles II 36:18 says he took "all the vessels of the house of God."
- **They stayed in royal hands.** In Daniel 5, Belshazzar drinks from the Temple vessels. [Megillah 12a] also describes Achashverosh using Temple vessels at his feast.
- **Only some were returned.** Ezra 1:7-11 records Cyrus returning the vessels, but a *paroches* is not mentioned. Some items could have been kept or lost.
- **Empires inherited the treasuries.** Persia fell to Alexander and Greece, and the Greek successor kingdoms later fell to Rome. Royal treasures moved with each conquest, so Rome could plausibly have held first-Temple items.

## The Blood Stains

The Gemara says the drops were from Yom Kippur blood sprinkling. That fits either Temple, since the High Priest sprinkled before the *paroches* area in both. The blood can't distinguish between them, and the debate would turn on tradition about the object itself.

## Caveat

If you can share the text of the Tosafos, I can address its reasoning directly. It may answer differently, for example by saying the first-Temple *paroches* was not among the items Bavel took, or by relying on a specific tradition about the stains. I am offering plausible resolutions, not Tosafos' own explanation.

answer:
Your question is open-ended, so I'm reading it as: what sources does the Talmud draw on, and what sources appear in the passages retrieved here? The Talmud rests on the **Written Torah**, the **Mishnah** and **baraitot** (Tannaitic teachings outside the Mishnah), and earlier midrashic collections. The retrieved passages show two examples: the Haggada's "four sons" passage, which has parallels in the Jerusalem Talmud and earlier rabbinic literature, and Kiddushin 26a, which grounds acquisition of land in verses.

## Key Takeaways

- The Talmud's sources are Tanakh, Mishnah, baraitot, and Tannaitic midrash (such as the Mekhilta, Sifra, and Sifrei).
- Talmudic rulings are typically anchored in a verse, as in Kiddushin 26a, where land acquisition is derived from Scripture.
- The Haggada's "four sons" text emerged from centuries of editing, with earlier "drafts" in Mishnaic-era sources and the Jerusalem Talmud [Jonathan Sacks Haggadah, "The Wicked Son: What Does He Say?"].
- Some early sources mention only the wicked son, not all four [Jonathan Sacks Haggadah].
- Please tell me which topic or passage you meant, and I can be more precise.

## General Sources of the Talmud (from my background knowledge)

- **Tanakh:** the Written Torah, Prophets, and Writings supply the proof-texts (*derashot*) for halachic and aggadic claims.
- **Mishnah:** the Gemara is built as a commentary on it.
- **Baraitot and Tosefta:** Tannaitic traditions not included in the Mishnah, often cited with "*tanu rabbanan*" (our Rabbis taught).
- **Halakhic midrashim:** the Mekhilta (Exodus), Sifra (Leviticus), and Sifrei (Numbers and Deuteronomy).
- **Amoraic traditions:** statements of the Amoraim, preserved in both the Babylonian and Jerusalem Talmuds.

## From the Retrieved Sources

### Four Sons: Earlier "Drafts"

According to the Sacks essay, the Haggada's text was the result of "several centuries of debate and a long process of editing." There are "sources that read like early drafts" in Mishnaic-period writings and the Jerusalem Talmud. Two of these refer only to the wicked son. This suggests the four-son structure developed over time from earlier traditions.

From my own knowledge, the four sons are tied to the four verses where the Torah speaks of a child's question: Exodus 12:26, Exodus 13:8, Exodus 13:14, and Deuteronomy 6:20. The parallel passages are found in the **Mekhilta de-Rabbi Yishmael** (Bo, Masekhta de-Pischa 18) and **Jerusalem Talmud Pesachim 10:4**. Check the exact wording of each before relying on my citations here.

### Kiddushin 26a: Land and *Hazakah*

The **Daf Shevui** commentary notes that the Talmud cites two sources showing that land is acquired by dwelling on it [Daf Shevui, Kiddushin 26a]. These verses concern land seized in war, which is treated as ownerless, so Israelites take possession by living there.

The commentary also stresses that *hazakah* (acquisition by presumption of ownership through use) does not mean you can take land by squatting. Elsewhere, the claimant must also assert that he bought it but lost the documents. *Hazakah* creates a presumption of ownership.

answer:
The shortest masechet in the Mishnah, and in the Shas as printed, is ***Kinnim*** (קִנִּים, "nests"). It has only 3 chapters and 15 mishnayot. It appears in **Seder Kodashim**, and it has no Gemara in either Talmud.

## Key Takeaways

- **Kinnim** is the shortest masechet, with 3 chapters and 15 mishnayot (from my general knowledge, not the retrieved passages).
- It deals with bird offerings (*chatat ha'of* and *olat ha'of*) brought by those of limited means, and with cases of mixed-up offerings.
- In the Bavli it takes up only a few pages near the end of Seder Kodashim (roughly 22b-25a).
- Other very short tractates are Middot (5 chapters) and Tamid (7 chapters), but Kinnim is shorter than both.
- Do not confuse it with "*seder kanim*" in Ben Yehoyada on Yoma 38a, which refers to the supports for the showbread.

## Detailed Answer

### What Kinnim covers
Kinnim discusses the bird offerings of the poor and the laws of *chovah* (obligatory) versus *nedarim* and *nedavot* (vows and freewill offerings). The retrieved Mishnah gives the basic procedure: "The sin offering of a bird is done below, and the sin offering of an animal above. The burnt offering of a bird is done above, and that of an animal below. If one switched them, it is invalid." [Mishnah Kinnim]

It also distinguishes a *neder* (a vow: "I take upon myself a burnt offering") from a *nedava* (a freewill offering: "This is a burnt offering"). In a neder, the person remains liable if the animal dies or is stolen. [Mishnah Kinnim]

### Kinnim in the Gemara literature
Kinnim has no Gemara in the Bavli or the Yerushalmi. In the Bavli it is printed with the Mishnah and commentaries only, as are Middot. Other sources still cite it. **Tosafot** on Kiddushin 13b begins "האשה שהביאה חטאתה ומתה" ("A woman who brought her sin offering and died"). It notes "משנה היא במס' קנים" ("it is a Mishnah in Tractate Kinnim") and uses it to raise a question about the order of offerings. [Tosafot, Kiddushin 13b]

### Other short tractates
- **Middot**, on the measurements of the Temple, has 5 chapters.
- **Tamid**, on the daily offering, has 7 chapters.
- **Orlah** is also short, but it is longer than Kinnim.

The precise counts and page numbers come from my general knowledge, not the retrieved passages, so check them in a printed Shas.

answer:
Understanding a *hava aminah* (the initial assumption) and the *maskanah* (the conclusion) in a Talmudic sugya shows what the Gemara was worried about and why the final halacha is what it is. The distance between the two is where the concepts live: each initial assumption is a path a reasonable person might take, and its rejection reveals the principle that blocks it. Studying this movement turns a sugya from a list of rulings into a map of legal logic.

## Key Takeaways

- The *hava aminah* is not an error but a serious option, and the Gemara's rejection of it defines the boundaries of a concept.
- Each shift from *hava aminah* to *maskanah* usually exposes a hidden distinction or principle (a *sevara*).
- Asking "why did the Gemara need to say this?" teaches why a ruling is needed and what it excludes.
- Rishonim and Acharonim often build entire systems (*yesodot*) from the gap between the two.
- This method is a source of *chiddush* (novel insight), though it must be applied carefully against the text.

*Note: No specific sources were retrieved for this question, so everything below comes from my general knowledge of Torah tradition.*

## What the Terms Mean

*Hava aminah* (הוה אמינא, "I would have thought") is the Gemara's first understanding of a verse, Mishnah, or case. *Maskanah* (מסקנא, "conclusion") is where the sugya ends up after challenges, *kushyot* (difficulties), and *terutzim* (resolutions).

Phrases like "*Mahu d'teima*" (you might have thought) and "*Mashma lan*" (it teaches us) often mark this movement. The Gemara asks, "*Mai ka mashma lan?*" (What is this teaching us?), forcing us to name the possibility that the statement is meant to exclude.

## Why the *Hava Aminah* Matters

### 1. It defines the boundaries of a rule

If a Mishnah rules in an unusual case, we ask why it did not simply rule in the common one. The *hava aminah* identifies the logic that would have led elsewhere. Once we see which logic was rejected, we understand which principle won.

### 2. It reveals a hidden machloket in *sevara*

Often the *hava aminah* reflects a legitimate line of reasoning that another Tannaitic or Amoraic opinion actually holds. A rejected assumption in one sugya may be the accepted view of a different authority elsewhere. Seeing this lets us connect sugyot across Shas.

### 3. It explains why a verse or Mishnah is needed

Many *derashot* depend on this. A verse is "needed" only if, without it, we might have assumed otherwise. The *hava aminah* shows which assumption the verse is correcting, and so what its scope is.

### 4. It trains precision in distinguishing cases

When a Gemara says "you might have thought X, so it teaches us Y," the exercise shows how close two cases can be and what small factor separates them, such as *ma'aseh* vs. *machshavah*, or *gufo* vs. *damav*.

## How Later Authorities Use It

**Rishonim** such as Tosafot regularly ask, "*Hava aminah* of what?" to pin down exactly what the Gemara was assuming. Their answer often changes the interpretation of the whole sugya.

**Acharonim** and the **Brisker** approach go further, defining the *hava aminah* and the *maskanah* as two different *chalot* (legal categories) or *havanot* (conceptual definitions). Here the gap becomes a full analytical tool: what is the nature of the thing such that one might have thought X, yet it turns out to be Y?

## A Practical Method

- **Identify** the exact point where the Gemara says "I would have thought."
- **Reconstruct** the reasoning behind it as strongly as possible.
- **Locate** the specific question or verse that overturns it.
- **Name** the principle that the *maskanah* establishes.
- **Look for parallels** elsewhere in Shas where the same principle appears.

## A Caution

Not every *hava aminah* is a deep concept. Sometimes it is simply the Gemara's way of clarifying a text. Also, a *hava aminah* that was rejected in one sugya does not automatically become invalid halachically in another context. The conclusion applies to the case at hand, and the principle must be tested against each sugya before it is extended.

Learning this way also reflects a broader Torah value: that the path of study, with its false starts and corrections, is itself part of Torah, as the Gemara preserves the arguments that did not prevail alongside those that did (see [Eruvin 13b], where the *halacha* follows Beit Hillel partly because they cited the opposing view as well as their own).

answer:
The primary Gemara discussion of **ma'aser behema** (the tithe of cattle, sheep, and goats) is in **Masechet Bekhorot**, in the ninth chapter, which begins around daf 53b and is named for this topic. The Torah source is Leviticus 27:32-33, and the New Year for the animal tithe is discussed in Rosh Hashanah. The retrieved passages here (Deut. 14:22, Gen. 28:22, Mal. 3:10) concern produce tithes and tithing generally, not animals, so what follows comes from my own knowledge of the tradition.

## Key Takeaways

- **Bekhorot, chapter 9** (roughly 53b-61a) is the main sugya, building on Mishnah Bekhorot 9.
- The Torah source is **Leviticus 27:32-33**: every tenth animal passing under the rod is holy.
- **Rosh Hashanah** (Mishnah 1:1 and the Gemara on it) discusses when the tithing "year" begins and ends.
- Related laws appear in the Torah's laws of *kodashim* (sacred offerings), such as *temura* (substitution), and in the Rambam's code.

## The Torah Source

Leviticus 27:32-33 says: "וְכָל־מַעְשַׂר בָּקָר וָצֹאן כֹּל אֲשֶׁר־יַעֲבֹר תַּחַת הַשָּׁבֶט הָעֲשִׂירִי יִהְיֶה־קֹּדֶשׁ לַה׳" ("And every tithe of herd or flock, whatever passes under the rod, the tenth shall be holy to the Lord"). Unlike produce tithes, which go to Levites and the poor, this tithe is itself a sacrifice, eaten by its owners after the blood and fats are offered.

## Bekhorot, Chapter 9

The chapter opens with Mishnah Bekhorot 9:1, which says ma'aser behema applies in the Temple's presence and absence, in Israel and abroad, and to unconsecrated animals. The Gemara covers:

- Which animals are obligated, and how kosher and non-kosher animals are treated.
- How animals born within the year are gathered into a pen and brought out one by one.
- The "rod" (*shevet*), which marks the tenth animal with red paint.
- Whether a mistake in counting still leaves the tenth animal sanctified.
- The status of the ninth and eleventh animals if they are mistakenly called "tenth."
- How the tithe differs from the firstborn (*bekhor*), including the rule against redemption and the prohibition on selling it.

## Rosh Hashanah

Mishnah Rosh Hashanah 1:1 lists the "new years" of the year. The Tannaim dispute the date for the animal tithe, **1 Elul** or **1 Tishrei** (Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon). The Gemara on that mishnah (around 2a and 8a) explains the reasoning and the practical consequences. Animals born before and after the cutoff cannot be combined into a single tithing.

## Related Sources

- **Temurah** discusses animals substituted into sanctified status.
- **Sifra** (Behar-Bechukotai) is the halachic midrash on Leviticus 27.
- **Rambam, Hilchot Bekhorot** (chapters 6-7) codifies the laws in a clear structure.

For personal guidance, consult your local rabbi or posek.

I can't say with certainty which side holds which view, because the retrieved passages (the *goses* laws and the stillborn child) don't contain this dispute. The likely crux is whether calling a non-Jew or slave a "righteous man" who lived by his own labor is true or appropriate, or whether it is flattery or inaccurate. What follows is my own reconstruction from related sources, not a quotation of Semachot.

## Key Takeaways

- The retrieved sources do not include this dispute, so the explanation below comes from my general knowledge, not the provided texts.
- I cannot reliably assign the lenient and strict positions to the Sages and Rabbi Yehuda without the text in front of me.
- The likely issues are the status of non-Jews and slaves in mourning law, whether a non-Jew can be called "righteous," and whether the phrase "his own labor" suits a slave.
- Please check the passage in a full edition of Semachot (e.g., Higger) before relying on any attribution.

## What the Retrieved Sources Do Say

Semachot 1 opens with the laws of the *goses* (a dying person), who is treated as a living person in every respect [Semachot 1]. The other retrieved source, Sefer Puah, rules that a stillborn child is not mourned or eulogized, based on the Rambam and Semachot 1 [Sefer Puah, Pregnancy and Birth, Miscarriages 63:48, citing Rambam and Semachot 1].

Both sources show that Semachot 1 decides who is owed mourning and eulogy. That is the framework for your question, but neither passage mentions the non-Jew or slave dispute.

## Likely Reasons for the Dispute

**1. The status of slaves in mourning.** The Talmud teaches that one does not stand in the mourners' line or offer formal condolences for slaves. The story of Rabban Gamliel mourning his slave Tavi is presented as an exception [Berakhot 16b]. A eulogy for a slave is therefore already a debated honor.

**2. Calling a non-Jew "righteous."** Tannaitic sources debate whether the righteous of the nations merit a share in the World to Come [Tosefta Sanhedrin 13:2]. Whether the title *tzaddik* may be applied to a non-Jew could depend on that question. A more lenient view might allow it as *darkei shalom* (maintaining peaceful relations).

**3. "Who lived by the labor of his own hands."** For a slave, this phrase is arguably inaccurate, since a slave's earnings belong to his master [Gittin 12a; Pesachim 88b]. A slave would not have "eaten from his own labor" in the usual sense. This may be the reason for a stricter position on slaves, though that is my inference.

**4. Truthfulness in eulogies.** The Sages generally hold that one eulogizes the deceased only with true praise [see Ketubot 17a on eulogizing as a matter of honoring the deceased]. A formula that fits a free, self-supporting person may not suit others.

I recommend checking the passage in Semachot directly, along with a commentary such as the Gra or the Meiri's treatment of Berakhot 16b. If you can share the text you are looking at, I can walk through the exact wording.

answer:
The Yissachar-Zevulun partnership (one tribe learning Torah, the other supporting it through commerce) has no explicit Talmudic passage that states it as a formal arrangement. Its basis lies in the Torah's blessings of the two tribes (Genesis 49, Deuteronomy 33), the Midrash, and the later halachic literature. The Talmud does contain related ideas: supporting Torah scholars, the merit of commerce that sustains Torah, and the idea of sharing in a scholar's reward.

## Key Takeaways

- The Talmud never names a "Yissachar-Zevulun contract" as such; the model is built from the Torah verses, Midrash, and later authorities.
- Talmudic sources do praise supporting Torah scholars and describe their supporters as sharing in the reward (e.g., Ketubot 111b, Berachot 34b).
- Other Talmudic passages speak of Torah and business as complementary (e.g., Kiddushin 82a, Berachot 35b).
- The explicit partnership model is found in Midrash (Bereishit Rabbah 99, Sifrei on Deuteronomy 33), Rashi, and later Rishonim and Acharonim.
- Practical halacha has to be sorted out carefully, and my citations below come largely from memory rather than the retrieved passages.

## Source Basis in the Retrieved Text

The retrieved **Zohar, Mishpatim 3:200** describes Yissachar and Zevulun as "two thighs" (שְׁתֵּי יְרֵכַיִם), the place from which the true prophets draw nourishment. It cites "And of the sons of Yissachar, men who understood the times" (I Chronicles 12:33) and "Rejoice, Zevulun, in your going out" (Deuteronomy 33:18). This is kabbalistic and pairs the tribes, but it does not describe a business arrangement. The Ramban passage retrieved (Genesis 37:3) concerns Yaakov's love for Yosef and is not relevant to this question.

## The Scriptural Foundation

In Deuteronomy 33:18, Moses blesses them together: "Rejoice, Zevulun, in your going out, and Yissachar, in your tents." **Rashi** (ad loc., drawing on the Midrash) explains that Zevulun went out to trade while Yissachar sat in the tent of Torah, and that Zevulun's profits supported Yissachar. The **Targum Yonatan** and **Midrash Tanchuma** (Vayechi) develop this. **Bereishit Rabbah 99:9** says that Zevulun would trade and feed Yissachar, and that Zevulun's name is mentioned first because Yissachar's Torah study was made possible through him.

## Talmudic Parallels

### Sharing in reward
- **Ketubot 111b** (as I recall it): "Whoever brings a gift to a Torah scholar, it is as if he offered first fruits." A related passage there asks how one may cleave to the Divine Presence, and answers: by marrying one's daughter to a scholar, doing business for scholars, or benefiting scholars from one's property.
- **Berachot 34b** speaks of the exalted place of those who support scholars: the prophets prophesied only for one who marries his daughter to a scholar, does business for a scholar, or benefits a scholar with his property.
- **Sotah 21a** and **Pesachim 53b** also discuss the standing of those who support Torah. Pesachim 53b mentions the scholar-supporter relationship in connection with the reward of a person who gives to scholars.

### The Torah and work balance
- **Berachot 35b** records the dispute between Rabbi Yishmael ("combine Torah with the way of the world") and Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai (who held that others will do one's work for him if he devotes himself to Torah). Abaye said that many followed Rabbi Yishmael and succeeded, while those who followed Rabbi Shimon did not.
- **Kiddushin 82a** and **Avot 2:2** (Rabban Gamliel's son, Yehuda HaNasi) praise Torah together with a worldly occupation.

### Supporting the scholar-partner
- **Pesachim 53b** and related Rishonim describe a person who supports Torah as being "close to" the scholar's merit.
- **Bava Batra 8a** discusses the exemption of scholars from taxes, showing the community's recognition of the scholar's role.

## Later Halachic Development

- **Rashi on Deuteronomy 33:18** and **Rashi on Genesis 49:13** state the model clearly.
- **Rambam, Hilchot Talmud Torah 3:10** strongly opposes scholars taking money from the public to support their Torah study, and calls it a desecration of God's name. This is the major counterpoint to the later partnership model.
- **Rema, Yoreh De'ah 246:1** (citing the Tur and Rashba) permits scholars to receive support and recognizes the agreements between merchants and scholars. **Rabbi Moshe Isserles** is among those who ruled leniently here.
- **Rabbi Yosef Karo, Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh De'ah 246:1** cites Rambam's view. The Rema quotes the Yissachar-Zevulun arrangement to justify support.
- The **Rashba**, **Rivash**, and **Rabbeinu Yonah** discuss supporting scholars. Some of these view the supporter as sharing in reward.

Whether the partner actually shares equally in the reward is itself debated, and many authorities, including the **Chafetz Chaim**, noted that the merchant's share depends on the arrangement and sincerity. Some say the full reward is shared; others say the scholar's reward is not reduced but the supporter receives a substantial portion. I am not certain of the details of each source here, so verify them inside.

## Underlying Tension

The disagreement turns on two principles. One is that Torah should not be used as a "spade to dig with" (Avot 4:5), which is Rambam's concern. The other is that supporting Torah is itself a mitzvah, and communities need full-time scholars, which is the position of the Rema and others.

For personal guidance, consult your local rabbi or posek.

answer:
The Mishnah contains **525 perakim** (chapters) across its 63 tractates, according to the standard printed division. This is the commonly cited total, and the count is based on my general knowledge rather than the retrieved passages, which do not state a total.

## Key Takeaways

- The standard count is 525 perakim in 63 masechtot, organized in 6 *sedarim* (orders).
- Some counts differ slightly (for example 524 or 523), depending on how Bava Kamma, Bava Metzia, and Bava Batra, or Makkot, are treated.
- The chapter divisions are later than the Mishnah's composition and vary between manuscripts.
- The Yerushalmi's manuscripts and editions show variation in the Mishnah chapters.

## Breakdown by Seder

These are the standard figures:

- **Zera'im** (11 tractates): 74 perakim
- **Mo'ed** (12 tractates): 88 perakim
- **Nashim** (7 tractates): 71 perakim
- **Nezikin** (10 tractates): 73 perakim
- **Kodashim** (11 tractates): 91 perakim
- **Tohorot** (12 tractates): 126 perakim

Together these total 523 by this tally, which is why you will see different sums. The commonly quoted figure of 525 (or 524) depends on whether certain tractates are split or merged, and on how the divisions are counted in different editions. I would treat the exact per-seder numbers above as approximate and check them against a printed Mishnah if you need precision.

## Why the Numbers Vary

The retrieved sources show that chapter divisions are an external, later layer. [Introduction to Tosefta, Introductions to Tannaitic Literature] says that the division into chapters in the Tosefta "is certainly later than its composition," and that manuscripts differ widely. Copyists tried to match the Tosefta's chapters to the Mishnah's but did not succeed. The same source notes that the division is "external," as it is in the Mishnah. As an example, Nezikin was divided into three *bavot* of 11 chapters each, which made the chapter "HaShutafin" part of chapter 11 of Bava Metzia.

This shows that the divisions of the Mishnah into chapters are not always rooted in the original editorial structure. That is part of why the totals differ.

## Manuscript Variation in the Yerushalmi

The retrieved sources also show how fluid the Mishnah chapter text is in the Yerushalmi tradition:

- [Addenda to Variae Lectiones for the Yerushalmi, Yevamot 258] notes that a manuscript copied two Mishnah chapters (15 and 16) consecutively.
- [Addenda, Niddah 67] explains that the copyist did not notice the loss of the end of chapter 15 and the beginning of chapter 16 of Yevamot. He did not know where chapter 16 began, so he copied the two chapters one after the other.
- [Ohr LaYesharim on Jerusalem Talmud Taanit and Moed Katan, Introduction] notes that the Academy of the Hebrew Language edition did not copy the Mishnah chapters from the manuscript at the head of each Yerushalmi chapter. The Mishnah text used for the commentary therefore does not fully match the manuscript.

For personal guidance on any practical learning schedule (such as Mishnah Yomit), consult your local rabbi or posek.

answer:
The man is **unnamed** in the Gemara. The story appears in **Sanhedrin 75a**, and he **died** rather than be allowed a forbidden remedy. The retrieved sources don't cover this passage, so what follows comes from my knowledge of the Talmud.

## Key Takeaways

- The Gemara says only "a certain man" (*ish echad*), without naming him.
- He became deathly ill from desire for a woman, and the doctors said only relations with her would cure him.
- The Sages refused, ruling "let him die and she not be given to him" [Sanhedrin 75a].
- They also rejected lesser cures, such as her standing before him unclothed or speaking with him behind a fence.
- The Gemara gives different reasons for the refusal, including concern for her dignity and for the moral standards of the community.

## The Story

A man fixed his eyes on a woman, and his heart was consumed with longing until he became gravely ill. The doctors said he would not recover until she had relations with him. The Sages answered: "Let him die, and she shall not be given to him" [Sanhedrin 75a].

The doctors then suggested easier alternatives: that she stand unclothed before him, or that she speak with him from behind a fence. The Sages rejected both. In the Gemara's account he died.

## Why Did the Sages Refuse?

This passage is a central source for the principle of *yehareg v'al ya'avor* (be killed rather than transgress) as it applies to forbidden relations. Even though *pikuach nefesh* (saving a life) overrides almost every commandment, it does not override *arayot*, the prohibitions on forbidden relations.

- **Rav Yaakov bar Idi** says the woman was married to someone else.
- **Rav Acha bar Chanina** says she was unmarried.

The Gemara asks why they would not permit marriage if she was unmarried. The answer given is concern for her honor, so that Jewish daughters not be treated casually. The Gemara also rejects the "fence" conversation, which shows how seriously the Sages treated the standards of modesty and the dignity of the community.

## Halachic Note

Poskim such as the **Rambam** and the **Shulchan Aruch** codify this rule: even in life-threatening illness, forbidden relations are not permitted as a cure.

For personal guidance, consult your local rabbi or posek.

answer:
The Gemara in Gittin 59b raises the question of why the Mishnah's list of *mipnei darkhei shalom* (for the sake of the ways of peace) enactments is needed, since the whole Torah is for the sake of peace. It cites Proverbs 3:17, "Its ways are ways of pleasantness, and all its paths are peace." The Gemara's point is that the Torah as a whole aims at peace, yet these specific rabbinic enactments are singled out because they respond to a concrete risk of strife, not just the general ideal.

## Key Takeaways

- The Gemara cites Proverbs 3:17 to show that peace is the overall purpose of the Torah's laws [Gittin 59b].
- The Mishnah's list covers specific takkanot (rabbinic enactments) designed to prevent concrete conflict [Gittin 59a].
- The general ideal of peace does not erase the distinction between these enactments and ordinary mitzvot.
- Examples include supporting non-Jewish poor, visiting their sick, and burying their dead [Gittin 61a].
- Explanations of the exact relationship between the general and specific uses of "peace" are partly my own, drawn from standard commentary themes, not from the retrieved passages.

## The Context in Gittin

The Mishnah opens, "These are things that were said *mipnei darkhei shalom*: a Kohen reads first, then a Levi, then a Yisrael; an *eiruv* may be made in an old house..." [Gittin 59a]. These are rules whose basis is avoiding quarrels, not a direct biblical command.

The Gemara then asks a challenge: "כל התורה כולה נמי מפני דרכי שלום היא" (the entire Torah is also for the sake of the ways of peace), as it is written, "דרכיה דרכי נועם וכל נתיבותיה שלום" (Her ways are ways of pleasantness, and all her paths are peace) [Gittin 59b, citing Proverbs 3:17]. In other words, if everything in the Torah is for peace, what is special about this list?

## What the Verse Means (Pshat)

Proverbs 3:17 describes the Torah (wisdom) as a path of pleasantness and peace. The verse is a statement about the Torah's character and aims: following it should produce harmony, in society and within a person. It is not a legal rule.

## How the Gemara Distinguishes the Specific Cases

The Gemara proceeds to differentiate (this is the general thrust, which I am supplying from my knowledge of the sugya, not from the retrieved text). The Torah's overall peaceful purpose is one thing. The Mishnah's category is another: laws where, without the rabbinic rule, the din itself might lead to an outcome that provokes hostility, so the Rabbis adjust or add to it explicitly for that reason.

Commentators generally understand that the Torah's peace is the deep, structural purpose. *Darkhei shalom* is a practical, operative criterion that the Rabbis invoke to set a particular rule.

## Examples of Operative *Darkhei Shalom*

- **Non-Jewish poor:** "We do not protest against poor non-Jews gathering *leket*, *shikhecha*, and *peah*, for the sake of peace" [Gittin 61a].
- **Sustaining the needy:** "We sustain the non-Jewish poor along with the Jewish poor, visit their sick, and bury their dead, for the sake of peace" [Gittin 61a].
- **Torah reading order:** A Kohen, then Levi, then Yisrael [Gittin 59a].

These show the idea in action: kindness and fairness toward others are framed as preventing enmity, which is itself an expression of the Torah's aim.

## A Related Theme

Deuteronomy 20:10 commands, "When you approach a city to fight against it, call out to it for peace" [Deuteronomy 20:10]. Even in warfare, the Torah mandates a peace offer first. This is an example of how peace is built into the Torah's structure, not only the rabbinic enactments, and supports the Gemara's broad claim.

## Why This Matters

The statement teaches that halacha is not merely technical. Its ultimate end is a just and harmonious world. Yet the Gemara also keeps the categories distinct, preserving the idea that a specific rabbinic rule made for peace is different from a Torah law whose broader purpose is peace.

For deeper study, look at Rashi and the Tosafot on Gittin 59b, which discuss how the Gemara resolves the challenge.

answer:
A good judge must adjudicate with constant awareness that the stakes are ultimate. The image of a **sword resting between his thighs** (*cherev munachat bein yerkhotav*) and **Gehenna open beneath him** (*Gehinom petucha mi-tachtav*) conveys the danger of corrupting judgment. Your phrasing, "feet together," seems to be a garbled version of "Gehenna beneath him." This is a Rabbinic teaching, not a verse, and it expresses the Torah's demand for *tzedek* (justice) in Deuteronomy 16:18-20.

## Key Takeaways

- The sword and Gehenna dramatize that a judge's decision carries both physical-life-and-death and spiritual consequences.
- The image rests on the Torah's command: "Justice, justice shall you pursue" [Deuteronomy 16:20].
- Judges are warned against perverting judgment, showing favoritism, and taking bribes [Deuteronomy 16:19].
- The Talmud's concern for judicial integrity appears in many places, including the sources on judges in [Ketubot 105a].
- I cannot give you the exact chapter-and-verse source for this wording from the retrieved passages; it comes from my general knowledge of the tradition, so please verify the precise citation.

## The Biblical Foundation

The Torah commands: "You shall appoint judges and officers in all your gates... and they shall judge the people with righteous judgment" (*shofetim ve-shoterim titen lekha... ve-shafetu et ha-am mishpat tzedek*) [Deuteronomy 16:18]. The next verse warns: "You shall not pervert judgment, you shall not show favoritism, and you shall not take a bribe, for a bribe blinds the eyes of the wise and corrupts the words of the righteous" [Deuteronomy 16:19].

The doubled phrase "*Tzedek, tzedek tirdof*" ("Justice, justice shall you pursue") [Deuteronomy 16:20] is tied to national survival: "so that you may live and inherit the land." The verse thus makes judicial integrity a condition of the nation's existence.

## The Meaning of the Image

**The sword.** The sword between the thighs suggests that a wrong ruling is not an abstract error. A judge who wrongly takes money, or worse, life, has in effect wielded a sword against someone. The image also suggests the judge himself is in danger: he lives with the blade at his own body.

**Gehenna beneath him.** This represents divine accountability. Judges stand before the ultimate Judge. This resonates with the teaching that a judge should know "before whom he is judging," and with the verse, "God stands in the congregation of God; in the midst of judges He judges" [Psalms 82:1].

**Why such frightening language?** A judge has power over others, often with no one to check him in the moment. The Rabbis answer this by making the judge internally terrified. They also teach that a judge who judges truthfully becomes a partner with God in creation [Shabbat 10a], so the role is both exalted and perilous.

## Related Talmudic Concern for Judges

The retrieved passage from [Ketubot 105a] discusses disputes about judicial procedure, such as when an oath is administered, and records the opinion of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai. It also mentions the three judges of Jerusalem who handled robbery cases. It shows that the sages treated judging as a serious, carefully regulated office. The same page in the Talmud goes on to a famous discussion of bribery, which expands on the verse "you shall not take a bribe" [Deuteronomy 16:19]. This is my supplement from general knowledge, not from the retrieved excerpt.

## Takeaway for Today

The image serves not only judges in formal courts but anyone who makes decisions affecting others: a person in authority must act with fear of Heaven, humility, and awareness of the consequences. For the exact source and wording, I would recommend checking the passage in the *Tur* and *Shulchan Aruch, Choshen Mishpat* chapter 1, and the Talmudic discussion in Sanhedrin, with your rabbi or a good reference work.

You're asking why the *tzadikim* couldn't carry on the world through mitzvah-driven procreation (*pru urvu*), without any *yetzer*. The Gemara's logic seems to assume otherwise: the drive for permitted and forbidden relations is not two separate faculties.

answer:
The first *mishnah* (teaching) of **Tractate Semachot** teaches that a *goses* (a person in the final throes of death) is a living person in every legal respect. Nothing may be done to hasten death, and the dying person must not be moved or touched in ways that could cause it. The text is often quoted from memory, and wording varies among editions, so I describe its core content and cite parallel sources where I'm confident of them. No sources were retrieved for this question, so everything below comes from my own knowledge of the tradition.

## Key Takeaways

- A *goses* is legally alive "for all matters" (*le-khol devarav*), with the full protections of a living person.
- It is forbidden to do anything that hastens death, such as removing the pillow, moving the person, or closing the eyes as the soul departs.
- The classic image is a flickering lamp that goes out at a touch (a parable attributed to Rabbi Meir; see [Shabbat 151b]).
- Preparations for death and burial may begin only after death is established.
- Tractate Semachot (also called *Evel Rabbati*) is a minor tractate that opens with dying before moving to mourning.

## Plain Meaning (*Pshat*)

The tractate's euphemistic name, *Semachot* ("joys"), covers the laws of death and mourning. It begins at the moment before death, which sets the principle for what follows. Until death is certain, the person is treated as fully alive.

The *mishnah* lists practices that were customary after death, such as binding the jaw, closing the orifices, and placing a cooling object on the abdomen. It forbids them for a *goses*, since any of them might hasten death. Doing so is treated as an act of bloodshed (*shefichut damim*).

## The Lamp Parable

The tradition compares the dying person to a flickering lamp. In the parable Rabbi Meir offers, a lamp about to go out is extinguished by the slightest touch. A person on the edge of death is the same, and a mere touch could be the cause. The parable draws on Proverbs 20:27, "The soul of man is the lamp of God" (*ner Hashem nishmat adam*). The parallel passage is in [Shabbat 151b].

## Why the Ruling Matters

- **Sanctity of life:** Even a moment of remaining life has infinite value, and life is not measured by its expected length. This ties to the principle of *pikuach nefesh* (saving a life).
- **Legal status:** A *goses* retains the legal status of a living person. Killing one is murder in principle, though practical court liability is limited because the victim is already dying (see [Sanhedrin 78a]; [Rambam, Hilchot Rotze'ach 2:7]).
- **Moral caution:** One may not assume that death is inevitable and then act on that assumption.

## Later Halachic Development

The ruling is codified in [Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh De'ah 339:1], which prohibits touching a *goses*. The **Rema** adds that one may remove an obstacle that is delaying the soul's departure, such as noise or salt placed on the tongue, since this removes an impediment rather than hastening death. Permitting this while forbidding active hastening is the key distinction in later discussion. Modern authorities apply it to difficult questions in end-of-life care, and they disagree about specific cases.

For personal guidance, consult your local rabbi or posek.

**מגילת סתרים** נכתבה על ידי האדמור רבי יצחק אייזיק יהודה ייחיאל safrin מקומרנא (1806–1874), בעל "נתיב מצותיך" ו"הכל ביד שמים" ומחבר "זוהר חי". החיבור הוא יומן רוחני אישי. הוא מתאר בו מסעות נפש, חלומות, גילויים וקשרים עם צדיקים, ובהם דודו רבי צבי הירש מזידיטשוב. הוא מזכיר גם התמודדויות עם כוחות הטומאה ועם מחלוקות בעולם החסידות.

אינני בטוח לאיזה "מעשה נורא" אתה מתכוון. יש בחיבור כמה קטעים שמתוארים כך, ואם אנחש אני עלול לבלבל בין סיפורים.

## איך למצוא את הקטע

- חפש באתר בצירוף "מגילת סתרים" עם מילים כמו "מעשה נורא", "חלום", "ראיתי", "נגלה אלי" או "הסטרא אחרא".

- אם אתה זוכר פרט מהסיפור, כמו דמות, מקום או נושא, כתוב לי אותו ואנסה לזהות את הקטע.

## איך אוכל לעזור הלאה

- אם תדביק כאן את הטקסט, אסביר אותו, אנתח את המונחים הקבליים והחסידיים שבו ואקשר אותו לשאר משנתו של האדמור.

answer:
Na parashá desta semana, **Vayishlach** (Gênesis 32:4–36:43), o Zohar lê o encontro de Yaakov com Esav como um confronto entre forças espirituais: a luta de Yaakov com o "homem" é a luta com o anjo-guardião de Esav, e a mudança de nome para *Yisrael* marca a elevação de Yaakov. Os trechos do Zohar recuperados para esta conversa não comentam Vayishlach diretamente, então o conteúdo zohárico abaixo vem do meu conhecimento geral, e indico o que vem das fontes recuperadas.

## Key Takeaways

- O verso inicial, "וַיִּשְׁלַח יַעֲקֹב מַלְאָכִים לְפָנָיו אֶל־עֵשָׂו אָחִיו" ("E Yaakov enviou mensageiros diante de si a Esav, seu irmão") [Gênesis 32:4], abre a porta para a leitura do Zohar sobre anjos e forças espirituais.
- Segundo a tradição, o "homem" que lutou com Yaakov é o anjo celestial de Esav (*sar shel Esav*), e o Zohar aprofunda essa ideia em chave mística.
- O Zohar vê Esav/Edom como a esfera do rigor e do mal (*din* e *sitra achra*), e Yaakov como o equilíbrio de *Tiferet*.
- O Zohar de Beha'alotcha descreve o próprio estudo do Zohar como uma "arca de Noé", um refúgio para poucos [Zohar, Beha'alotcha 16:88].
- A Haftará (Ovadia) fecha o tema do destino de Edom.

## Pshat primeiro: o verso

O texto simples diz que Yaakov, voltando de Charan, envia mensageiros (*malachim*) a Esav, que estava em "Seir, campo de Edom" [Gênesis 32:4]. A palavra *malachim* pode significar "mensageiros" ou "anjos".

Segundo a tradição midráshica, citada por Rashi, eram anjos de verdade [Rashi sobre Gênesis 32:4, citando Bereishit Rabbah 75:4]. Essa ambiguidade é a porta de entrada para a leitura zohárica.

## Temas do Zohar em Vayishlach
*(do meu conhecimento; o Zohar sobre esta parashá está no volume I, aproximadamente 166a–179a, mas confira a paginação numa edição)*

### 1. O medo de Yaakov
O verso diz "וַיִּירָא יַעֲקֹב מְאֹד וַיֵּצֶר לוֹ", "E Yaakov temeu muito e angustiou-se" [Gênesis 32:8]. O Talmud já pergunta por que ele temia, apesar da promessa divina, e responde que talvez o pecado pudesse causar a perda dela [Berachot 4a]. O Zohar desenvolve a ideia de que Yaakov enfrentava uma força espiritual, e não só um irmão de carne e osso.

### 2. A luta com o "homem"
O verso diz "וַיִּוָּתֵר יַעֲקֹב לְבַדּוֹ וַיֵּאָבֵק אִישׁ עִמּוֹ עַד עֲלוֹת הַשָּׁחַר", "E Yaakov ficou só, e um homem lutou com ele até o raiar da aurora" [Gênesis 32:25]. A tradição identifica esse homem como o anjo de Esav [Rashi sobre Gênesis 32:25, citando Bereishit Rabbah 77:3].

O Zohar relaciona isso com a "outra esfera" (*sitra achra*), cuja força se manifesta na escuridão e enfraquece com a luz da manhã. Por isso o anjo pede para partir quando a aurora chega.

### 3. O nervo ciático (*gid hanasheh*) e o nome Yisrael
Yaakov é ferido na coxa, e a Torá proíbe comer o *gid hanasheh* [Gênesis 32:32]. Em chave mística, a ferida mostra que o contato com o mal deixa marcas, mesmo na vitória.

O nome novo, *Yisrael* ("pois lutaste com anjos e homens e prevaleceste"), é lido como elevação a um grau espiritual superior [Gênesis 32:29].

### 4. Esav e Edom
O Zohar associa Edom ao rigor sem misericórdia. Isso se liga à Haftará de Ovadia, que anuncia a queda de Edom e que "a realeza será do Eterno" [Ovadia 1:21]. Os reis de Edom listados no fim da parashá [Gênesis 36:31] são lidos pela Cabalá como uma alusão a mundos que "se quebraram" antes da rearmonização, mas essa leitura é mais desenvolvida em Zohar posterior e no Ari.

## Sobre estudar o Zohar
Os trechos recuperados oferecem uma moldura para o estudo:

- O Zohar de Yitro descreve a estrutura de "rei" e "sacerdote", em cima e embaixo, uma imagem das *sefirot* e de seus reflexos [Zohar, Yitro 1:9-15].
- O Zohar de Beha'alotcha cita Daniel: "וְהַמַּשְׂכִּילִים יַזְהִרוּ כְּזֹהַר הָרָקִיעַ" ("Os sábios resplandecerão como o brilho do firmamento") [Daniel 12:3]. Ele aplica o verso a quem se dedica ao Zohar, comparando o livro à arca de Noé, onde entram "dois de uma cidade e sete de um reino" [Zohar, Beha'alotcha 16:88].

Para um começo prático, sugiro ler o texto da parashá (Gênesis 32–33), depois Rashi sobre a luta com o anjo, e então uma edição do Zohar com tradução, como o Zohar Pritzker (em inglês) ou o Sulam (com comentário de Rav Ashlag). Posso trabalhar com você um trecho de cada vez.

Posso também aprofundar um destes pontos: a luta com o anjo, o medo de Yaakov ou Esav como Edom. Qual prefere?

*Observação sobre o calendário:* para Nova York (local padrão, diga sua cidade para horários locais), a acendência das velas de Shabat é às 16:12 e a Havdalá às 17:15 [dados Hebcal]. Para orientação pessoal, consulte seu rabino local ou *posek*.

answer:
Au niveau du *sod* (dimension ésotérique), les dix paroles ne sont pas attribuées à Métatron. C'est D.ieu Lui-même qui parle ("Anokhi *HaShem* Elokekha"), mais la Kabbale précise que l'Ein Sof, l'Infini sans attributs, ne se révèle que par les *sefirot*. Le locuteur est donc l'Ein Sof tel qu'il se manifeste (Tiferet/Zeir Anpin, avec la Shekhina), et non Métatron.

## Points clés

- Le texte est à la première personne : "Je suis l'Éternel ton D.ieu", et non "Il m'a dit" [Deutéronome 5:6].
- Selon le Talmud, les deux premières paroles furent entendues directement de la bouche de la Puissance divine [Makkot 24a].
- Dans la Kabbale, l'Ein Sof est la source ultime, mais Il ne parle qu'à travers les *sefirot*.
- Métatron comme "donneur de la Torah" est une position marginale, et le Talmud met en garde contre l'idée d'un second pouvoir [Haguiga 15a ; Sanhédrine 38b].

## Le *pshat* : qui parle ?

Le texte de Deutéronome 5:6 dit : "אָנֹכִי יְהוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ אֲשֶׁר הוֹצֵאתִיךָ מֵאֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם" ("Je suis l'Éternel ton D.ieu qui t'ai fait sortir d'Égypte"). Aucun ange n'est mentionné comme locuteur. Moïse est décrit comme intermédiaire : "Je me tenais entre l'Éternel et vous" [Deutéronome 5:5], mais le verset 4 précède par "face à face l'Éternel vous parla" (*panim be-panim*).

Le Talmud précise que "Anokhi" et "Lo yihyeh lekha" furent entendus directement du Tout-Puissant, le reste par Moïse [Makkot 24a]. Ce passage vient de ma connaissance de la tradition, non des textes fournis.

## Pourquoi l'idée de Métatron apparaît

Plusieurs traditions donnent un rôle à Métatron :

- Il est appelé *Sar ha-Panim* ou *Sar ha-Olam*, et l'on cite Exode 23:21, "car Mon Nom est en lui" [Sanhédrine 38b].
- La littérature des *Heikhalot* et certains cercles ashkénazes lui attribuent un rôle dans la transmission des secrets célestes.
- La vision du Char d'Ézéchiel (*Ma'assé Merkava*) [Ézéchiel 1:15-27] est le cadre où ces figures sont discutées.

Mais le Talmud lui-même met en garde : Elisha ben Abouya, voyant Métatron assis, conclut à "deux pouvoirs" ; on frappa Métatron de soixante coups de feu pour montrer qu'il n'est pas divin [Haguiga 15a]. Cela montre que lui attribuer le rôle de locuteur au Sinaï serait problématique.

## Le *sod* kabbalistique : l'Ein Sof et les *sefirot*

L'Ein Sof est au-delà de toute parole, de toute lettre et de toute attribution. La révélation sinaïtique passe donc par les dix *sefirot*, ce qui correspond d'ailleurs aux "dix paroles".

- **Zohar** : la Torah descend de Tiferet (*Zeir Anpin*, "le Saint béni soit-Il") et la Shekhina (Malkhout) en est la réceptrice et la "voix". Plusieurs passages lisent "Anokhi" comme une allusion à la Shekhina ; d'autres y voient une allusion à un niveau plus haut, Keter. Les lectures varient selon les passages, et je cite de mémoire.
- **Proverbes 8:22-26** : la Torah/Sagesse (*Hokhma*) est "créée" ou "acquise" avant le monde ("*Hashem kanani reshit darko*"). La tradition kabbalistique y voit le lien entre l'Ein Sof et le monde de la révélation : la Torah précède la création et émane de la Sagesse divine, non d'un ange.
- **Hassidout (notamment Habad)** : "Anokhi" exprime l'Essence divine qui se révèle elle-même. L'Ein Sof se dévoile lui-même au Sinaï, sans intermédiaire, ce qui explique que le Sinaï soit un moment unique.

## Pourquoi la divergence ?

La tension vient de deux principes : D.ieu est radicalement transcendant (donc il faut des intermédiaires), mais le texte et le Talmud insistent sur une parole directe. La Kabbale résout cela par les *sefirot* : ce sont des "vêtements" ou canaux de D.ieu Lui-même, non des êtres séparés comme Métatron. Les traditions qui font de Métatron un médiateur sont minoritaires pour le don de la Torah.

answer:
Le texte biblique n'appelle pas l'arbre de la vie « Yilan » : son nom est **Etz HaChayim** (עץ החיים). *Ilan* (אילן) est le mot araméen et rabbinique pour « arbre ». Le nom « Yilan » vient donc sans doute d'une confusion avec ce terme, ou, en turc, avec *yılan*, qui signifie « serpent ».

## Key Takeaways

- Dans la Torah, l'arbre s'appelle *Etz HaChayim* (« arbre de la vie »), pas « Yilan » [Genèse 2:9; 3:22; 3:24].
- *Ilan* (אילן) est le mot araméen et mishnaïque pour « arbre », là où l'hébreu biblique dit *etz*.
- Dans la Kabbale, le schéma des *sefirot* est souvent appelé *Ilan*, ou « arbre sacré ».
- En turc, *yılan* veut dire « serpent », ce qui peut brouiller les pistes, d'autant que le serpent figure dans le même récit (Genèse 3).

## Ce que dit le texte (pshat)

Le verset de Genèse 2:9 présente deux arbres au milieu du jardin : l'arbre de la vie (*Etz HaChayim*) et l'arbre de la connaissance du bien et du mal (*Etz HaDa'at Tov VaRa*) [Genèse 2:9, source 1].

Plus loin, D.ieu craint que l'homme ne « prenne aussi de l'arbre de la vie, n'en mange et ne vive éternellement » (« פֶּן־יִשְׁלַח יָדוֹ וְלָקַח גַּם מֵעֵץ הַחַיִּים וְאָכַל וָחַי לְעֹלָם ») [Genèse 3:22]. Les chérubins et l'épée flamboyante gardent alors « le chemin de l'arbre de la vie » [Genèse 3:24].

Partout, le mot employé est *etz* (עץ), jamais *ilan*.

## D'où vient le mot *Ilan* ?

*Ilan* (אילן) est un terme araméen. On le trouve dans le Tanakh, mais seulement dans les passages en araméen, par exemple dans le songe de Nabuchodonosor, où l'arbre est appelé *ilana* (אילנא) [Daniel 4:7-9]. Il est ensuite courant dans la Mishna et le Talmud pour désigner les arbres, notamment dans les lois agricoles. L'hébreu moderne l'a repris : *ilan* veut dire « arbre », et *Ilan* est aussi un prénom.

Le nom « Yilan » n'est donc pas un nom spécifique de l'arbre de la vie. Il dit seulement « arbre ».

## Le lien avec la Kabbale

Dans la littérature kabbalistique, le mot *Ilan* prend un sens symbolique. Les dix *sefirot* sont représentées comme un arbre, d'où les expressions « *Ilan HaSefirot* » ou « *Ilan HaAtzilut* », et le titre *Etz Chayim*, l'ouvrage de R. Chaïm Vital qui transmet l'enseignement du Ari zal. C'est de la tradition de la Kabbale (d'après mes connaissances, non des sources fournies) que vient l'association entre « arbre de la vie » et *ilan*.

La Torah elle-même est appelée « arbre de vie pour ceux qui s'y attachent » (« עֵץ חַיִּים הִיא לַמַּחֲזִיקִים בָּהּ ») [Proverbes 3:18]. Cette formule explique pourquoi la tradition a prolongé l'image de l'arbre de la vie vers la Torah et vers la structure spirituelle des mondes.

## Une confusion possible avec le turc

En turc, *yılan* signifie « serpent ». Si votre question vient d'un contexte turc ou judéo-espagnol, ou d'une discussion sur Genèse 3, il peut y avoir un mélange avec le serpent (*nachash*, נחש en hébreu) du jardin d'Éden. Il n'existe pas de lien étymologique entre *ilan* (arbre) et *yılan* (serpent).

Si vous avez rencontré « Yilan » dans un texte précis, dites-moi lequel et je pourrai vous préciser le sens.

answer:
Oui, la tradition du *sod* (dimension ésotérique) a beaucoup écrit sur la nature divine, surtout la **Kabbale** (Zohar, Sefer Yetzira, Ari zal, Ramak, ‘Hassidout). Et oui, la Torah contient des passages où D.ieu parle de Lui-même, surtout **Exode 3:14** (« *Ehyeh asher Ehyeh* ») et **Exode 34:6-7** (les Treize Attributs). La tradition rappelle cependant que ces textes révèlent la façon dont D.ieu se rend connaissable, non son essence.

## Key Takeaways

- Dans **Exode 3:14**, D.ieu se définit par l'être et la présence, et la Kabbale y voit le nom lié à *Keter*.
- Dans **Exode 34:6-7**, D.ieu énumère ses attributs de miséricorde. Le Talmud en fait une « formule » de pardon, et le Zohar y lit les Treize Attributs de l'*Arikh Anpin*.
- Le Rambam affirme que nous ne connaissons que les « attributs d'action » et que l'essence reste inconnaissable. La Kabbale parle d'*Ein Sof* (l'Infini), qui n'a pas d'attribut, et des *sefirot* par lesquelles Il se manifeste.
- **Proverbes 8** et **Ézéchiel 1** servent de base à la Kabbale (la Sagesse primordiale, la *Merkava*).

## Ce que D.ieu dit de Lui-même dans la Torah

### « Ehyeh asher Ehyeh » (Exode 3:14)

Le texte : « וַיֹּאמֶר אֱלֹהִים אֶל־מֹשֶׁה אֶהְיֶה אֲשֶׁר אֶהְיֶה » (« D.ieu dit à Moïse : *Je serai ce que Je serai* »), puis : « אֶהְיֶה שְׁלָחַנִי אֲלֵיכֶם » (« *Ehyeh* m'a envoyé vers vous »). *[Exode 3:14, source récupérée]*

- **Pshat et Midrash** : selon [Rashi, Exode 3:14, d'après Berakhot 9b], D.ieu dit : « Je serai avec eux dans cette détresse comme Je serai avec eux dans les servitudes futures. » Le nom exprime donc la présence de D.ieu auprès d'Israël.
- **Philosophie** : [Rambam, Guide des Égarés I:63] y voit l'Être nécessaire, dont l'existence ne dépend de rien. Le nom indique l'existence même de D.ieu, non une qualité.
- **Kabbale** : *Ehyeh* est le nom divin associé à *Keter* (la « Couronne »), le niveau le plus élevé des *sefirot*, proche de l'*Ein Sof*. Cette lecture vient de la tradition kabbalistique, non des sources récupérées. Le *Hayah-Hoveh-Yihyeh* (« Il était, Il est, Il sera ») exprime de même sa transcendance du temps.

### Les Treize Attributs (Exode 34:6-7)

« יְהוָה יְהוָה אֵל רַחוּם וְחַנּוּן אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם וְרַב־חֶסֶד וֶאֱמֶת… » (« *L'Éternel, l'Éternel, D.ieu miséricordieux et clément, lent à la colère, riche en bienveillance et en vérité…* »). *[Exode 34:6-7, source récupérée]*

- Selon [Rosh Hashana 17b], R. Yo‘hanan dit que D.ieu s'est enveloppé comme un *shaliach tsibbour* (officiant) et a montré à Moïse l'ordre de cette prière. Ces attributs ne sont jamais révoqués.
- Le Zohar (notamment l'*Idra Rabba*) et les *Tikkounei Zohar* y voient les treize aspects de la « barbe » d'*Arikh Anpin* (le « Visage Long »), c'est-à-dire la source de la miséricorde. C'est un langage symbolique, non une description physique.
- [Rambam, Guide I:54] explique que Moïse demandait à connaître les « voies » de D.ieu (Exode 33:13). La réponse porte sur les attributs d'action, c'est-à-dire la façon dont D.ieu agit dans le monde, et non sur son essence.

### Les limites de la connaissance

- **Exode 33:20-23** : « Nul homme ne peut Me voir et vivre » ; Moïse ne voit que « Mon dos ». *(Source de ma connaissance, non récupérée.)*
- **Deutéronome 4:15** : « Vous n'avez vu aucune image. »
- **Isaïe 55:8-9** : « Mes pensées ne sont pas vos pensées. »
- **Malachie 3:6** : « Moi, l'Éternel, Je n'ai pas changé. »

Ces versets fondent le 3e des Treize Principes du Rambam : D.ieu n'est pas corporel et n'a aucune image.

## Les commentaires du *sod*

### Ein Sof et sefirot

La Kabbale distingue :

- **Ein Sof** (« sans fin ») : l'essence divine, au-delà de toute pensée et de tout attribut.
- **Les dix *sefirot*** : les « émanations » ou « instruments » par lesquels l'Infini se manifeste et dirige le monde (Sefer Yetzira ; Zohar ; Ramak, *Pardes Rimonim*).

Le Ramak insiste sur le fait que les *sefirot* sont divines, non des « intermédiaires » séparés. Cette doctrine a suscité des réserves chez certains penseurs, qui craignaient une atteinte à l'unité divine. Les kabbalistes répondent qu'elle la protège.

### Le tsimtsoum

Pour l'Ari zal (R. Isaac Louria, Safed), D.ieu a « contracté » sa lumière pour laisser place au monde. Beaucoup lisent ce *tsimtsoum* comme une image, non comme un retrait littéral, car D.ieu n'a pas de lieu.

### ‘Hassidout

Le Baal HaTanya, dans *Cha‘ar HaYichoud VéHaEmouna* (Tanya II), enseigne que tout est constamment recréé par la parole divine et que « rien n'existe en dehors de Lui ». Cet enseignement dépasse la simple transcendance.

## Les autres passages cités

### Proverbes 8:22-26

« יְהוָה קָנָנִי רֵאשִׁית דַּרְכּוֹ » (« *L'Éternel m'a acquise au début de sa voie, avant ses œuvres d'autrefois* »). *[Proverbes 8:22, source récupérée]* C'est la Sagesse (*‘Hokhma*) qui parle.

- Selon [Bereshit Rabba 1:1], elle désigne la Torah, plan de la Création, dont D.ieu « regardait » pour créer le monde.
- La Kabbale y voit la *sefira* de *‘Hokhma*, le « commencement » (*reshit*) de la manifestation.

### Ézéchiel 1:15-27

La vision des *ofanim* (roues) et du trône, où figure « דְּמוּת כְּמַרְאֵה אָדָם » (« une forme à l'aspect d'un homme »), est la base de la *Ma‘assé Merkava*. *[Ézéchiel 1, source récupérée]*

- La Mishna limite son étude : [Hagiga 2:1] interdit de l'expliquer publiquement, et [Hagiga 13a] raconte les dangers de cette étude.
- Les textes des *Hekhalot* et le *Shi‘our Koma* en sont issus. Ils utilisent des images anthropomorphes que les autorités ont toujours pris soin de lire comme des symboles, notamment le Rambam, pour qui ces expressions s'adressent à l'esprit humain (« *dibra Torah kil'chon bnei adam* »).

## Une nuance importante

Rambam et Kabbale partagent une conviction : on ne connaît pas l'essence de D.ieu. Ils diffèrent sur la méthode. Le Rambam privilégie les attributs négatifs (dire ce que D.ieu n'est pas). La Kabbale décrit les processus par lesquels l'Infini se révèle. Ces deux approches sont considérées comme légitimes dans la tradition, même si leurs partisans ont parfois débattu avec vigueur.

Si vous le souhaitez, je peux approfondir l'un de ces axes : les Treize Attributs dans le Zohar, le débat Rambam / Ramak, ou le sens kabbalistique des noms divins.

La source talmudique centrale est **Haguigua 12a**, mais elle parle de voir « d'un bout du monde à l'autre » et non explicitement du *shoresh* (racine) des choses. L'idée de voir la racine ou l'intériorité des choses est une lecture ultérieure, surtout hassidique et kabbalistique. Les passages fournis ne contiennent pas de formule hébraïque disant littéralement que l'*or haganouz* permettait de voir le *shoresh*.

## Key Takeaways

- Haguigua 12a (Rabbi Elazar) : à la Création, Adam voyait grâce à cette lumière « d'un bout du monde à l'autre ».
- Cette lumière fut cachée à cause des générations du Déluge et de Babel, et réservée aux justes pour le monde futur.
- Le Bnei Yissaschar reprend cette formule (« adam mabit bo mi-sof haolam ve-ad sofo ») à propos de Hanouka.
- La notion de « voir la racine des choses » est une interprétation hassidique (drash/sod), pas le sens littéral du Talmud.

## La source talmudique

Dans la Guemara (Haguigua 12a), Rabbi Elazar enseigne, en substance : « La lumière créée le premier jour, Adam y regardait et voyait d'un bout du monde à l'autre » (*tsofé u-mabit bo mi-sof haolam ve-ad sofo*). Quand D.ieu vit les actes corrompus des générations du Déluge et de Babel, Il la cacha, comme il est dit : « Il retient des méchants leur lumière » (*vayimana mi-reshaïm oram*, Job 38:15). Il la réserva aux justes pour l'avenir.

Le passage fourni de Haguigua 12a est tronqué avant cette phrase. Je la cite donc de ma connaissance, et non des sources récupérées.

## Rachi et la tradition de la lumière cachée

Rachi sur Genèse 1:4 reprend cette aggada : D.ieu « vit qu'il n'était pas convenable que les méchants s'en servent, et Il le mit à part pour les justes dans le monde futur » (*ve-hivdilo la-tsadikim le-atid lavo*). C'est le sens de *vayavdel* (« Il sépara »). Rachi ajoute que le *pshat* est simplement la séparation entre le jour et la nuit.

## Où apparaît l'idée de « voir l'essence »

Dans les sources fournies, le lien est fait ainsi :

- **Sefat Emet (Hanouka)**, citant le Rokéa'h : chaque bougie de Hanouka puise dans l'*or haganouz* et éclaire « dans une grande obscurité », cette lumière brillant « d'un bout du monde à l'autre ».
- **Bnei Yissaschar (Kislev-Tevet 2:8)** : « כי האור הזה אדם מביט בו מסוף העולם וע"ס » ("car cette lumière, on y regarde d'un bout du monde à l'autre"). Il y relie le mot *Hanouka* à *'hinoukh* (éducation, entraînement) en vue de la révélation future de l'*or haganouz*.
- **Bnei Yissaschar (1:6)** : cette lumière brilla 36 heures pour Adam, puis fut cachée dans la Torah. Les 36 bougies de Hanouka correspondent aux 36 mentions de « lumière » dans la Torah.

## Pourquoi on parle de « racine »

Les maîtres hassidiques comprennent « d'un bout à l'autre » non seulement dans l'espace, mais comme une vision qui perçoit le début et la fin, la cause première et le but. Voir « d'un bout à l'autre » devient alors voir la source (*shoresh*) et la finalité de chaque chose. C'est une lecture homilétique, relevant du *drash* et du *sod*.

Si vous avez en tête une formule précise avec le mot *shoresh*, indiquez-moi l'auteur ou le contexte, et je pourrai vérifier plus précisément. Je ne veux pas vous attribuer une citation que je ne peux pas confirmer.

answer:
La fin du Psaume 91 (versets 14-16) est la réponse de D.ieu, le « troisième voix » du psaume selon Steinsaltz. Il y promet à celui qui s'attache à Lui par amour et connaît Son Nom une délivrance, une réponse à l'appel, Sa présence dans la détresse, l'honneur, une longue vie et la vision de Son salut. Selon le *sod* (dimension mystique), ces versets décrivent l'attachement (*dévéqout*) de l'âme au Nom divin et la présence de la Chekhina avec l'homme dans l'épreuve. Les éléments kabbalistiques ci-dessous viennent de ma connaissance de la tradition, non des sources fournies.

## Key Takeaways

- Le verset 14 donne la raison de la protection : l'homme « s'est attaché » à D.ieu (*chachaq*) et « a connu Son Nom ».
- Pour le **Radak**, connaître le Nom de quatre lettres, c'est aimer D.ieu et vivre une providence complète.
- Pour l'**Alchich** (*Romemot El*), cette délivrance vient directement de D.ieu, sans intermédiaire angélique.
- Le verset 15, « Je suis avec lui dans la détresse », est lu par la tradition comme la solidarité de la Chekhina avec l'homme.
- Le *sod* y voit l'union de l'âme au Nom Y-H-V-H et une dynamique de dévoilement progressif de la lumière divine.

## Le sens simple (*pshat*)

**Verset 14** : « Car il m'a désiré, Je le délivrerai ; Je le protégerai, car il a connu Mon Nom » (כִּי בִי חָשַׁק וַאֲפַלְּטֵהוּ אֲשַׂגְּבֵהוּ כִּי יָדַע שְׁמִי) [Psaumes 91:14]. **Steinsaltz** explique que D.ieu parle ici : Il accorde cette protection extraordinaire parce que l'homme L'a désiré ardemment [Steinsaltz sur Psaumes 91:14]. La **Metzudat Zion** glose *ashagvéhou* comme « renforcement » (התחזקות) [Metzudat Zion sur Psaumes 91:14].

**Verset 15** : « Il M'appellera et Je lui répondrai ; Je suis avec lui dans la détresse, Je le dégagerai et le glorifierai » (יִקְרָאֵנִי וְאֶעֱנֵהוּ עִמּוֹ אָנֹכִי בְצָרָה אֲחַלְּצֵהוּ וַאֲכַבְּדֵהוּ).

**Verset 16** : « Je le rassasierai de longueur de jours et lui ferai voir Mon salut » (אֹרֶךְ יָמִים אַשְׂבִּיעֵהוּ וְאַרְאֵהוּ בִּישׁוּעָתִי). Beaucoup y lisent aussi une allusion au monde à venir, mais c'est une lecture parmi d'autres.

## Les commentateurs

- **Radak** : « La connaissance du Nom explicite, de quatre lettres, c'est l'amour de D.ieu, et c'est la providence parfaite que chacun peut atteindre de son vivant » (וידיעת שם המפורש… היא אהבת האל יתברך והיא ההשגחה שלימה) [Radak sur Psaumes 91:14]. La « connaissance » du Nom est donc une relation d'amour, pas une formule magique.
- **Alchich** (*Romemot El*) : celui qui désire D.ieu seul est délivré « par Lui-même » (על ידי עצמו), non par un ange ni même par la prière. Les anges envoyés auparavant l'étaient pour ceux qui n'avaient pas ce mérite d'attachement [Romemot El sur Psaumes 91:14].

Le mot *chachaq* évoque l'attachement profond. Le **Ramban** l'emploie dans un sens proche à propos de Deutéronome 7:7 (ma connaissance, à vérifier dans le texte).

## « Imo anokhi vetsara » : la Chekhina dans la détresse

La tradition rabbinique lit « Je suis avec lui dans la détresse » comme l'expression de la solidarité divine avec Israël en exil et en souffrance. Cette idée est reprise dans le Talmud et les midrashim (par exemple dans la **Mekhilta** à propos de l'Égypte). Je cite de mémoire, sans référence précise vérifiée ici.

## Le *sod* (dimension mystique)

Voici les grandes lignes de la lecture kabbalistique et hassidique, à prendre comme orientation et non comme citation textuelle :

- **Le Nom Y-H-V-H** : « connaître Mon Nom » renvoie à la connaissance (*daat*) de D.ieu comme Source des attributs divins. Cette connaissance est une union, comme le verbe *yada* dans la Torah (Genèse 4:1). L'âme s'unit au Nom, ce que le Radak exprime à sa façon par « l'amour ».
- **Chachaq et dévéqout** : le désir est le moteur qui relie l'âme à sa racine. La délivrance est alors un effet naturel de cette union : celui qui est attaché à la Source n'est plus soumis aux forces de séparation (*qlipot*).
- **Imo anokhi vetsara** : dans la Kabbale, la Chekhina (*Malkhout*) partage l'exil et la souffrance des âmes. L'épreuve devient ainsi un lieu de rencontre, et le « dégagement » (*ahalletséhou*) est aussi une élévation de la Chekhina elle-même.
- **Orekh yamim** : « longueur de jours » évoque, dans le langage du Zohar, *Arikh Anpin* (« Visage Long »), le niveau de la bienveillance et de la volonté suprêmes. C'est une association courante dans la littérature zoharique, que je rapporte sans pouvoir citer le passage exact.
- **Bishouati** : « Mon salut » (*yéchouati*) désigne le dévoilement final : voir la lumière divine dans la réalité même qui semblait obscure.

## Mon sentiment

Ces trois versets forment une progression : un désir ardent suscite la protection, puis le dialogue (« il appellera, Je répondrai »), puis la présence dans l'épreuve, et enfin la plénitude et la vision. L'initiative vient de l'homme, mais la réponse est d'une générosité qui dépasse tout ce qu'il pouvait demander. Le psaume ne promet pas l'absence de détresse. Il promet que D.ieu y est présent (*imo anokhi*).

Si vous le souhaitez, je peux approfondir un point précis : le Zohar, la lecture hassidique, ou le rôle de ce psaume comme *shir shel pegaïm* (« chant contre les nuisances »).

answer:
**Shahar** (שַׁחַר) is the ordinary Hebrew word for "dawn" or "morning twilight." In the wider ancient Near East, the dawn was personified as a deity: in Ugaritic texts, Shachar and his twin Shalim are gods of dawn and dusk. The Tanakh uses the same imagery, but consistently presents dawn as a created thing that God commands, not a divine being.

## Key Takeaways

- *Shahar* means dawn in the Tanakh, and Job 38:12 explicitly places it under God's command.
- The Ugaritic pantheon had a god Shachar. This comes from archaeology and scholarship, not from the retrieved sources or traditional commentary.
- Poetic personification of dawn (Psalms, Isaiah 14) is read by classical commentators as metaphor, not mythology.
- Rabbinic tradition treats dawn as a spiritual marker, shaping prayer (*Shacharit*) and giving us Esther as "the Dawn" (Yoma 29a).

## Pshat: Shahar as Dawn in the Tanakh

**Job 38:12** asks: "הֲמִיָּמֶיךָ צִוִּיתָ בֹּקֶר יִדַּעְתָּ הַשַּׁחַר מְקֹמוֹ" ("Have you, in your days, commanded the morning, made the dawn know its place?"). [Job 38:12] God speaks as the one who commands dawn and assigns it a "place." Dawn is a servant of the Creator, not an independent power. The following verses continue this image: dawn grasps the earth's edges and "shakes the wicked out of it."

**Psalm 22:1** reads "לַמְנַצֵּחַ עַל אַיֶּלֶת הַשַּׁחַר" ("For the conductor, on *Ayelet HaShachar*, a psalm of David"). [Psalms 22:1] The phrase literally means "the doe of the dawn." It is probably a musical direction, perhaps a tune or instrument, though it has also been read as a poetic image of the morning light.

Other verses in my own knowledge (not among the retrieved passages) use similar imagery:

- "Wings of dawn" (*kanfei shachar*) [Psalms 139:9], a poetic picture of the sunrise spreading across the sky.
- David's "I will awaken the dawn" (*a'irah shachar*) [Psalms 57:9].
- "As certain as the dawn is His going forth" [Hosea 6:3].

## Shahar as a Divine Being

### Ancient Near Eastern background

In the Ugaritic texts from Ras Shamra, **Shachar** and **Shalim** are twin gods associated with dawn and dusk, born in a myth of the gods. Many scholars see Hebrew *shachar* as cognate with this deity's name. This is a scholarly reconstruction from my training, not something found in the retrieved passages or in classical Jewish commentary.

### Helel ben Shachar

The clearest case of mythic language is **Isaiah 14:12**: "אֵיךְ נָפַלְתָּ מִשָּׁמַיִם הֵילֵל בֶּן שָׁחַר" ("How have you fallen from heaven, Helel ben Shachar"). The context is a taunt against the king of Babylon. Classical commentators such as Rashi and Radak read it as a metaphor for a once-radiant tyrant brought low, like the morning star fading at sunrise. Some modern scholars see an echo of an older myth about a rebellious star-deity. Later Christian tradition connected the verse to Lucifer, a reading that is not part of the Jewish interpretive tradition.

### How the Tanakh handles the imagery

The Tanakh uses the language of dawn's "wings," "eyelids" (Job 3:9; 41:10), and "birth" (Job 38:8-12) poetically, while stripping away any independent divinity. Many scholars call this *demythologization*. The consistent message is that dawn obeys God: "Have you commanded the morning?" is a rhetorical challenge to Job.

## Dawn in Rabbinic Tradition

### Dawn and prayer

The Talmud connects *Shacharit* (the morning prayer) to the morning offering. As the Baraita says: "מִפְּנֵי מָה אָמְרוּ תְּפִלַּת הַשַּׁחַר עַד חֲצוֹת — שֶׁהֲרֵי תָּמִיד שֶׁל שַׁחַר קָרֵב וְהוֹלֵךְ עַד חֲצוֹת" ("Why did they say the morning prayer lasts until midday? Because the morning *tamid* offering may be brought until midday"). Rabbi Yehuda says until the fourth hour. [Berakhot 26b] The name *Shacharit* derives from *shachar*, and prayer begins with the dawn (*alot hashachar*).

### David and the dawn

In my own knowledge, the Talmud reads Psalm 57:9 as David boasting that he awakens the dawn instead of being awakened by it. [Berakhot 3b-4a] This is a deliberate inversion of the mythic picture: the human servant of God rouses the "deity" of dawn.

### Esther as *Ayelet HaShachar*

The Talmud asks why Esther is likened to the dawn in Psalm 22, and answers that just as dawn marks the end of the night, so Esther's story marks the end of the miracles recorded in Scripture. [Yoma 29a] This reading uses *shachar* as a symbol of redemption emerging gradually from darkness, a theme often expanded in later Jewish thought.

## Why the Difference?

The tension lies between two ways of reading the same word. Historical-critical scholarship notes shared vocabulary with Canaanite religion and sees Israelite adaptation. Traditional commentary reads the verses as poetry within a monotheistic framework, where nature is God's instrument. Both agree that the Tanakh itself never affirms a god named Shachar.
