answer:
**Resposta curta:** no judaísmo não existe um "diabo" nos moldes cristãos ou popular, isto é, um rival independente de D'us. O **Satan** é descrito como um acusador ou agente a serviço de D'us, e a tradição o identifica com o ***yetzer hara*** (inclinação ao mal) dentro do homem. Há uma divisão real entre os sábios: alguns o tratam como um anjo de fato, outros (como o Rambam) como uma alegoria da nossa própria inclinação interna. Em ambos os casos, a responsabilidade pelo ato é sempre da pessoa.

## Key Takeaways

- *Ha-Satan* ("o opositor/acusador") é um servo de D'us, sem poder próprio; o judaísmo rejeita o dualismo.
- O Talmud identifica Satan, *yetzer hara* e o Anjo da Morte como uma só coisa [Bava Batra 16a].
- O *yetzer hara* não é "mau" por essência: foi criado por D'us e tem função construtiva.
- "Ego" é parecido com o *yetzer hara*, mas não equivale a ele exatamente.
- Nunca se pode dizer "o diabo me obrigou": [Gênesis 4:7] diz "e tu o dominarás".

## O Satan na Torá e nos Profetas (pshat)

Na Bíblia, *satan* é um substantivo funcional: "opositor". Em [Números 22:22] o anjo que bloqueia Bil'am é chamado *satan*. Em [Jó 1–2] e [Zacarias 3] ele aparece na corte celestial como um promotor, e só age com permissão divina. Não há um reino do mal concorrente: "Formo a luz e crio a escuridão... Eu, o Eterno, faço tudo isto" [Isaías 45:7].

## O que dizem as fontes recuperadas

**Rashi** em [Gênesis 22:1], citando o Talmud [Sanhedrin 89b], explica que "depois dessas coisas" (*achar hadevarim ha'eleh*) pode ser "depois das palavras de Satan", que acusou Avraham de não ter oferecido nem um boi ou carneiro em todos os seus banquetes. D'us responde que Avraham faria tudo por seu filho, e que se Ele pedisse Yitzchak, Avraham não hesitaria. Aqui o Satan é um **acusador** que serve de ocasião para a prova, não um inimigo de D'us.

O **Or HaChaim** em [Gênesis 23:2] diz que "a terra de Canaã" alude a este mundo, comparado ao *yetzer hara*, ao Satan, porque a existência dele é o incentivo para vencê-lo e alcançar santidade. Ou seja, o adversário existe **para que haja mérito e crescimento**.

## "Ele é o yetzer hara" (conhecimento complementar)

O Talmud afirma: "Ele é o Satan, ele é o *yetzer hara*, ele é o Anjo da Morte. Desce e engana, sobe e acusa, recebe permissão e toma a alma" [Bava Batra 16a]. O Talmud também descreve a estratégia dele: hoje diz "faça isto", amanhã "faça aquilo", até chegar à idolatria [Shabbat 105b].

## Existe de verdade, ou é só o ego? Duas leituras

- **Leitura literal:** o Satan é um anjo real, com função de acusador e tentador. Essa é a leitura mais simples de Rashi e do Talmud, e grande parte da tradição cabalística ampliou o tema (*Sitra Achra*, Samael), sempre sob o controle de D'us.
- **Leitura psicológica/alegórica:** o **Rambam** [Guia dos Perplexos 3:22] vê a história de Jó como parábola e identifica o Satan com a inclinação humana, ligada à matéria e à imaginação. Esta é uma leitura filosófica minoritária entre os comentaristas, mas respeitada.

## O yetzer hara é o ego?

Em parte. O *yetzer hara* inclui o egoísmo e o impulso de satisfazer a si mesmo, mas a Torá o vê de modo mais amplo:

- Ele é inerente: "a inclinação do coração do homem é má desde a juventude" [Gênesis 8:21].
- Não é inimigo a ser eliminado, mas força a ser canalizada. Os sábios dizem que o "muito bom" de [Gênesis 1:31] inclui o *yetzer hara*, pois sem ele ninguém construiria casa, casaria ou teria filhos [Bereshit Rabá 9:7].
- D'us diz: "Criei o *yetzer hara*, criei a Torá como antídoto" [Kiddushin 30b].

"Ego" é um conceito psicológico moderno; o *yetzer hara* é um conceito moral e teológico. Há sobreposição, mas não são sinônimos.

## Responsabilidade

Em [Gênesis 4:7] D'us diz a Caim que o pecado "espreita à porta... mas tu o dominarás". Seja o Satan um anjo ou uma força interior, a Torá coloca a escolha, e portanto a culpa e o mérito, sobre o ser humano.

answer:
Não tenho certeza do que você quis dizer com "segu do departamento", então entendi como "o segundo compartimento (departamento) do Gan Éden". Segundo a tradição midráshica tardia (*Seder Gan Eden*), o Gan Éden tem sete divisões, e o segundo compartimento é o dos *baalei teshuva* (os que se arrependeram), descrito como feito de prata. Isso **não vem das fontes recuperadas**, mas do meu conhecimento da tradição, e os detalhes variam entre as versões.

## Key Takeaways

- O texto bíblico não descreve compartimentos: apenas diz que D'us plantou um jardim no Éden e colocou ali o homem [Gênesis 2:8].
- A divisão em sete moradas aparece em midrashim tardios, como o *Seder Gan Eden*, e na literatura mística.
- Nessa tradição, o segundo compartimento é associado aos penitentes (*baalei teshuva*).
- Há base talmúdica para a grandeza dos penitentes: "no lugar onde os *baalei teshuva* estão, os justos completos não podem estar" [Berakhot 34b].
- As descrições variam entre as fontes, e muitas são alegóricas.

## Fontes recuperadas: o pano de fundo

O versículo diz: "וַיִּטַּע יְהֹוָה אֱלֹהִים גַּן־בְּעֵדֶן מִקֶּדֶם" (e D'us plantou um jardim no Éden, ao oriente) [Gênesis 2:8]. Esse é o *pshat*: um jardim concreto, sem divisões internas.

O **Kohelet Rabbah 7:13** acrescenta que D'us conduziu Adão por todas as árvores do Gan Éden e disse: "Veja como são belas as minhas obras; tudo o que criei, criei para você. Cuide para não corromper o meu mundo." Isso mostra o jardim como lugar de responsabilidade, mas não fala de compartimentos.

## A tradição dos compartimentos

O *Seder Gan Eden* (publicado em Jellinek, *Beit HaMidrash*) fala de sete moradas para diferentes categorias de justos. Cito de memória, e a ordem e os detalhes (materiais, personagens) mudam conforme a versão:

- **Primeiro compartimento:** associado aos mártires e aos conversos justos (*gerei tzedek*).
- **Segundo compartimento:** dos *baalei teshuva*, descrito como de prata. Algumas versões associam a ele o rei Menashé, símbolo do arrependimento depois de grande pecado.
- **Compartimentos seguintes:** habitados por patriarcas, tribos, grandes justos e assim por diante, em graus crescentes de proximidade com a Presença Divina.

## Por que os penitentes?

A ideia tem raiz no Talmud: "No lugar onde os *baalei teshuva* estão, os completamente justos não podem estar" [Berakhot 34b]. Rabi Avahu e outros divergem sobre quem é maior, mas essa passagem mostra o grau elevado do arrependimento. Maimônides, em *Hilchot Teshuva* 7:4, também ressalta que o penitente é "amado e querido" diante de D'us.

## Como entender essas descrições

Muitos comentaristas, como Maimônides (*Hilchot Teshuva* 8) e o Ramban (*Shaar HaGemul*), entendem o Gan Éden do mundo vindouro como realidade espiritual, e não física. Os "compartimentos" seriam graus de percepção de D'us, e não salas literais.

Se você tinha outro sentido em mente (por exemplo, o Gan Éden superior e o inferior, ou outra divisão), diga-me e eu aprofundo.

answer:
Sim, segundo a tradição, um **ben Noach** (não judeu que observa as sete leis de Noé) que apoia generosamente o kiruv e as sinagogas pode ter mérito, inclusive uma parte no *Olam Haba* (Mundo Vindouro). Isso vale sobretudo se ele age por fidelidade ao mandamento Divino e não só por simpatia. Nas fontes clássicas, porém, o mérito do não judeu é tratado como parte do Mundo Vindouro e da recompensa geral dos justos. Não há uma categoria específica de "mérito messiânico" por financiar projetos de kiruv.

## Key Takeaways

- **Os justos das nações têm parte no Mundo Vindouro** [Tosefta, Sanhedrin 13:2; Rambam, Hilchot Melachim 8:11].
- **Segundo o Rambam, a motivação importa**: o ben Noach deve cumprir as sete leis por serem ordem de D'us, e não apenas por lógica.
- **Tzedaka e chesed** são valorizadas também nas nações [Bava Batra 10b], e a Torá dá lugar à oração e à contribuição do não judeu [I Reis 8:41-43; Isaías 56:6-7].
- **Era messiânica e Mundo Vindouro são conceitos distintos**, e as fontes falam de um papel positivo das nações na redenção [Isaías 2:2-4; Zacarias 14:16].
- **As fontes recuperadas** (Rambam, Teshuvá 3:5, e Zohar, Mishpatim) tratam do tema só de forma indireta.

## Sobre as fontes recuperadas

O **Rambam, Hilchot Teshuvá 3:5** trata da pesagem de mérito e culpa: "אין מחשבין עליו עון שחטא בו תחלה ולא שני, אלא משלישי ואילך" ("não se contam o primeiro e o segundo pecado, mas do terceiro em diante"). Ele fundamenta isso em "הן כל אלה יפעל אל פעמים שלש עם גבר" (Jó 33:29). A passagem fala do indivíduo judeu e do conceito de que os méritos são pesados contra as transgressões. Não se refere diretamente ao ben Noach. Serve apenas como pano de fundo: a ideia de balança de mérito é central ao julgamento Divino.

O **Zohar, Mishpatim** menciona os "חֲסִידֵי אוּמוֹת הָעוֹלָם" (*chasidei umot ha'olam*, os piedosos das nações do mundo). O trecho está fragmentado e não permite concluir muito sobre o seu caso. Apenas confirma que a literatura mística reconhece essa categoria. O restante da resposta vem de fontes que conheço da tradição, não do material recuperado.

## O princípio básico: os justos das nações

A **Tosefta (Sanhedrin 13:2)** registra a discussão entre R. Eliezer e R. Yehoshua. R. Eliezer limitava o Mundo Vindouro aos judeus. R. Yehoshua ensinou: "יש חסידי אומות העולם שיש להם חלק לעולם הבא" (há justos das nações que têm parte no Mundo Vindouro). A halachá segue R. Yehoshua.

O **Rambam, Hilchot Melachim 8:11** codifica isso: quem aceita as sete leis e cuida de cumpri-las é dos *chasidei umot ha'olam* e tem parte no Mundo Vindouro. A condição é que as cumpra porque o Santo, Bendito Seja, as ordenou na Torá e nos informou por Moshé Rabenu. Se as cumpre apenas por raciocínio próprio, não é considerado *ger toshav* nem dos piedosos, mas dos seus sábios. Há variantes de leitura nesse trecho, e os comentaristas discutem a precisão da formulação.

## Tzedaka e apoio a instituições judaicas

**Bava Batra 10b** interpreta Provérbios 14:34 ("וְחֶסֶד לְאֻמִּים חַטָּאת"). Segundo R. Nechunya ben HaKaná, a *tzedaka* eleva Israel e o *chesed* (bondade) expia pelas nações. Isso mostra que o bem praticado pelo não judeu tem peso espiritual real.

A Torá também valoriza o apoio do não judeu à Casa de D'us:

- **Salomão**, na dedicação do Templo, pediu que D'us atenda o estrangeiro que vier orar naquela casa, "para que todos os povos da terra conheçam Teu nome" [I Reis 8:41-43].
- **Isaías 56:6-7** diz que os estrangeiros que se unem a D'us serão trazidos ao Seu monte santo, e que "ביתי בית תפלה יקרא לכל העמים" (Minha casa será chamada casa de oração para todos os povos).
- O **Rambam, Hilchot Maaseh HaKorbanot 3:2** aceita oferendas voluntárias de não judeus no Templo, o que mostra que sua contribuição era valorizada.

Um ben Noach que apoia sinagogas e kiruv, ou seja, o estudo e a continuidade da Torá, se encaixa nesse espírito. Ainda assim, o texto não faz da doação, por si só, um "bilhete" para o mérito. O que o Rambam exige é a base: aceitar as sete leis como ordem Divina.

## E na era messiânica?

É preciso distinguir dois conceitos. Para o Rambam, o **Mundo Vindouro** é a recompensa da alma, enquanto a **era messiânica** (*Yemot HaMashiach*) é uma época histórica neste mundo [Rambam, Hilchot Melachim 11-12].

Os profetas descrevem um papel positivo para as nações nessa era:

- Todas as nações afluirão ao monte do Senhor para aprender Seus caminhos [Isaías 2:2-4].
- Sofonias 3:9 diz: "אָז אֶהְפֹּךְ אֶל עַמִּים שָׂפָה בְרוּרָה לִקְרֹא כֻלָּם בְּשֵׁם ה'" (então darei aos povos lábios puros, para que todos invoquem o Nome do Senhor).
- Zacarias 14:16 prevê as nações subindo a Jerusalém para celebrar Sucot.

Quem já viveu segundo a vontade de D'us, e apoiou a Torá, está em harmonia com esse futuro. Mas as fontes não dizem que contribuições específicas rendem um mérito messiânico definido. Afirmar isso seria especulação.

## Observações finais

- A sinceridade e a motivação contam: agir por reconhecer a autoridade Divina é o que o Rambam valoriza.
- O mérito é julgado por D'us, e nenhuma fonte permite prever o resultado individual.
- Se o objetivo é a prática, o mais seguro é cumprir bem as sete leis de Noé e manter a doação como expressão de *chesed*.

Para orientação pessoal, consulte seu rabino local ou *posek*.

answer:
Há pontos de contato reais, mas também diferenças importantes. O judaísmo clássico ensina que o *Gehinnom* (geralmente traduzido como "inferno") é, para a maioria das pessoas, um lugar temporário de purificação, o que lembra o conceito espírita. A reencarnação (*gilgul*) existe na tradição judaica, mas só na Cabala e em parte do pensamento medieval, não como dogma central. Já a comunicação com os mortos, base do espiritismo, é proibida pela Torá.

## Key Takeaways

- No judaísmo, o Gehinnom é majoritariamente temporário, em torno de até 12 meses para a maioria, segundo o Talmud [Rosh Hashanah 16b-17a].
- A reencarnação (*gilgul*) vem da Cabala (Zohar, Arizal) e foi rejeitada por grandes filósofos como Saadia Gaon.
- Os princípios mais amplamente aceitos são a ressurreição dos mortos e o *Olam Haba* (mundo vindouro), não a reencarnação.
- A Torá proíbe consultar os mortos [Deuteronômio 18:10-11], o que é uma diferença fundamental em relação ao espiritismo.
- O judaísmo não tem um "purgatório" no sentido católico, embora a ideia de purificação seja parecida.

## Sobre as fontes recuperadas

Das fontes recuperadas, **Rosh Hashanah 16b** é a mais relevante. **Isaías 30:33** menciona o *Tofet*, mas no contexto original (*pshat*) trata da queda da Assíria, e só depois a tradição associou essa imagem ao Gehinnom. A passagem de **Sanhedrin 90a** recuperada trata de uma discussão legal técnica sobre idolatria e não se aplica diretamente à sua pergunta. O restante vem do meu conhecimento da tradição.

## O Gehinnom como purificação

O Talmud discute o julgamento divino em Rosh Hashanah 16b-17a. Segundo a *Beit Shammai*, as pessoas "intermediárias" (nem totalmente justas, nem totalmente perversas) descem ao Gehinnom e depois sobem. A *Beit Hillel* diz que D'us "se inclina para a misericórdia" (*rav chesed*) e as poupa.

O mesmo texto fala de um período de **doze meses** de julgamento para os pecadores [Rosh Hashanah 17a; Mishná Eduyot 2:10]. É por isso que o *Kaddish* de luto é recitado por 11 meses: para não sugerir que o falecido é um pecador completo.

Há exceções. O Talmud menciona categorias de pecados muito graves cujo castigo é mais longo. Mesmo assim, a visão predominante é que o sofrimento é limitado, e muitos ensinam que o Gehinnom serve para purificar a alma. A Mishná afirma: "Todo Israel tem parte no mundo vindouro" [Sanhedrin 90a]. Os justos de todas as nações também têm parte nele (Tosefta Sanhedrin 13:2; Rambam, Leis de Teshuvá 3:5).

## Reencarnação (*gilgul*)

- **Talmud**: não ensina a reencarnação de forma clara.
- **Cabala**: o *Sefer HaBahir*, o *Zohar* e o **Arizal** (séc. XVI) desenvolveram o *gilgul* amplamente. Ele é muito aceito no hassidismo e entre sefarditas místicos.
- **Rejeição**: **Saadia Gaon** a rejeitou em *Emunot VeDeot* 6:8. **Rabi Yosef Albo** (*Ikkarim* 4:29) a viu como não fundamental. O Rambam, em seus 13 princípios de fé, não a inclui.

A reencarnação judaica costuma servir para a **correção** (*tikkun*) de uma alma que não cumpriu sua missão. Não é uma evolução contínua através de muitos mundos, como no espiritismo de Allan Kardec.

## Onde divergem

- **Comunicação com espíritos**: a Torá proíbe o *ov* e o *yidoni*, ou seja, médiuns e necromantes [Deuteronômio 18:10-11]. O episódio da necromante de Ein Dor [I Samuel 28] é visto como transgressão de Saul.
- **Autoridade**: o judaísmo se baseia na revelação do Sinai e na tradição transmitida, não em mensagens espirituais contemporâneas.
- **Visão de Jesus e do pecado**: o espiritismo tem uma cristologia própria, que o judaísmo não aceita.
- **Ressurreição**: o judaísmo ortodoxo afirma a ressurreição corporal dos mortos (Rambam, 13º princípio).

## Uma observação sobre o cristianismo

A ideia de um inferno eterno para quase todos os pecadores não é a visão judaica majoritária. Isso pode ajudá-lo a entender por que o judaísmo e o espiritismo parecem próximos nesse ponto.

Se quiser, pode me mandar suas perguntas uma a uma, e posso aprofundar qualquer tema, como Gehinnom, *Olam Haba*, gilgul ou a visão judaica do pecado. Para orientação pessoal, consulte seu rabino local ou *posek*.

answer:
Não encontrei nenhuma fonte clássica que descreva uma recompensa específica e exclusiva do *sofer* (escriba de STaM: Sefer Torá, tefilin e mezuzot) na era messiânica ou no *Olam Haba*. O que existe são fontes sobre a grandeza da mitsvá da escrita e princípios gerais de recompensa. Essa resposta vem do meu conhecimento da tradição, pois nenhuma fonte foi recuperada.

## Key Takeaways

- Não há fonte talmúdica clara que prometa ao escriba uma recompensa messiânica ou do Mundo Vindouro diferente da de outros que cumprem mitsvot.
- A tradição enfatiza a **seriedade e o mérito** da escrita: "seu trabalho é trabalho do Céu" [Eruvin 13a].
- Quem escreve ou participa da escrita de um Sefer Torá é considerado como se o tivesse recebido no Sinai [Menachot 30a; Rambam, Hilchot Sefer Torá 7:1].
- A era messiânica e o *Olam Haba* são conceitos distintos; a recompensa plena das mitsvot é associada ao *Olam Haba* [Kiddushin 39b].
- Afirmações populares sobre recompensas específicas para escribas devem ser tratadas com cautela, a menos que citem fonte.

## Fontes sobre a grandeza do escriba

**Eruvin 13a:** Rabi Yishmael diz a Rabi Meir, que era escriba: "Meu filho, seja cuidadoso em seu trabalho, pois seu trabalho é o trabalho do Céu; se omitir uma letra ou acrescentar uma letra, destruirá o mundo inteiro." Isso indica o peso da função, não uma recompensa específica.

**Menachot 30a e Rambam, Hilchot Sefer Torá 7:1:** a escrita de um Sefer Torá é a última mitsvá da Torá (derivada de Deuteronômio 31:19, "escrevei para vós este cântico"). Quem escreve, ou corrige uma única letra, é tido como se tivesse escrito o rolo inteiro. O Rambam acrescenta que é como se o tivesse recebido no Sinai.

**Kiddushin 30a:** os primeiros sábios eram chamados *sofrim* porque contavam todas as letras da Torá. Isso mostra a honra da função na tradição.

## Recompensa: princípios gerais

- **Olam Haba:** o Talmud ensina que a recompensa das mitsvot é no Mundo Vindouro [Kiddushin 39b]. O escriba a recebe pelo mesmo critério que os demais: a mitsvá cumprida com sinceridade e *lishmá* (pela própria mitsvá).
- **Era messiânica:** o Rambam a distingue do *Olam Haba*. Ela é uma era de paz e de dedicação ao conhecimento de D'us [Rambam, Hilchot Melachim 12:4–5]. O *Olam Haba* é a existência da alma além do mundo físico [Rambam, Hilchot Teshuvá 8].
- **Aplicação por analogia:** Daniel 12:3 diz que "os que justificam a muitos brilharão como as estrelas" (cf. Bava Batra 8b). O escriba permite que muitos cumpram mitsvot com tefilin, mezuzot e rolos kasher, então é plausível aplicar-lhe esse verso. Isso é uma extensão minha, não uma afirmação explícita das fontes.

## Cautela

Em círculos de *sofrut* circulam ditos sobre grandes recompensas para escribas, às vezes atribuídos a fontes cabalísticas ou ao *Sefer Chasidim*. Não consigo confirmar uma fonte precisa para eles. Se você encontrou uma afirmação específica, posso ajudar a analisá-la caso me diga onde a viu.

answer:
Segundo a Halachá, uma pessoa pode se converter quando é sincera, aceita o jugo das mitzvot por inteiro e passa pelo processo completo: instrução, *brit milá* (circuncisão, para homens), *tevilá* (imersão no mikvê) e um *beit din* (tribunal rabínico) de três juízes. Ela não pode ser aceita quando o motivo é claramente interesse externo (dinheiro, poder, casamento) ou quando recusa parte das mitzvot. Também não há conversão válida sem o processo formal. Os impedimentos bíblicos contra certos povos já não se aplicam hoje.

## Key Takeaways

- O candidato deve ser testado e advertido sobre as dificuldades do povo judeu [Yevamot 47a].
- Quem diz "sei disso e não sou digno" é aceito imediatamente [Yevamot 47a].
- Exigem-se *milá*, *tevilá* e *beit din* [Shulchan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 268].
- Motivos ocultos, ou a rejeição de qualquer parte das mitzvot, invalidam a aceitação no início, embora a Halachá trate o caso depois de realizado (*bedi'avad*) de forma mais complexa.
- As proibições bíblicas contra amonitas, moabitas, egípcios e edomitas não se aplicam mais.

## Quando a pessoa PODE se converter

### O teste de sinceridade
O Talmud ensina: quando um candidato vem, pergunta-se: "O que viste para vires te converter? Não sabes que Israel hoje é *dvuyim, dchufim, sehufim umeturafin* (sofrido, empurrado, perseguido e atormentado)?" [Yevamot 47a]. Se ele responde: "Sei, e não sou digno", é aceito de imediato.

Em seguida, informam-lhe algumas mitzvot leves e algumas graves, as dádivas aos pobres (*leket, shikhchá, peá, maaser ani*) e o castigo pela transgressão das mitzvot [Yevamot 47a; Shulchan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 268].

### Os requisitos formais
O **Shulchan Arukh** estabelece [Yoreh De'ah 268]:

- *Milá* (circuncisão) primeiro. Se já foi circuncidado, tira-se uma gota de sangue da aliança (*hatafat dam brit*), sem bênção.
- *Tevilá* (imersão) diante de um beit din.
- Aceitação das mitzvot (*kabalat mitzvot*).
- Se o órgão foi amputado, a milá não é exigida e basta a imersão.

### O modelo de Rut
Rut é o arquétipo do convertido sincero. Ela insistiu mesmo depois que Noemi tentou dissuadi-la: "Para onde fores, irei... teu povo é o meu povo, e teu D'us é o meu D'us" (*Amech ami velohayich elohai*) [Rut 1:16-17]. O Talmud deriva daí o processo de dissuasão e de instrução [Yevamot 47b].

## Quando a pessoa NÃO PODE (ou não deve) se converter

### Motivos externos
O Talmud discute convertidos por casamento, riquezas, poder ou medo [Yevamot 24b]. Alguns sábios rejeitam todos eles. Rabi Nechemiá aceita o caso consumado, e a Halachá ensina que, uma vez realizada a conversão, a pessoa é considerada judia (veja Rambam, *Issurei Bi'á* 13:14-17). Mesmo assim, o beit din não deve aceitar candidatos nessas circunstâncias desde o início. Esta síntese vem do meu conhecimento da tradição, não das passagens recuperadas.

### Aceitação parcial
Quem aceita toda a Torah exceto um detalhe não é aceito [Bekhorot 30b]. A aceitação das mitzvot precisa ser completa.

### Épocas especiais
Não se aceitavam convertidos nos tempos de David e Salomão, para evitar conversões por interesse na grandeza do reino [Yevamot 24b].

### Povos proibidos: já não se aplicam
A Torah proíbe amonitas e moabitas (Deuteronômio 23:4) e restringe egípcios e edomitas até a terceira geração (23:8-9). A Mishná ensina que Senaqueribe misturou as nações, de modo que ninguém sabe mais a origem de ninguém [Mishná, Yadayim 4:4]. Por isso essas restrições deixaram de ser aplicadas na prática.

## Restrições de parentesco após a conversão
O convertido mantém algumas proibições. Pela Torah, ele poderia se casar com a mãe ou irmã (também convertidas), mas os sábios proibiram, para que não se diga que "passamos de uma santidade grave para uma mais leve" [Shulchan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 269]. Se o casal já era casado antes da conversão em outras relações proibidas, não precisa se separar [ibid.]. Segundo o Rambam, duas irmãs convertidas por parte de mãe obrigam o homem a se separar de uma delas [Mishneh Torah, Forbidden Intercourse 14:15]. Isso afeta o casamento, não a possibilidade de converter-se.

## Observações práticas

- As práticas variam entre comunidades e entre beit dins, especialmente quanto ao grau de observância exigido hoje.
- Menores podem ser convertidos por um beit din (Ketubot 11a) e têm o direito de protestar ao atingir a maioridade. Esta informação vem do meu conhecimento, não das fontes recuperadas.

Para orientação pessoal, consulte seu rabino local ou *posek* (For personal guidance, consult your local rabbi or posek).

answer:
It sounds like your friend is staying because of who you are together, not out of convenience, though no one can promise the future. A friend who is calm and honest with you, who credits you for helping her become social, and who stayed close even when others mocked her choice is showing real loyalty. Jewish tradition also says that friendship like this is something you tend, not just something you hope will last.

## Key Takeaways

- Real friendship shows in how someone acts with you, and she is her calmest, most honest self with you.
- Pirkei Avot teaches "acquire a friend for yourself," which means friendship is built and kept by both people.
- Ecclesiastes says two are stronger than one, and you each gave the other that strength.
- Being called "the weird kids" is painful, but you two chose each other anyway, which is rare and valuable.
- The retrieved sources (about Bilam in Numbers 23:3) don't address friendship, so what follows draws on my knowledge of Torah tradition.

## What You're Describing

You say she may have "mirrored" other people's personalities, but with you she is calm and honest. That matters. Someone who adapts to everyone may be unsure who she is, and with you she doesn't need to perform. She even said you made her social, because watching you showed her she could do it too. That is a person giving you credit, not using you.

You also never cared when people bullied you over your friend. That is *chesed* (loving-kindness) and loyalty, and it likely built her trust in you.

## What Jewish Sources Say About Friendship

- **Pirkei Avot 1:6** says "*Aseh lecha rav, u'kneh lecha chaver*," "Make for yourself a teacher, and acquire for yourself a friend." The word "acquire" suggests you invest in friendship, and it doesn't just happen.
- **Ecclesiastes 4:9–10, 12** says "Two are better than one... for if one falls, the other will lift up his friend... and a threefold cord is not quickly broken." You each lifted the other out of loneliness.
- **Proverbs 17:17** says "A friend loves at all times." True friends stay in hard times, as you both did.
- **Ta'anit 23a** tells of Choni, who said "*O chavruta o mituta*," "Either companionship or death." The Sages understood how deeply people need a true companion.
- **Proverbs 27:17** says "Iron sharpens iron." Your friend credits you for helping her grow, and you've likely grown from her too.

## A Connection to Bilam

The sources retrieved here show Bilam going to seek God's word and report back to Balak [Numbers 23:3]. Bilam is a figure who bends his words to please those who hire him. This is my own drash, not a classical reading, but it contrasts with what you describe. A true friend doesn't reshape herself for whoever is in front of her, and honesty is where trust begins.

## Will She Stay?

I can't know the future, and friendships change as people grow. Still, these things tend to help a friendship last:

- **Keep being honest** with each other, including when something bothers you.
- **Let each other grow.** She became more social, and a good friendship can hold that without jealousy.
- **Make room for other people** without it feeling like betrayal. Having other friends doesn't mean she values you less.
- **Tell her what she means to you**, the way she told you.

If you're ever unsure, you can simply ask her, calmly and honestly, which is how the two of you work best. If the school's teasing or loneliness weighs on you, a trusted teacher, parent, or counselor can help too.

answer:
Job's **Sabeans** are the people of **Sheba** (*Shva*, שבא), a trading people of Arabia, and nothing in the text or in historical evidence links them to Shiva worship. The Quranic **Sabians** (*Sabi'un*) are a different group with a different name, and the similarity in English spelling is misleading.

## Key Takeaways

- Job 1:15 says "וַתִּפֹּל שְׁבָא וַתִּקָּחֵם" ("Sheba fell upon them and took them"), referring to a people named Sheba, not a religion.
- Genesis 10:7 places Sheba in the line of Cush, through Raamah, as an ethnic or geographic grouping.
- The Quranic Sabians (*al-Sabi'un*) are a separate term, probably referring to a baptizing or astral-worshipping community such as the Mandaeans.
- There is no evidence connecting Sheba or Arabian religion with Shiva worship. Phallic-looking standing stones in the Near East belong to local traditions.
- Your underlying question, whether the Tanakh knows of India, is a fair one, and there are real texts to consider.

## The Sources: Who Is Sheba?

**Job 1:15** describes a raid in which Sheba took the oxen and donkeys and killed the servants. The text names a nation acting as raiders, not a cult.

**Genesis 10:7** lists "וּבְנֵי רַעְמָה שְׁבָא וּדְדָן" ("and the sons of Raamah: Sheba and Dedan"). This is the Cushite Sheba.

The Torah has other Shevas, which is likely why the name is confusing:

- Sheba son of Yoktan, in the line of Shem [Genesis 10:28].
- Sheba son of Yokshan, a son of Keturah and Abraham [Genesis 25:3].

Scholars generally connect these to the Sabaean civilization of southern Arabia (modern Yemen), known from its own inscriptions. This is the same kingdom as the **Queen of Sheba** [I Kings 10]. Other verses depict Sheba as a caravan and spice-trading people [Ezekiel 27:22, Job 6:19]. A raiding party coming from the south or east of Uz fits that picture. This historical background comes from my general knowledge, not the retrieved passages.

## Sabeans vs. Quranic "Sabians"

These are different words in Arabic. The kingdom is *Saba'* (سبأ), which the Quran discusses in Surah 27 and 34 as the land of the queen who met Solomon. The *Sabi'un* (الصابئون, Quran 2:62, 5:69, 22:17) is a religious community, with a name related to immersion. It is usually linked to the Mandaeans or to star-worshippers of Harran. English "Sabean" has been used for both, which causes the confusion. Neither is connected to Shiva.

## The Shiva *Linga* Hypothesis

I would not accept this theory, for several reasons:

- Ancient South Arabian religion centered on deities such as Almaqah (a moon-associated god), with its own temples and inscriptions. Nothing identifies Shaivism there.
- Upright stones (*matzevot*, מצבות, and Arabian *baetyls*) were widespread in the ancient Near East. Resemblance in shape does not show a shared origin. The Torah prohibits them [Deuteronomy 16:22].
- Ancient Indian Ocean trade between Arabia and India certainly existed, so some cultural contact is plausible. But contact is not the same as Sabeans being "disciples of Shiva."

## Does the Tradition Ignore India?

It doesn't entirely. Several texts touch on it:

- **Hodu** (הוד), usually identified with India, appears in Esther 1:1, "מֵהֹדּוּ וְעַד־כּוּשׁ" ("from India to Kush").
- The Talmud says Abraham gave his sons by concubines "the name of impurity" [Sanhedrin 91a], and Genesis 25:6 says he sent them "eastward" (*kedmah*). Some later commentators and writers connected this to eastern religions and magic, though this is an interpretive tradition, not a clear identification.
- Rabbinic and medieval writers, including Maimonides, knew of Eastern idolatry, but they generally describe it in broad categories of *avodah zarah* rather than by specific Hindu names.

The Tanakh's focus is on the nations that interacted with Israel: Canaan, Egypt, Mesopotamia, Arabia, and Persia. Silence about Hindu practice largely reflects geography and not a deliberate omission.

answer:
Your question points to a famous debate in **Eruvin 13b**, where the School of Shammai and the School of Hillel argue for two and a half years over whether it would have been better for humanity not to have been created. The conclusion is that it would have been better not to have been created, but now that humanity exists, "let him examine his deeds" (*yefashpesh b'ma'asav*). Job 3 does voice a similar wish, but he speaks from personal agony, while the Talmud poses the question as a general, almost philosophical one.

## Key Takeaways

- Eruvin 13b records Beit Shammai's view that it is better for man not to have been created and Beit Hillel's view that it is better that he was created.
- The sages "voted" that non-creation would have been better, but they turned the conclusion into a call for moral accountability.
- Job 3:3 and 3:11 express a personal wish never to have been born. He does not claim that humanity as a whole should not exist.
- The Torah's opening chapters, especially humanity in God's image, are the background against which Beit Hillel and Job's critics respond.
- The Talmud converts a despairing question into an ethical task: if we are here, our deeds are what matter.

## The Talmudic Debate (Eruvin 13b)

*Note on sources:* The retrieved passage from Eruvin 13b is from the same page, but it deals with Rabbi Meir and the laws of writing a *get*, not with the creation debate. What follows about the debate comes from my knowledge of the Talmud.

The Gemara reports that for two and a half years Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel disagreed:

- **Beit Shammai:** it would have been better for man not to have been created than to have been created.
- **Beit Hillel:** it is better that he was created than that he was not.

They counted votes and concluded: "It would have been better had man not been created, but now that he has been created, let him examine his deeds" (some versions: "let him scrutinize his future actions"). Rashi explains the pessimism in terms of sin and its consequences: a human being can fail morally, and that risk makes existence precarious.

## Job's Parallel, and Where It Differs

**Job 3:3** says: "יֹאבַד יוֹם אִוָּלֶד בּוֹ" ("Let the day on which I was born perish"), along with the night that said "a man-child is conceived." **Job 3:11** says: "לָמָּה לֹּא מֵרֶחֶם אָמוּת, מִבֶּטֶן יָצָאתִי וְאֶגְוָע" ("Why did I not die from the womb; why did I not expire as I came out of the belly?").

The overlap is real, because both texts say that non-existence would have been preferable. But there are important differences:

- **Scope:** Job curses his own birth. Beit Shammai makes a claim about the human condition in general.
- **Cause:** Job's wish comes from catastrophic loss and suffering, and it is not about sin. Beit Shammai's view, as Rashi reads it, is about moral risk.
- **Tone:** Job's statement is a lament, and he is not offering a theory. The Talmud's is a formal legal-style deliberation, ending in a vote.
- **Resolution:** Job's wish is eventually met by God's speech from the whirlwind (Job 38–41), which does not answer "why" but widens the frame beyond human experience. The Talmud's resolution is the practical charge to examine our deeds.

Similar laments appear elsewhere, such as Jeremiah 20:14–18 and Kohelet 4:2–3, so Job is part of a wider biblical stream of existential protest.

## The Creation Texts as Backdrop

Beit Hillel's position fits the Torah's affirmation of creation. **Genesis 1:26–27** says God made humanity "בְּצַלְמֵנוּ כִּדְמוּתֵנוּ" ("in Our image, after Our likeness") and "בְּצֶלֶם אֱלֹהִים בָּרָא אֹתוֹ" ("in the image of God He created him"). If humans bear the divine image, their existence has dignity and purpose. Genesis 1:31 also declares creation "very good" (*tov me'od*), and the Midrash (Bereishit Rabbah 9:5) famously links this "very good" to humanity, even to death. Both of these are from my own knowledge, not the retrieved passages.

**Genesis 1:1** and **2:4** describe heaven and earth being created and brought forth deliberately. Creation is presented as purposeful, not accidental, which gives Beit Hillel their footing.

## Why the Debate Resolves the Way It Does

The tension is between two true observations. Human beings are capable of great sin and suffering, which supports Beit Shammai. Human beings are also made in God's image and capable of great good, which supports Beit Hillel. The vote does not declare Beit Hillel wrong about the value of life. It acknowledges honestly how much can go wrong, and then moves to the only question that can be acted on: what do we do now?

Later Jewish thought leans toward Beit Hillel's spirit. The Ramchal (*Derekh Hashem*, *Mesillat Yesharim*) teaches that creation exists so God can bestow good, and that humanity's task is to earn closeness to God. Seen this way, "examine your deeds" does not concede defeat. It names the purpose of being created at all.

answer:
Pshat sources suggest that a lasting spiritual impression forms through a few things: words and experiences that reach the heart, repeated review, concrete action, and early, sustained transmission. No sources were retrieved for this question, so everything below comes from my own knowledge of the tradition. Please verify the citations before relying on them.

I'm reading your question as "Can you give sources, more *pshat*-based (straightforward), on how a lasting spiritual impression is made?" Tell me if you meant something else.

## Key Takeaways

- The Torah's own model is words "on your heart," repeated until sharp, and tied to daily life [Deuteronomy 6:6-9].
- Experience must be remembered and handed down, or it fades [Deuteronomy 4:9].
- Repetition matters: the Talmud says reviewing 100 times is not the same as 101 [Chagigah 9b].
- Action shapes the heart, and deeds are the "roots" of wisdom [Sefer HaChinuch 16; Avot 3:17].
- Early learning sticks most strongly, but real understanding can take years [Avot 4:20; Deuteronomy 29:3 with Rashi].

## Torah Text: The Basic Method

### Words on the heart, repeated

"וְהָיוּ הַדְּבָרִים הָאֵלֶּה... עַל לְבָבֶךָ. וְשִׁנַּנְתָּם לְבָנֶיךָ" (*"And these words shall be upon your heart. And you shall teach them diligently to your children"*) [Deuteronomy 6:6-7].

The verse gives a sequence: first the words are on your heart, then you repeat them. *Rashi* on 6:7, drawing on the *Sifrei*, explains *veshinantam* as words "sharp" in your mouth, so that you answer without hesitation when asked.

The verse then ties this to ordinary life: sitting at home, walking, lying down, rising. Lasting impressions come from constant, embedded exposure rather than one peak moment.

### Experience plus memory

"רַק הִשָּׁמֶר לְךָ... פֶּן תִּשְׁכַּח אֶת הַדְּבָרִים אֲשֶׁר רָאוּ עֵינֶיךָ" (*"Only guard yourself... lest you forget the things your eyes saw"*) [Deuteronomy 4:9].

Even Sinai, the most powerful experience imaginable, needs active guarding and retelling. The text assumes spiritual impressions fade unless they are deliberately preserved and passed on. *Ramban* on this verse stresses the obligation to keep Sinai alive in memory.

### Song as a memory device

God tells Moses to write a song and "put it in their mouths" so it will be a witness that is "not forgotten from the mouths of their descendants" [Deuteronomy 31:19-21]. Rhythm and melody make content durable.

### A new heart

Jeremiah describes the ideal as Torah written inwardly: "נָתַתִּי אֶת תּוֹרָתִי בְּקִרְבָּם וְעַל לִבָּם אֶכְתֲּבֶנָּה" (*"I will put My Torah within them and write it on their hearts"*) [Jeremiah 31:32]. Proverbs uses similar imagery: "write them on the tablet of your heart" [Proverbs 3:3].

## Rabbinic Sources

### Repetition

- **Chagigah 9b**: one who reviews his chapter 100 times is not like one who reviews it 101 times. Small amounts of added effort create real differences.
- **Eruvin 54b**: the Talmud describes teaching in repeated rounds until the material is fixed, and learns from the verse "שִׂימָהּ בְּפִיהֶם" (*"place it in their mouths"*) that a teacher must repeat until the student has it.

### Action shapes the inner self

- **Sefer HaChinuch, Mitzvah 16**: "אַחַר הַפְּעֻלּוֹת נִמְשָׁכִים הַלְּבָבוֹת" (*"hearts are drawn after actions"*). External practice forms inner character.
- **Rambam, Hilchot De'ot 1:7** teaches that one acquires traits by repeating the corresponding actions again and again.
- **Avot 3:17** (3:22 in some editions) compares one whose wisdom exceeds his deeds to a tree with many branches and few roots, which the wind uproots. One whose deeds exceed his wisdom is like a tree with many roots, which stands firm. Lasting impact requires practice, not just knowledge.

### Timing and age

**Avot 4:20** quotes Elisha ben Avuya: learning as a child is like ink on fresh paper, while learning in old age is like ink on erased paper. This is a pshat-level observation about how early impressions endure. Note that this teaching comes from a figure who ultimately abandoned the tradition, though it is preserved in the Mishnah.

### Understanding takes time

"וְלֹא נָתַן ה' לָכֶם לֵב לָדַעַת... עַד הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה" (*"God did not give you a heart to know... until this day"*) [Deuteronomy 29:3]. *Rashi*, citing **Avodah Zarah 5b**, explains that it took forty years for Israel to truly grasp their teacher's mind. A deep impression can lag behind the experience.

## Why These Sources Seem to Differ

They emphasize different entry points:

- **Heart first**: Deuteronomy 6:6 and Jeremiah 31 stress inner receptivity.
- **Action first**: Sefer HaChinuch and Avot 3:17 hold that deeds build the heart.
- **Memory and repetition**: Chagigah and Eruvin focus on retention.

These approaches are generally read as complementary. Na'aseh venishma ("we will do and we will hear") [Exodus 24:7] is often cited as the model that combines commitment, action, and understanding.

If you'd like, I can go deeper on one angle, such as the Chassidic reading of *al levavecha* or the educational ideas in Proverbs 22:6.

answer:
Judaism does not teach that non-Jews, or people who hold different beliefs, are condemned to hell. The mainstream Jewish view is that **the righteous of all nations have a share in the World to Come** (*Olam Haba*), and that hell (*Gehinnom*) is generally understood as temporary purification rather than eternal damnation. This answer draws on my general knowledge of the tradition, since no specific sources were retrieved.

## Key Takeaways

- The **Tosefta** and **Maimonides** teach that righteous non-Jews have a share in the World to Come.
- For non-Jews, the baseline expectation is keeping the **Seven Noahide Laws**, not conversion.
- *Gehinnom* is typically understood as a period of purification, lasting up to 12 months for most souls.
- There is a real debate about what counts as "belief," and about whether specific theology is required of non-Jews.
- Ultimate judgment belongs to God, not to us.

## The Core Source: Righteous of the Nations

The **Tosefta** states: "The righteous of the nations of the world have a share in the World to Come" (*chasidei umot haolam yesh lahem chelek le'olam haba*) [Tosefta Sanhedrin 13:2]. This is the view of **Rabbi Yehoshua**, against **Rabbi Eliezer**, who read Psalms 9:18 more restrictively.

**Maimonides** rules like Rabbi Yehoshua [Mishneh Torah, Laws of Kings 8:11]. He writes that whoever accepts and observes the Seven Noahide Laws is among the "righteous of the nations."

Maimonides adds a condition: this must be done because God commanded it, not merely out of logic. Some texts have a variant reading of this passage, and later authorities discuss it.

## The Seven Noahide Laws

These are the universal baseline [Sanhedrin 56a]:

- Do not worship idols
- Do not blaspheme
- Do not murder
- Do not commit sexual immorality
- Do not steal
- Establish courts of justice
- Do not eat a limb torn from a living animal

## What Is Gehinnom?

Most classical sources describe *Gehinnom* as a place of cleansing, not eternal punishment. The Mishnah says the judgment of the wicked in Gehinnom lasts **twelve months** [Mishnah Eduyot 2:10].

The Talmud notes that Jewish sinners are also judged there, so it is not reserved for outsiders [Rosh Hashanah 16b-17a]. Some categories of exceptionally wicked people are described as being destroyed or cut off, but this is a minority of cases and is debated.

## Where Opinions Differ

- **Maimonides** also lists foundational beliefs (the 13 Principles) as necessary for a Jew's share in the World to Come. For non-Jews, his requirement is Noahide observance.
- **Rabbi Menachem Meiri** (13th-14th century) held that nations bound by law and morality are not subject to the harsh rulings applied to ancient idolaters.
- **Rabbi Eliezer's** stricter view in the Talmud [Sanhedrin 105a] exists, but it is not the accepted halacha.
- Some mystical sources discuss souls' journeys in more complex ways, including reincarnation (*gilgul*).

## Why It Matters Theologically

Judaism sees a covenant with Noah's descendants (all humanity) and a separate covenant with Israel. Jews have 613 commandments, and others are not expected to keep them. Being good and doing right is the path for everyone.

Our tradition also stresses humility. We do not claim to know exactly how God judges any individual, since "the Judge of all the earth will do justice" [Genesis 18:25].

If you're asking out of personal curiosity or concern about someone you know, it's worth discussing with a rabbi who can speak to your specific situation. For personal guidance, consult your local rabbi or posek.

answer:
Your question seems to have been cut off, so I'm assuming you're asking **why joy is permitted, or even required, in Judaism**. Joy is allowed when it is joy in serving God and in the good He gives, and Deuteronomy treats the absence of that joy as a serious failing. Ecclesiastes warns only against joy as an end in itself, cut off from purpose. If you meant something else, tell me and I'll adjust.

## Key Takeaways

- **Deuteronomy 28:47** names the lack of joy in serving God, despite abundance, as the reason for the curses.
- **Ecclesiastes 2:1-2** critiques joy and laughter pursued for their own sake, not joy itself.
- Rambam and the Talmud present *simcha shel mitzvah* (joy in a commandment) as a spiritual ideal.
- Joy is allowed when it is directed toward God, gratitude, and meaning.

## The Plain Meaning of the Sources

### Deuteronomy 28:47: joy as part of service

The verse reads: "תַּחַת אֲשֶׁר לֹא־עָבַדְתָּ אֶת־יְהוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ בְּשִׂמְחָה וּבְטוּב לֵבָב מֵרֹב כֹּל" ("Because you did not serve the LORD your God with joy and goodness of heart, out of abundance of everything") [Deuteronomy 28:47].

The complaint here is not only about neglected mitzvot. It is about the *spirit* in which they were done, especially given the abundance God had provided. Joy is part of gratitude, so serving God without it can reflect a failure to appreciate what one has been given.

### Ecclesiastes 2:1-2: joy as an end in itself

Kohelet says: "אָמַרְתִּי אֲנִי בְּלִבִּי לְכָה־נָּא אֲנַסְּכָה בְשִׂמְחָה וּרְאֵה בְטוֹב וְהִנֵּה גַם־הוּא הָבֶל" ("I said in my heart, 'Come, let me test you with joy, and see goodness'; but behold, that too is vanity"). He continues: "לִשְׂחוֹק אָמַרְתִּי מְהוֹלָל וּלְשִׂמְחָה מַה־זֹּה עֹשָׂה" ("Of laughter I said, 'It is mad,' and of joy, 'What does it accomplish?'") [Ecclesiastes 2:1-2].

Here joy is a *experiment*, pursued as a way to find meaning. It fails because it was sought for its own sake. Elsewhere Kohelet praises joy when it is received as a gift from God (e.g., Ecclesiastes 8:15, 9:7; this is from my own knowledge, not the retrieved passages). The two passages are therefore not in conflict. Joy detached from purpose is empty, while joy rooted in service and gratitude is a divine expectation.

## Later Tradition

- **Rambam** rules that the joy a person feels in doing a mitzvah and in loving God is itself a great act of service. He says one who holds back from this joy deserves to be called a sinner and a fool, and he cites Deuteronomy 28:47 [Rambam, Mishneh Torah, Hilchot Lulav 8:15].
- **The Talmud** teaches that the Divine Presence rests on a person not out of sadness, laziness, frivolity, or idle talk, but out of the joy of a mitzvah [Shabbat 30b].
- **Psalms** says "עִבְדוּ אֶת־יְהוָה בְּשִׂמְחָה" ("Serve the LORD with joy") [Psalms 100:2].
- **Rebbe Nachman of Breslov** taught that it is a great mitzvah to be happy always [Likutei Moharan II:24].

## Why the Apparent Tension?

The sources differ because they speak about different kinds of joy:

- **Hedonistic joy** (Kohelet's experiment) is pleasure pursued to fill an inner void, and it fails.
- **Joy of mitzvah and gratitude** (Deuteronomy, Rambam) comes from recognizing purpose and blessing, and it is encouraged.

Judaism does not ask us to avoid joy. It asks us to anchor it in something larger than ourselves.

answer:
## Direct Answer

The Torah contains real precursors to many of Freud's ideas, including the hidden layers of the mind, dreams as expressions of inner thoughts, the healing power of speech, and the inner struggle of drives. It would be inaccurate, though, to say it contains *all* of them. Freud's core claims, such as pansexual drive theory, religion as collective neurosis, and psychological determinism, conflict with Torah, so a fair dvar Torah should show both the parallels and the limits.

## Key Takeaways

- Chazal anticipated the idea of a hidden inner life, especially in how they understood dreams and the *yetzer hara* (evil inclination).
- The retrieved sources show the "talking cure" intuition: a suffering person is revived when someone listens (Sichot HaRan), and emotional state affects spiritual functioning (Kol Bo).
- The Torah's defense mechanisms (denial, projection, rationalization) appear in narrative form, though the Torah treats them as moral failures, not just mental mechanisms.
- Torah rejects Freud's determinism and his view of religion as illusion, because *bechira* (free will) is foundational.
- "Precursor" is more accurate than "source": the Torah describes the human heart, but it is not a psychoanalytic textbook.

## Parallels That Hold Up

### 1. The Unconscious and the Hidden Chambers of the Heart

"נֵר ה׳ נִשְׁמַת אָדָם חֹפֵשׂ כׇּל חַדְרֵי בָטֶן", "The soul of man is the lamp of the Lord, searching all the chambers of the innermost being" [Proverbs 20:27]. The Torah assumes there are inner chambers a person doesn't fully see.

Chazal went further regarding dreams: "אֵין אָדָם רוֹאֶה בַּחֲלוֹמוֹ אֶלָּא מֵהִרְהוּרֵי לִבּוֹ", "A person is shown in a dream only the thoughts of his own heart" [Berakhot 55b]. The Gemara also says "חֲלוֹמָא דְלָא מִתְפַּשַּׁר כְּאִגַּרְתָּא דְלָא מִתְקְרְיָא", "An uninterpreted dream is like an unread letter" [Berakhot 55a]. This is close to Freud's view that dreams carry meaning needing interpretation. Yosef's interpretations (Genesis 40–41) are the biblical model.

### 2. The Talking Cure

The retrieved sources speak directly to this. **Sichot HaRan** (Rebbe Nachman of Breslov) says that some people carry great and terrible suffering and cannot tell what is in their hearts. They want to speak but have no one to speak to. He adds that when someone comes with a cheerful face, he can "literally revive them" (*lehachayot otam mamash*), and reviving a person is "a very great thing" [Sichot HaRan 43:6].

This echoes the Talmudic reading of "דְּאָגָה בְלֶב אִישׁ יַשְׁחֶנָּה", "Worry in a man's heart weighs him down" [Proverbs 12:25]. One opinion says to dismiss it from the mind. The other reads *yasichena* as "let him tell it to others" [Yoma 75a]. Hannah's words, "וָאֶשְׁפֹּךְ אֶת נַפְשִׁי לִפְנֵי ה׳", "I poured out my soul before the Lord" [I Samuel 1:15], and the verbal *vidui* (confession) of *teshuva* show the same idea: speech releases and transforms.

### 3. The State of the Mind Shapes Function

The **Kol Bo** rules that if a person finds his mind and heart disturbed, he may not pray until his mind settles. One who returns from a journey exhausted or distressed should not pray until his mind cools [Kol Bo 11:108]. Halacha thus recognizes that emotional disturbance affects the ability to function spiritually. Freud's insight into the weight of inner states is more clinical, but the premise is shared.

### 4. Inner Drives in Conflict

"כִּי יֵצֶר לֵב הָאָדָם רַע מִנְּעֻרָיו", "The inclination of man's heart is evil from his youth" [Genesis 8:21]. Chazal describe the *yetzer hara* as present from birth and the *yetzer hatov* as maturing later (this is from my own knowledge; see Avot d'Rabbi Natan 16 and Nedarim 31b).

Some compare this to the id and superego. The comparison is loose. Chazal say the *yetzer hara* is necessary for building, marriage, and livelihood, and that it is "very good" in Genesis 1:31 [Bereishit Rabbah 9:7]. It is a drive to be channeled, not a pathology to be explained away.

### 5. Channeling Drives (Sublimation)

"If this repulsive one meets you, drag him to the beit midrash" [Kiddushin 30b]. The Rambam, in *Shemoneh Perakim* ch. 3 and *Hilchot De'ot* 2:1, compares the sages to physicians of the soul who diagnose and treat character illnesses. This is psychological thinking in a Torah framework, aimed at *avodat Hashem* and not at self-understanding alone.

### 6. Defense Mechanisms in Narrative

- **Denial:** Sarah says "לֹא צָחַקְתִּי", "I did not laugh" [Genesis 18:15].
- **Projection and blame-shifting:** Adam blames Chava, and she blames the snake [Genesis 3:12–13].
- **Rationalization:** Aharon says "I threw it into the fire and out came this calf" [Exodus 32:24].
- **Repressed guilt resurfacing:** Years later the brothers say, "We saw the anguish of his soul when he pleaded with us and we did not listen" [Genesis 42:21].
- **Suppression with warning:** "לַפֶּתַח חַטָּאת רֹבֵץ", "Sin crouches at the door" [Genesis 4:7], God's warning to Kayin before he acts.

## Where Torah and Freud Diverge

- **Free will:** Torah insists on *bechira*, "וּבָחַרְתָּ בַּחַיִּים", "choose life" [Deuteronomy 30:19]. Freud's psychic determinism is incompatible with this.
- **Religion as illusion:** Freud's *The Future of an Illusion* treats belief as wish-fulfillment, and *Moses and Monotheism* claims Moses was Egyptian and was murdered. These contradict the Torah's account.
- **Sexuality as the root of everything:** The Torah recognizes the power of desire but does not reduce all motivation to it. The Oedipal theory has no basis in the Torah. Cases like Reuven and Bilhah [Genesis 35:22] are treated as specific sins, not universal drives.
- **Goal of the healing:** Freud aims at adjustment and insight. The Torah aims at *teshuva*, *kedusha*, and relationship with God.

## A Dvar Torah Framing

You could build the dvar Torah around Proverbs 20:27: the Torah says there are "chambers of the innermost being," and the task is to let the *ner Hashem* illuminate them. Freud noticed the chambers, but the Torah insists on whose lamp does the searching and why. Chazal's language of hearts, dreams, speech, and inclinations shows a sophisticated awareness of the inner life, even though it uses different categories and has a different goal.

I'd suggest picking two or three parallels (dreams, the talking cure, and the *yetzer*) and going deep, rather than claiming every Freudian idea is in the Torah. That framing is more intellectually honest and will hold up better with a thoughtful audience. Sources 1 and 2 above come from the retrieved passages. The remaining citations come from my own knowledge of the tradition and are worth verifying inside before you present.

answer:
Your framing is a classic one in Jewish thought: the Torah's permission of slavery sits in real tension with God's absolute morality, and the tradition's response is to **ask** without claiming to **judge** God. The Torah does not abolish slavery outright, but it surrounds it with restrictions, and the Sages and later commentators wrestled openly with why. Abraham, Jeremiah, and Kohelet all model protest and questioning that stay within covenantal faith.

## Key Takeaways

- Jewish tradition treats questioning God's ways as legitimate, even exemplary, when it comes from within the covenant (Abraham, Jeremiah).
- The Torah regulates and humanizes slavery (limits, release, Shabbat rest, covenantal inclusion) rather than simply endorsing it.
- Maimonides and others explain the lack of abolition as divine gradualism, which is a historical-pedagogic answer, not a full resolution.
- "Torah speaks in human language" (*dibra Torah kilshon bnei adam*) suggests the text meets people where they are.
- Your caution is sound, but "we don't know" should motivate moral seriousness, not complacency.

## The Plain Text: Regulation, Not Idealization

**Leviticus 25:44-46** permits acquiring "eved v'amah" (male and female slaves) from the surrounding nations, and the passage ends by contrasting this with fellow Israelites: "וּבְאַחֵיכֶם בְּנֵי־יִשְׂרָאֵל אִישׁ בְּאָחִיו לֹא־תִרְדֶּה בוֹ בְּפָרֶךְ" ("But over your brothers, the children of Israel, one over another, you shall not rule with rigor"). This verse is not easy, and it should not be softened. But it sits within a larger framework (from my own knowledge, not the retrieved passages):

- **Exodus 21:2** requires the Hebrew servant to go free in the seventh year.
- **Exodus 21:26-27** frees a slave whose master injures him.
- **Deuteronomy 5:14** grounds Shabbat rest in the slave's dignity: "so that your servant and maidservant may rest as you do," followed by "remember that you were a slave in Egypt."
- **Deuteronomy 23:16** forbids returning an escaped slave, which is remarkable for the ancient world.

**Genesis 17:12-13** is also relevant. Slaves, whether "born in the house" or "bought with money," are included in the covenant of circumcision. The slave is a covenantal person, not mere property.

## Why Not Abolish? The Classical Answers

**Maimonides** [Guide for the Perplexed 3:32] argues that God works through gradual process, as with sacrifices. A people cannot be moved abruptly from the universal practice of its age, so the Torah channels and restricts the practice, planting seeds that point beyond it. Some modern thinkers extend this into a trajectory of moral development. Others are uneasy with this, since it implies the text's ethics are bounded by its era.

**Berakhot 31b** and other passages state that "the Torah speaks in the language of human beings." This is Talmudic precedent for the idea that the Torah's legislation addresses human reality, which is close to your point about how the infinite engages the finite.

**Kiddushin 22b** reads Leviticus 25:55, "For the children of Israel are My servants," as: "My servants, and not servants of servants." This is a theological limit. Ultimate ownership belongs to God, so no human lordship is absolute.

**Kiddushin 20a** says "whoever acquires a Hebrew servant acquires a master for himself," because the master must treat him as an equal in food and lodging.

**Maimonides** [Mishneh Torah, Laws of Slaves 9:8] writes that although one may work a Canaanite slave permanently, the path of piety and wisdom is not to be cruel, and he should provide them with the same food and drink. He cites that God's compassion extends to all creatures. This is the tradition's own moral critique of the legal minimum.

## Your Framework: Tension as Productive

Your point about the "unitary infinite" meeting the physical world touches a real theme. The text itself preserves the tension rather than hiding it.

**Genesis 18:25** has Abraham say, "Shall the Judge of all the earth not do justice?" Tradition reads this as praiseworthy, not presumptuous.

**Jeremiah 12:1** begins "צַדִּיק אַתָּה יְהוָה כִּי אָרִיב אֵלֶיךָ" ("You are righteous, O Lord, when I contend with You, yet I would speak of judgments with You"). The prophet affirms God's righteousness and, in the same breath, presses his complaint about the prosperity of the wicked. That is your formula exactly: faith plus protest.

**Ecclesiastes 8:14** names the same dissonance as *hevel* (vapor, absurdity), where the righteous receive what the wicked deserve. Kohelet does not resolve it. The canon includes his unresolved voice.

These two passages concern theodicy rather than slavery directly, so the connection is by analogy. The same posture, however, applies: the tradition protects the right to ask.

## Asking vs. "Making Ourselves God"

Your distinction is a good one. Abraham and Jeremiah argue *from* the premise that God is just, not *against* it. They don't replace divine authority with their own. Job's ending is the counterweight: the questioner is reminded of limits (Job 38).

Still, two caveats:

- **Asking should produce action.** The Torah's repeated "remember you were slaves in Egypt" points toward empathy and ethical conduct, not quiet acceptance. The tradition's later halachic development, including Maimonides' extension of kindness, shows moral intuition working within the system.
- **Humility cuts both ways.** We should avoid assuming ancient law was simply primitive, and also avoid assuming that our uncertainty means the question lacks force.

## A Hasidic Angle

The retrieved **Bat Ayin** passage (Ha'Azinu 37) is truncated, but it speaks of *avodah* (service) as the core of one's relationship to God, in Torah, prayer, and even eating and drinking when done for the Creator's will. The Hebrew root *ayin-bet-dalet* means both "slave" and "serve." In this reading, true servitude is to God alone, which echoes Kiddushin 22b: the ultimate "eved" relationship is the one that frees us from being servants of other people. This is a homiletic reading, not a direct comment on legal slavery.

answer:
The Torah does not give a single verdict on AI, since AI is not addressed directly, but Jewish tradition supplies principles for judging it. Human creativity and wisdom are widely seen as divinely sanctioned, and the Talmud treats artificially created beings with fascination rather than horror. At the same time, tradition insists that a creation is not a person, and that technology be judged by its purposes and results as well as its technical permissibility.

## Key Takeaways

- The Talmud describes sages creating artificial beings, suggesting that such creation is not inherently forbidden [Sanhedrin 65b].
- Rava's creation could not speak, and Rabbi Zeira ordered it back to dust, which marks a boundary between a human-made thing and a human being.
- Halacha often permits new technologies on technical grounds, as in the debate over electricity prepared before Shabbat [Mishpetei Uziel, OC 28].
- Some thinkers worry about technologies that comply with the letter of the law but empty it of its spirit [Karati Bekhol Lev, Re'eh 2:11].
- Whether AI is "approved" depends on its use: whether it serves wisdom, justice, and human dignity.

## The Talmudic Precedent: Rava's Man

The most direct source is [Sanhedrin 65b]: "Rava created a man (*gavra*) and sent him before Rabbi Zeira. He spoke to him, but he did not answer. He said: 'You are from the colleagues; return to your dust'" (רָבָא בְּרָא גַּבְרָא... מִן חַבְרַיָּא אַתְּ, הֲדַר לְעַפְרָיךְ).

Three points stand out:

- **Creation is possible.** Just before this passage, the Gemara says that Rabbi Hanina and Rabbi Oshaya would study *Hilchot Yetzirah* (laws of creation) and produce a calf to eat (from my background knowledge of the surrounding passage).
- **The creation was lacking.** Its inability to speak is the decisive flaw. In Jewish thought, speech (*medaber*) is the mark of the human being, as in Targum Onkelos on Genesis 2:7, where "a living soul" becomes "a speaking spirit."
- **Rabbi Zeira did not treat undoing it as murder.** This implies it lacked human status. Later authorities, such as the Chacham Tzvi (Responsa 93), discuss whether a golem can count in a *minyan* and conclude it cannot (from my training, not the retrieved passages).

Modern AI that converses fluently complicates the Talmud's test, because it does "answer." Tradition would still likely ask whether fluent speech is the same as a soul (*neshama*) or moral responsibility (*chiyuv*).

## Human Creativity as a Divine Mandate

From my background knowledge: God tells humanity to "fill the earth and subdue it" (Genesis 1:28). Bezalel is filled with "wisdom, understanding, and knowledge" to build the Mishkan (Exodus 31:3). Tradition therefore treats skilled invention as a form of partnership with creation.

The counterweight is the Tower of Babel (Genesis 11), which many read as a warning about technology that serves human pride rather than divine purpose.

## Technology and Halacha: Method vs. Outcome

The retrieved responsum from **Rabbi Ben-Zion Meir Hai Uziel** discusses preparing electricity before Shabbat so it operates on Shabbat. It engages the Yerushalmi's reasoning that Shabbat prohibits one's *act* of work, while something that proceeds on its own is judged differently (from the Yerushalmi cited in [Mishpetei Uziel, Vol. VIII, OC 28:12]). The passage shows halacha evaluating new technology through careful analogy to older categories, and that the question was contested among authorities.

By contrast, **Karati Bekhol Lev** raises a deeper worry: "Even if the technique meets the rules of halacha, the result will be problematic and will raise a question about the essence of halacha." It imagines devices operated by thought alone, making Shabbat like a weekday, and asks whether halacha is "a system of formal rules" or one that carries a value statement [Karati Bekhol Lev, Re'eh 2:11]. The source is cut off at that point, so I cannot say how the author resolves it.

This applies to AI directly. Even if a use of AI is technically permitted, one can still ask whether it undermines the values the law protects.

## Ethical Guardrails from Torah

From my own knowledge, several principles would shape a Torah view of AI:

- **Safety:** "Make a parapet for your roof" (Deuteronomy 22:8) obligates us to prevent foreseeable harm from what we build.
- **Truth and honesty:** "Distance yourself from a false matter" (Exodus 23:7) and the prohibitions on deception (*geneivat da'at*) bear on deepfakes and misleading outputs.
- **Human dignity and justice:** Judges must act with personal accountability, and Jewish law generally requires human beings, not instruments, to bear responsibility.
- **Privacy:** The concept of *hezek re'iyah* (damage by seeing) suggests concern about surveillance.
- **Torah study:** Whether AI can assist learning is debated. It may help find sources, but it cannot replace a teacher or bear halachic authority, since a *posek* must be a person accountable for the ruling.

## Why Opinions Differ

The disagreement turns on whether one stresses the permissive precedent (Rava, Hanina and Oshaya, creative partnership) or the cautionary one (Babel, the creation that cannot speak, the concern that technical compliance hollows out meaning). Both strands are authentically Jewish, and most contemporary rabbis evaluate specific uses rather than AI as a whole.

For personal guidance, consult your local rabbi or posek.

answer:
Feeling that Hashem's presence is gone after you stumbled and tried to return is very common, and it is not proof that the connection is broken. In the Torah's view, the pain you feel is part of teshuva, not evidence that it failed. Hashem is described as close to people in exactly this state, and the sources below say the door is open.

## Key Takeaways

- Hosea calls you to return even when you have "stumbled" (*kashalta*), and promises healing: "I will heal their backsliding."
- Hashem is described as especially near to the broken-hearted, so feeling broken doesn't mean being abandoned.
- Chazal and the Rambam teach that one who returns is beloved and close, not damaged or distant.
- Feelings of loss, like memory problems or feeling "less whole," deserve real care, including from a rabbi and a mental health professional.

## The Plain Meaning of Hosea

[Hosea 14:2] says, "שׁוּבָה יִשְׂרָאֵל עַד יְהֹוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ כִּי כָשַׁלְתָּ בַּעֲוֺנֶךָ" ("Return, Israel, to Hashem your God, for you have stumbled in your iniquity"). The verb *kashalta* describes a stumble, something that happens to a person on the way, not a verdict on who they are. The call to return comes *because* of the stumble.

The next verse gives the method: "קְחוּ עִמָּכֶם דְּבָרִים" ("Take words with you") [Hosea 14:3]. You don't need a perfect emotional state, just honest words: "כָּל תִּשָּׂא עָוֺן וְקַח טוֹב" ("Forgive all iniquity and accept what is good"). Then comes the promise: "אֶרְפָּא מְשׁוּבָתָם אֹהֲבֵם נְדָבָה כִּי שָׁב אַפִּי מִמֶּנּוּ" ("I will heal their backsliding, I will love them freely, for My anger has turned away from them") [Hosea 14:5].

The word "heal" (*erpa*) matters here. Hashem doesn't only forgive. He repairs.

## You Are Not Left Alone in the Exile

[Deuteronomy 30:1-3] describes a person who "returns it to his heart" (*vahashevota el levavecha*) after being driven far away. The verse says "וְשָׁב ה' אֱלֹהֶיךָ אֶת שְׁבוּתְךָ," literally "Hashem will return your captivity."

Rashi notes the unusual phrasing and, citing the Talmud [Megillah 29a], says it teaches that the Shechina is, so to speak, in exile with Israel, and that Hashem will return together with them. This is from my training, not the retrieved passages. When you feel far away, the tradition says Hashem is not standing outside the place where you feel lost.

## Closeness When Broken

These verses are from my own knowledge of Tanakh, not the retrieved passages:

- "קָרוֹב ה' לְנִשְׁבְּרֵי לֵב" ("Hashem is close to the broken-hearted") [Psalms 34:19].
- "לֵב נִשְׁבָּר וְנִדְכֶּה אֱלֹהִים לֹא תִבְזֶה" ("A broken and crushed heart, God, You will not despise") [Psalms 51:19].
- "אֶת דַּכָּא וּשְׁפַל רוּחַ" ("with the crushed and lowly of spirit I dwell") [Isaiah 57:15].

The sense of absence is often what a sensitive soul feels after a fall, and it is not the same as absence itself.

## What Chazal Say About Returning

- **Great is teshuva**, for it reaches the Throne of Glory [Yoma 86a].
- **Where baalei teshuva stand**, even completely righteous people cannot stand [Berakhot 34b].
- **Rambam, Hilchot Teshuva 7:7** says a person who returns should not imagine he is far from the level of the righteous because of his sins. He is beloved and desirable to the Creator as if he had never sinned. Rambam adds that the one who was separate from Hashem yesterday now clings to the Shechina.

Rambam also teaches that teshuva has stages: stopping, regret, confession, and resolving for the future. Even if you slip again, each sincere return counts.

## About the "Piece of Me" You Feel Is Missing

I can't know exactly what you saw or what you're experiencing, but I want to be careful. Feeling that you lost memory, a piece of yourself, or your sense of Hashem can be a spiritual experience of shame and grief. It can also be your mind and body reacting to distress, guilt, or something disturbing you saw. These can overlap, and neither is a sign that you are spiritually ruined.

Shame tends to say "I am ruined." Teshuva says "I did something, and I can return." Those are different messages, and the Torah speaks in the second voice.

Some practical suggestions:

- Talk to a rabbi or mentor you trust, ideally someone experienced with teshuva and recovery. You don't need to share details.
- If you are having memory trouble, numbness, intrusive images, or anxiety, please see a doctor or therapist. Seeking care is also an expression of *venishmartem lenafshoteichem* (guarding your life and well-being) [Deuteronomy 4:15].
- If you ever feel hopeless or unsafe, contact a crisis line or emergency services right away.
- Keep your return simple: a few honest words to Hashem each day, like those Hosea describes.

For personal guidance, consult your local rabbi or posek.

answer:
The "plaything" image most likely comes from Proverbs 8:30-31, where personified Wisdom, identified by tradition with the Torah, is "delight" (*sha'ashuim*) and "playing" (*metsachekes*) before God. It is a poetic way of saying that Torah preceded creation, accompanied it, and is a source of joy to both God and humanity. If you meant a different "plaything," such as Leviathan, let me know and I'll address that instead.

## Key Takeaways

- Proverbs 8 pictures Wisdom as God's constant delight and as "playing" before Him during creation.
- **Bereshit Rabbah 1:1** reads the key word *amon* in several ways, including "pedagogue," "hidden," and "great," and, in the well-known reading, "craftsman's tool," meaning God "looked into the Torah and created the world."
- Verse 31 shifts the image: Wisdom plays in God's world and delights in human beings, linking the cosmic Torah to mankind.
- **Ibn Ezra** warns that Torah's pre-existence is not literal but a *sod* (secret), since time requires the movement of the heavens.
- The "play" is not frivolity; it expresses joy, purposefulness, and the intimate bond between Creator, Torah, and humanity.

## Pshat: The Verses

[Proverbs 8:30]: "וָאֶהְיֶה אֶצְלוֹ אָמוֹן וָאֶהְיֶה שַׁעֲשׁוּעִים יוֹם יוֹם מְשַׂחֶקֶת לְפָנָיו בְּכׇל־עֵת" ("Then I was beside Him as an *amon*, and I was His delight day by day, playing before Him at all times").

[Proverbs 8:31]: "מְשַׂחֶקֶת בְּתֵבֵל אַרְצוֹ וְשַׁעֲשֻׁעַי אֶת־בְּנֵי אָדָם" ("Playing in His inhabited world, and my delight is with the children of man").

In context, Wisdom is speaking about her presence before and during creation. The word *sha'ashuim* means delight or joyful absorption, as with a child's play. The "playing" is the joy of something fitting perfectly into its purpose.

## Midrash: Bereshit Rabbah 1:1

R. Hoshaya opens the Midrash with this verse and explains *amon* through several readings:

- ***Amon* as pedagogue or nurse**, citing "as the *omen* carries the nursing child" [Numbers 11:12]. The Torah nurtures the world.
- ***Amon* as covered**, citing "those *ha-emunim* upon scarlet" [Lamentations 4:5]. The Torah was concealed before creation.
- ***Amon* as hidden**, citing "and he was *omen* to Hadassah" [Esther 2:7].
- ***Amon* as great**, from the name of the great city *No-Amon* [Nahum 3:8].

The Midrash then continues, from my knowledge since the retrieved text cuts off, with the reading *uman* (craftsman or artisan). Just as a king building a palace consults blueprints, God "looked into the Torah and created the world." Here the Torah is the instrument of creation, which is why the Torah begins with *Bereishit* [Genesis 1:1], read as "with the *reishit*," the Torah.

## Why "Play"?

The commentators and the wider tradition suggest several layers:

- **Delight, not necessity:** Creation flows from joy and not from need. God's relationship with His Torah is affectionate, not merely functional.
- **Effortless wisdom:** Play suggests mastery, so the world's design reflects wisdom that unfolds naturally.
- **Connection to humanity:** Verse 31 says Wisdom's delight is with "the children of man." The Torah, though pre-existent and cosmic, finds its fulfillment in being given to human beings, who are created "in God's image" [Genesis 1:26-27].

## Caution: Ibn Ezra on Pre-Existence

Ibn Ezra, in his Genesis introduction, addresses the teaching that the Torah preceded the world by two thousand years. He calls it a midrash that "has a secret and is not explained," true only "by way of the hidden path."

Taken literally, it cannot be. Days and years are measured by the motion of the celestial sphere, so "if there is no sphere there is no day, let alone two days or a year." He therefore treats the idea as symbolic of the Torah's priority in God's purpose, not as a chronology.

## Other "Playthings" (From My Knowledge)

Another famous image is Leviathan, "whom You formed to play with" [Psalms 104:26]. The Talmud [Avodah Zarah 3b] says God spends part of the day playing with it. That is a separate image from Proverbs 8, but both express the idea that God's relationship to creation includes joy.

If you had a specific source in mind, tell me where you saw it and I can focus on that.
